https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A board narrative summary dated June 2026 presents the Troy School District's proposed special education budget reductions, developed through a structured scoring process in which each proposal was evaluated across six weighted criteria — impact on student learning, equity, legal and compliance risk, cost savings, feasibility, and stakeholder support — and then sorted into tiers. Eight proposals, four in classroom instruction and four in non-instructional support, carry $3,229,885 in combined annual savings. The stated rationale is cost growth outpacing enrollment: special education costs rose 74%, from $16,744,610 in 2018–2019 to $29,210,999 in 2024–2025, an increase of $12,466,389, while the number of students served moved from 1,332 to 1,367.

**Document**
Board Narrative Summary — Special Education Budget Reductions, Proposed Reduction Scenario, June 2026, Troy School District.

**Method**
Each proposal was evaluated across six weighted criteria: impact on student learning, equity, legal and compliance risk, cost savings, feasibility, and stakeholder support. Weighted scores placed each proposal into a tier. Tier 1 = strong candidate (4.0–5.0); Tier 2 = consider (3.0–3.9); Tier 3 = high risk, requires further study (below 3.0). Savings figures reflect actual FTE and actual dollar savings as entered in the scoring matrix.

**Why special education is in the reduction scenario**
Costs grew far faster than the population served over the six-year window cited.

| Description | 2018–2019 | 2024–2025 | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Special Education Costs – IEP & non-IEP | $16,744,610 | $29,210,999 | +$12,466,389 (74%) |
| Special Education Student Count | 1,332 | 1,367 | +35 (3%) |

The summary also cites a state-led shift in how certain special education services are delivered; several proposals align district staffing to new county-level service plans and county targets.

**Category summary**

| Category | # of Proposals | Annual Savings | Tier Mix (T1/T2/T3) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| Special Education – Non-Instructional | 4 | $1,833,312 | 2 / 2 / 0 |

| Proposal | Annual Savings | Score | Tier | Status |

The Teacher Consultant / Resource Room (TC/RR) adjustment is the only Tier 3 proposal in the special education set and, per the scoring framework, warrants further study before adoption.

**Non-instructional reductions — $1,833,312**

The Student Support Aide reduction is described as the largest single special education reduction in the entire scenario, accounting for more than $1.3 million in savings. Social worker and psychologist reductions are noted as candidates for phased implementation.

**Risk and planning**
Of the eight proposals, four are Tier 1 (recommended), three are Tier 2 (consider, with additional planning), and one is Tier 3 (high risk). The four Tier 1 proposals are described as totaling roughly $1.95 million and are recommended for inclusion. Proposals scoring below 4.0 may still be included if savings are critical to meeting the reduction goal, but require additional planning, communication, and mitigation.

**Commitments to students**
All special education programs will continue to be staffed in alignment with state and county requirements, including certified teachers, paraprofessionals, and related service providers. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Titled "Board Narrative Summary — Special Education Budget Reductions, Proposed Reduction Scenario" and dated June 2026, the paper explains to the Troy School District Board of Education how the proposed special education reductions were developed and how those specific reductions connect to the broader budget plan presented to the Board. It opens by stating that special education remains one of the district's highest priorities and one of its largest areas of investment.

SCORING METHOD AND TIER DEFINITIONS
The proposals were produced through the district's structured scoring process. Each was evaluated across six weighted criteria: impact on student learning, equity, legal and compliance risk, cost savings, feasibility, and stakeholder support. Weighted scores then determined tier placement. Tier 1 is defined as a strong candidate, scoring 4.0–5.0; Tier 2 as "consider," scoring 3.0–3.9; Tier 3 as high risk, requiring further study, scoring below 3.0. The summary states that savings figures reflect actual FTE and actual dollar savings as entered in the scoring matrix.

WHY SPECIAL EDUCATION IS PART OF THE CONVERSATION
The narrative attributes the inclusion of special education in the reduction scenario to six years of cost growth that is described as no longer sustainable within the district's structural budget. Between 2018–2019 and 2024–2025, special education costs rose 74% — an increase of more than $12.4 million — while the number of students served grew by only 3%. The accompanying comparison table reports Special Education Costs (IEP and non-IEP) of $16,744,610 in 2018–2019 and $29,210,999 in 2024–2025, a change of +$12,466,389 (74%); and Special Education Student Count of 1,332 in 2018–2019 and 1,367 in 2024–2025, a change of +35 (3%). The gap between cost growth and enrollment growth is identified as the central reason special education is included in the scenario.

A second driver is a state-led shift in how certain special education services are delivered. Several of the proposals align district staffing to new county-level service plans and county targets. Taken together, the reductions are described as intended to right-size staffing to current requirements while preserving the services students are entitled to.

COMMITMENTS TO STUDENTS
The summary states that the district's core obligations to students with disabilities do not change. All special education programs will continue to be staffed in alignment with state and county requirements, including certified teachers, paraprofessionals, and related service providers. Decisions are guided by each student's Individualized Education Program (IEP) and are mandated to comply with all legal and educational standards. As the district adapts to the state-led shift in service delivery, it will continue to provide services based on IEP needs and state requirements while making responsible adjustments to ensure the long-term sustainability of its programs.

SUMMARY OF PROPOSED REDUCTIONS
The proposed reductions fall into two categories, classroom instruction and non-instructional supports. Special Education – Classroom Instruction comprises 4 proposals with annual savings of $1,396,573 and a tier mix of 2 Tier 1 / 1 Tier 2 / 1 Tier 3. Special Education – Non-Instructional comprises 4 proposals with annual savings of $1,833,312 and a tier mix of 2 / 2 / 0. Total Special Education Reductions are stated as 8 proposals, $3,229,885 in annual savings, with a tier mix of 4 / 3 / 1.

CLASSROOM INSTRUCTION REDUCTIONS — $1,396,573
These proposals adjust instructional special education staffing to align with new county-level service plans and county staffing targets. Three of the four are described as strong or consider-level candidates; one — the adjustment of Teacher Consultant and Resource Room (TC/RR) staff to county targets — carries the highest risk in the special education set and is flagged for further Board discussion. The itemized proposals are:
• Adjust TC/RR staff to meet county targets (3.7 Elementary, 3.6 Secondary) — annual savings $635,100, weighted score 2.95, Tier 3, status "Flag for review."
• Teacher reduction based on new county level plan (3 L4, 1 ECP) — annual savings $348,000, score 4.10, Tier 1, status "Recommended."
• Paraprofessional reduction based on new county level plan — annual savings $236,270, score 4.10, Tier 1, status "Recommended."
• Elementary Resource Room paraprofessionals reduction — annual savings $177,203, score 3.85, Tier 2, status "Consider."
The subtotal for the category is $1,396,573. The narrative repeats that the TC/RR adjustment is the only Tier 3 proposal in the special education set, with a weighted score of 2.95, and that per the scoring framework it warrants further study before adoption.

NON-INSTRUCTIONAL REDUCTIONS — $1,833,312
These proposals reduce non-instructional support staffing. The largest single special education reduction in the entire scenario sits in this category: the reduction of general education Student Support Aides from 158 to 104 FTE, which the narrative says accounts for more than $1.3 million in savings. The remaining proposals adjust social worker, psychologist, and clerical staffing. The itemized proposals are:
• Student Support Aide – Gen Ed (from 158 to 104 FTE) — annual savings $1,334,362, score 4.15, Tier 1, status "Recommended."
• Social Workers reduction (from 24.4 to 21.4 FTE) — annual savings $348,000, score 3.90, Tier 2, status "Consider."
• Psychologist reduction (from 10 to 9 FTE) — annual savings $116,000, score 3.90, Tier 2, status "Consider."
• Special Education Secretary — annual savings $34,951, score 4.35, Tier 1, status "Recommended."
The subtotal for the category is $1,833,312. The narrative notes that the social worker and psychologist reductions are Tier 2 (consider) proposals and may benefit from phased implementation.

RISK AND PLANNING CONSIDERATIONS
Of the eight special education proposals, four are Tier 1 (recommended), three are Tier 2 (consider, with additional planning), and one is Tier 3 (high risk). In practical terms, the narrative states that the four Tier 1 proposals — totaling roughly $1.95 million — are strong candidates with low risk and high feasibility and are recommended for inclusion; that the three Tier 2 proposals — the Elementary Resource Room paraprofessional, social worker, and psychologist reductions — may be included with additional planning, communication, or phased implementation; and that the single Tier 3 proposal, the TC/RR staffing adjustment to county targets, is flagged for further Board conversation before it is adopted. It adds that proposals scoring below 4.0 may still be included if savings are critical to meeting the reduction goal, but that they require additional planning, communication, and mitigation efforts.

HOW THE REDUCTIONS FIT THE OVERALL PLAN
Because special education is governed by IEPs and by state and county requirements, the proposals were scored with particular attention to legal and compliance risk and to equity impact. The stated intent is to bring staffing back into alignment with current service requirements and the state-led delivery model — not to reduce services students are entitled to receive — while contributing meaningfully toward closing the structural budget gap.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Regular meeting minutes of the Troy Board of Education for Tuesday, June 16, 2026, held at the Troy School District Services Building (Service Center), 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:18 p.m. In addition to Mrs. Anne, Board members Alic, Melton, Potts, and Zendler were present; Mr. Haupt and Dr. Philippart were absent. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Moran, Anderson, Montante, Pagel, and Trudel. Approximately 50 members of the audience attended. The meeting opened with the Pledge of Allegiance and adjourned at 9:03 p.m.

PUBLIC HEARING: 2026/2027 PROPOSED BUDGET
Mr. Trudel shared an overview of the 2025-2026 final budget amendments as well as the 2026-2027 budget proposals. His presentation addressed taxable values, the Headlee amendment, homestead millage comparisons, general fund versus ancillary funds, the capital project fund, the common debt fund, the sinking fund, the capital maintenance fund, special revenue funds, the food service fund, the Troy Career Center fund, the community service fund, the Troy Preschool fund, and the student activities fund.

RECOGNITION: RESOLUTION IN SUPPORT OF GUN SAFETY AND SAFE GUN STORAGE
Moved by Mrs. Zendler and supported by Mrs. Alic. The whereas clauses state that the safety and well-being of students, teachers, and staff is a top priority in the Troy School District; that firearms are now the leading cause of death among U.S. children and adolescents due to rising rates of homicide, suicide, and unintentional shootings, compounded by social inequities, increased access to guns, and insufficient safety measures; that rates of death from firearms among ages 14 to 17 are higher than motor vehicle-related death rates, and that middle and high school age children in the U.S. are now more likely to die as the result of a firearm injury than from any other single cause of death; that according to a report from the US Secret Service, in incidents of gun violence on school grounds 76% of attackers acquired a firearm from the home of a parent or another close relative; that since 2025 there have been over 240 unintentional shootings by children, resulting in 39 deaths and 72 injuries nationally; that more than 28,000 Americans are estimated to have died by suicide using firearms in 2025; that research indicates close to 5 million US children live in a home with a loaded and unlocked firearm; that evidence strongly suggests secure firearm storage is an essential component of any effective strategy to keep the community safe; that keeping students, teachers, and staff safe from the threat of gun violence should be the responsibility of all adult stakeholders within the school district; and that preventative measures require action now.

The resolved clauses direct the Superintendent to periodically communicate the importance of safe firearm storage and other firearm safety and violence prevention measures during gun violence awareness month, and to disseminate material on an annual basis stressing the importance of secure storage of firearms by including it in the district's annual notification materials; commit the Board and Superintendent to continue working with local law enforcement agencies, medical and mental health agencies, and non-profit organizations to inform district parents of their obligations regarding secure storage of firearms in their homes as well as other gun violence prevention safety measures; and state that the resolution shall not be construed to conflict with any existing Michigan or federal law. The vote was Yes 5, No 0, with Haupt and Philippart absent; the resolution was declared adopted. A certification by Matt Haupt, Secretary, Board of Education, attests that the resolution was duly adopted at a regular meeting held on the 16th day of June, 2026, conducted with public notice given in full compliance with the Open Meetings Act, being Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976.

RESOLUTION URGING PASSAGE OF THE 2026/2027 SCHOOL AID BUDGET BY JULY 1ST
Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Zendler. The whereas clauses note that with only two weeks remaining in the fiscal year for schools the Legislature had not yet passed a School Aid Budget; that last year the budget was not passed until after the Constitutional October 1 deadline, forcing districts to make critical staffing and programming decisions based on speculation rather than certainty, and that without a budget schools cannot responsibly plan for staffing, class sizes, transportation, or essential services; that Troy School District is legally obligated to complete its budget by the end of June and will fulfill that obligation, but without certainty from Lansing will again be forced to consider freezing programs, delaying hires, and laying off staff; that the framework for a responsible School Aid fund budget already exists within the three proposals under consideration; that focus should remain on passing a responsible, balanced budget rather than beginning discussions on major reforms, with significant property tax changes or other structural changes deserving thorough debate separate from the budget; and that policymakers must complete a School Aid budget including an inflationary increase to the foundation allowance, weighted funding for at-risk and ELL students, an end to the diversion of K12 dollars away from the classroom, and a fix to school safety and mental health funding. The resolved clauses call on the Legislature and the Governor to pass the School Aid Budget before July 1 and direct that a copy be forwarded to the district's representatives in the Michigan House of Representatives and the Michigan Senate as well as the Governor's office. The vote was Yes 5, No 0, with Haupt and Philippart absent; the motion was declared adopted, certified by Matt Haupt, Secretary.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS / PUBLIC COMMUNICATION
Additions and deletions: none. During public communication on agenda items, five community members addressed the Board; no action was taken. Public communication on non-agenda items: none. Personnel: none. Curriculum: none. Other: none.

GENERAL – CONSENT AGENDA
Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Dr. Melton that the Board approve items A through J on the consent agenda: minutes of the May 19, 2026 Special Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report – April 2026; Food Service Contract Renewal; Michigan High School Athletic Association (MHSAA) Membership – 2026/2027; 2025/2026 Budget Amendment; 2026/2027 Budget Appropriations Resolution; Common Debt Fund Resolution; approval of OCSBA Association Bylaws Amendment; approval of an OCSBA new resolution opposing tying any school funding to waiving the attorney-client privilege; and AP Precalculus Textbook Adoption. The vote was Yes 4 – Alic, Anne, Melton, Zendler; No 1 – Potts; Absent Haupt and Philippart.

MacBook/iPad Purchases: moved by Dr. Melton and supported by Mrs. Alic that the district purchase Apple MacBooks and iPads in the amount of $2,420,430.00, approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Vote Yes 5, No 0, Absent Haupt and Philippart.
Bus Purchase: moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Dr. Melton that the bid for school buses be awarded to Hoekstra Transportation in the amount of $2,464,089.00, approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Vote Yes 5, No 0, Absent Haupt and Philippart.
Smith Printers: moved by Mrs. Potts and supported by Mrs. Zendler that the purchase of printers be awarded to Applied Innovation in the amount of $733,985.55, approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Vote Yes 5, No 0, Absent Haupt and Philippart.

BOARD COMMENTS
Listed comments included encouraging the community to reach out to legislators to pass the budget on time; thanks to speakers who spoke during public comment, with the note that the board hears them; congratulations to the Class of 2026 graduates; Men's Mental Health Awareness Month; appreciation for secretaries; Board members requesting a special meeting to discuss budget reductions further; counselor ratios and special education positions; the August 4th ballot countywide millage, under which $780 per student would come from the Enhancement Millage, just under $9,000,000 to Troy School District; a comment that the public education landscape is not good; and Happy Father's Day and Juneteenth celebration.

ADJOURNMENT AND NEXT MEETING
The next Board meeting was announced for Tuesday, July 21st at 9:30 a.m. in the Administration Building. The meeting was adjourned at 9:03 p.m. Minutes respectfully submitted by Matt Haupt, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the notation MH/jh.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A letter dated June 15, 2026 from Matt Jansen, Troy School District Director of Athletics, Continuing Education and Enrichment, asks the MHSAA Executive Board to waive the cooperative team enrollment limitation so Troy High School and Troy Athens High School may form a combined "Troy United" boys lacrosse program beginning in 2026-27. The two schools' combined enrollment of 3,936 students exceeds the enrollment cap established for cooperative agreements. The request is framed by a projected $12.1 million district budget deficit and by declining participation, with only 41 players projected to return across the two programs before incoming freshmen.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Document**
Letter dated June 15, 2026 to the Members of the MHSAA Executive Board, on Troy School District District Athletics letterhead — Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D., Superintendent of Schools; Matt Jansen, Director, Athletics; 1522 E. Big Beaver Rd., Troy, Michigan 48083; 248.823.5154, fax 248.823.5133. Signed by Matt Jansen, Director of Athletics, Continuing Education and Enrichment.

**Request**
Approval of a waiver to the current cooperative team enrollment limitation to allow Troy High School and Troy Athens High School to form a cooperative boys lacrosse program beginning with the 2026-27 school year, operating as a single "Troy United" program.

**Enrollment**

| School | Enrollment |
| --- | --- |
| Troy High School | 2,127 |
| Troy Athens High School | 1,809 |
| Combined | 3,936 |

The combined figure exceeds the enrollment cap established for cooperative agreements, which is why a waiver is sought.

**Financial context**
The district is facing a projected $12.1 million budget deficit entering the 2026-27 school year. As part of district-wide reductions, the Athletics Department has been tasked with reducing expenditures by approximately $100,000. The district recently discontinued financial support for non-MHSAA sanctioned sports, including synchronized swimming and boys and girls water polo; those programs moved to self-funded club status, generating approximately $50,000 in annual savings. A cooperative boys lacrosse program would provide an estimated annual savings of approximately $25,000.

**Participation**

| Measure | Troy High School | Troy Athens High School |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2026 season participants | 48 | 31 |
| Graduating seniors | 21 | 13 |
| Projected returning participants | 26 | 15 |

Combined returning participation is stated as 41 players before the addition of incoming freshmen. Of the 15 projected returners at Athens, only one participated at the varsity level during the 2026 season; the remaining 14 had never played lacrosse prior to 2026. Athens attempted to field both varsity and junior varsity teams but could not consistently maintain enough healthy student-athletes to sustain junior varsity competition through the season.

**Program stability**
Following the 2026 season, the Troy Athens varsity boys lacrosse coach informed the district of his decision to step down, citing as a significant factor the ongoing difficulty of building and sustaining a program with limited participation. Troy Athens has historically participated in a cooperative arrangement with Avondale Schools, which in recent years has yielded no more than two players annually and contributed no participants during the 2026 season; the letter concludes that partnership is no longer viable.

**Precedent cited**
Within the Oakland Activities Association and surrounding communities: Farmington and North Farmington; Royal Oak and Berkley; Birmingham Groves and Birmingham Seaholm; Waterford Mott and Waterford Kettering; Milford and Lakeland; the Livonia Public Schools combined program; South Lyon's combined program; Bishop Foley and Clawson; Brandon and Holly; the St. Clair Shores cooperative program; and Eisenhower and Utica.

**Position**
The letter states the request is not intended to create a competitive advantage but to preserve participation opportunities, maintain both varsity and junior varsity levels of competition, and sustain access to boys lacrosse. It notes the proposal has the full support and approval of Troy School District administration, including the Superintendent, Assistant Superintendent, both high school principals, and the Athletic Department.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Correspondence dated June 15, 2026, addressed to the Members of the MHSAA Executive Board, sent on Troy School District District Athletics letterhead listing Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D., Superintendent of Schools, and Matt Jansen, Director, Athletics, at 1522 E. Big Beaver Rd., Troy, Michigan 48083, telephone 248.823.5154, fax 248.823.5133. The letter is signed by Matt Jansen, Director of Athletics, Continuing Education and Enrichment, and carries the footer "An Equal Opportunity/Affirmative Action Employer."

THE REQUEST
On behalf of the Troy School District, the letter requests approval of a waiver to the current cooperative team enrollment limitation to allow Troy High School and Troy Athens High School to form a cooperative boys lacrosse program beginning with the 2026-27 school year. The combined enrollment of the two high schools is 3,936 students, with Troy High School enrolling 2,127 students and Troy Athens High School enrolling 1,809 students. The letter acknowledges that this total exceeds the enrollment cap established for cooperative agreements but argues that the circumstances warrant special consideration and approval.

FINANCIAL CONTEXT
The Troy School District is described as currently facing a projected $12.1 million budget deficit entering the 2026-27 school year. As part of district-wide reductions, the Athletics Department has been tasked with reducing expenditures by approximately $100,000. To address these financial challenges, the district recently discontinued financial support for non-MHSAA sanctioned sports, including synchronized swimming and boys and girls water polo. Those programs have transitioned to self-funded club status, generating approximately $50,000 in annual savings. The letter calls this a difficult decision and states that additional measures are necessary to maintain sustainable athletic opportunities for students. A cooperative boys lacrosse program between Troy High School and Troy Athens High School would provide an estimated annual savings of approximately $25,000 while preserving participation opportunities for student-athletes at both schools.

PARTICIPATION AND PROGRAM SUSTAINABILITY
The letter emphasizes that the request is driven more by participation numbers and program sustainability than solely by financial considerations. During the 2026 boys lacrosse season, Troy High School had 48 participants while Troy Athens High School had 31 participants. Troy High School is graduating 21 seniors and Troy Athens High School is graduating 13 seniors. This leaves projected returning participation numbers of only 26 student-athletes at Troy High School and 15 student-athletes at Troy Athens High School, for a combined total of 41 returning players before the addition of incoming freshmen.

The situation at Troy Athens is described as particularly concerning. Of the 15 projected returning players, only one participated at the varsity level during the 2026 season; the remaining 14 players had never played lacrosse prior to the 2026 season. Although Athens attempted to field both varsity and junior varsity teams in the spring, the program was unable to consistently maintain enough healthy student-athletes to sustain junior varsity competition throughout the season.

COACHING AND PRIOR COOPERATIVE ARRANGEMENT
These challenges are said to have affected program leadership and long-term stability. Following the 2026 season, the Troy Athens varsity boys lacrosse coach informed the district of his decision to step down, with a significant factor being the ongoing difficulty of building and sustaining a program with limited participation numbers. The letter presents this as further illustration of the challenges facing the Athens program and the need for a more sustainable model. Historically, Troy Athens has participated in a cooperative arrangement with Avondale Schools, but that partnership has not provided the participation numbers necessary to sustain the program: in recent years the cooperative agreement has yielded no more than two players annually, and during the 2026 season Avondale contributed no participants. The letter concludes that the Avondale partnership is no longer a viable long-term solution.

RATIONALE FOR A COMBINED PROGRAM
The letter states that one of the fundamental goals of interscholastic athletics is to provide meaningful participation and developmental opportunities for as many student-athletes as possible. A cooperative program would allow the district to maintain both varsity and junior varsity competition, ensuring that beginning and developing players have an appropriate environment in which to learn, improve, and remain engaged in the sport; without sufficient numbers to sustain a junior varsity program, opportunities for skill development and long-term participation are significantly diminished. Establishing a single "Troy United" boys lacrosse program is presented as a stable structure that supports program numbers while preserving access and opportunity for student-athletes from both schools, aligning with the educational mission of the MHSAA by prioritizing participation, student development, and the long-term viability of boys lacrosse within the community.

REGIONAL PRECEDENT
The letter argues the request is consistent with cooperative programs that already exist throughout the region. Within the Oakland Activities Association and surrounding communities, numerous school districts have been permitted to combine programs to preserve participation opportunities. Examples cited include Farmington and North Farmington, Royal Oak and Berkley, Birmingham Groves and Birmingham Seaholm, and Waterford Mott and Waterford Kettering. Additional area examples cited are Milford and Lakeland, the Livonia Public Schools combined program, South Lyon's combined program, Bishop Foley and Clawson, Brandon and Holly, the St. Clair Shores cooperative program, and Eisenhower and Utica. The Troy School District states it is simply seeking the same opportunity to preserve a viable boys lacrosse program for its students.

CLOSING POSITION AND APPROVALS
Approval of the waiver would allow the district to establish a single "Troy United" boys lacrosse program representing both Troy High School and Troy Athens High School, providing the participation numbers necessary to maintain both varsity and junior varsity opportunities while supporting the district's ongoing financial sustainability efforts. The letter states the request is not intended to create a competitive advantage but rather to preserve participation opportunities, maintain both levels of competition, and ensure that student-athletes in the Troy School District continue to have access to boys lacrosse in a sustainable and educationally sound manner. The proposal is reported to have already received the full support and approval of the Troy School District administration, including the Superintendent, the Assistant Superintendent, both high school principals, and the Athletic Department. The letter closes by respectfully requesting that the Executive Board grant the waiver to the cooperative enrollment limitation and approve the cooperative boys lacrosse program, thanking the board for its consideration and offering to provide any additional information the Council may require.

**Meeting**
Troy Board of Education regular meeting, Tuesday, May 19, 2026, at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. Called to order by President Anne at 7:00 p.m.; adjourned at 8:27 p.m. Filed under the June 16, 2026 packet.

**Attendance**
Board members Anne, Alic, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts and Zendler. Also present: Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Keegan, Cottone, Wallace, Cronin, Griffin, Hall, Montante, Pagel and Trudel, plus approximately 125 members of the audience.

**Recognitions**
- Outstanding Support Person of the Year: Matt Snitgen, a paraprofessional in the MOCI Room at Athens High School, nominated by Rebecca Roy from a field of 25 nominees.
- Legislative Career Accelerator Program: teachers Brynn Lawrence (Troy Center for Transition) and Mark Chrzanowski (International Academy East) introduced Ava Pittman and Nathan Kohnert; participating students were Ayush Jaganath, Aarshia Soni, Harini Shrii Vengata Raghavan (Troy High), Tasnia Jannah, Sulayma Setiaarif (Athens), Amal Surti and Syeda Tarannum (IAE).
- Schools of Character: Hamilton Elementary and Troy Union Elementary named National Schools of Character by Character.org, two of just 72 schools nationwide; Schroeder Elementary, Troy Union and Boulan Park Middle School named State Schools of Character; Wattles and Barnard Elementary received Honorable Mention; Troy Union and Wattles were the only Michigan schools recognized for Promising Practices.
- Volunteers: Athens - Kristin Kennaugh, Heather and Kevin Blum, Samantha Zoll; IAE - Harj Deol, Minal Kulkarni, Surya Saladi; Troy High - Cheri Armstrong, Sherry Gillespie.

**Actions and votes**

| Item | Moved / supported | Vote |
| --- | --- | --- |
| National Teacher Appreciation Week, May 4-8, 2026 | Zendler / Potts | Yes 7, No 0 |
| Mental Health Awareness Month, May 2026 | Potts / Philippart | Yes 7, No 0 |
| Consent agenda items A through L | Haupt / Alic | Yes 7, No 0 |
| Boulan Park renovation bid, $297,803.00 | Philippart / Zendler | Yes 7, No 0 |
| Food Service and Operations vehicles, $205,610.00 | Alic / Haupt | Yes 7, No 0 |
| Oakland Schools biennial election resolution | Philippart / Haupt | Yes 7, No 0 |

The mental health resolution cited Oakland Community Health Network, stated that one in five Americans experience mental health issues, and referenced National Children's Mental Health Awareness Day on May 7, 2026 and Children's Mental Health Acceptance Week, May 3 through May 9, 2026.

**Consent agenda (A through L)**
Minutes of the April 7, 2026 special meeting and workshop, the April 14, 2026 special meeting, the April 21, 2026 regular meeting, and the April 28, 2026 special meeting, closed session and workshop; the Treasurer's Report for March 2026; approval of the Oakland Intermediate School District budget; a resolution to hold a public hearing on the proposed 2026/2027 school year budget; IA budget approval for 2026/2027; and a K-8 literacy pilot purchase. Personnel and Curriculum had no items.

**Business**
The bid for a complete renovation of Boulan Park Middle School covering architectural, mechanical, electrical and structural work (recommendation 3 of 3) was awarded at $297,803.00 as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund. The bid for a Food Services vehicle and an Operations vehicle was awarded to Gorno Ford at $205,610.00, charged to the Food Services Fund and the Maintenance Improvement Fund.

**Oakland Schools biennial election**
Under Mich. Comp. Laws 380.614, the board designated Kendra Montante as its representative, with a member of the district administration team as alternate, to the 2026 electoral body electing the Oakland Schools Intermediate School District Board of Education; supported candidate Gary Hauff for the one position, a six-year term ending June 30, 2032; and directed Montante to vote for Hauff at least on the first ballot at the June 1, 2026 election.

**Reports and comments**
Student representatives Chloe Gentilini (Troy College and Career High School), Ahyoung Song (International Academy-East), Sara Graunstadt (Athens High School) and Bella Doss (Troy High School) reported. One community member spoke during non-agenda public communication; no action was taken. Board comments covered the Oakland County enhancement millage, budget reductions against a $12 million deficit, the TFEE Golf Outing on June 9, retiree recognition June 1 at Troy High, and Coffee with the Superintendent and Board on May 21 at 5:00 pm. The next workshop was set for Tuesday, June 1 at Troy High and the next regular meeting for Tuesday, June 16 at the Services Building. Submitted by Matt Haupt, Secretary.

**Identification**
Regular meeting minutes of the Troy Board of Education, Tuesday, May 19, 2026, held at the Troy School District Services Building (Service Center), 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The record is filed as M051926BdMtg within the June 16, 2026 board packet. President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. and it was adjourned at 8:27 p.m. Minutes were respectfully submitted by Matt Haupt, Secretary of the Troy Board of Education, with typist initials MH/jh.

**Attendance**
In addition to Mrs. Anne, board members Alic, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts and Zendler were present. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Keegan, Cottone, Wallace, Cronin, Griffin, Hall, Montante, Pagel and Trudel. Approximately 125 members of the audience attended. The meeting opened with the Pledge of Allegiance.

**Recognition: Outstanding Support Staff**
The board presented the Outstanding Support Person of the Year award, a category covering bus drivers, secretaries, paraprofessionals, student support aides, custodial staff, food service, technology, childcare, security and more. There were 25 nominees. The 2026 honoree is Matt Snitgen, a paraprofessional at Athens High School in the MOCI Room, nominated by Rebecca Roy. The nomination praised his unwavering belief in his students, noting that he sees potential where others often see limitations, and cited his positivity, compassion and work ethic. It described how he models and encourages communication in all forms, including body language, gestures, facial expressions and AAC devices, treating every communicative attempt as meaningful. A student was quoted saying, "We have a secret handshake. Mr. S is a great person because he's nice and he makes me feel happy and excited to be at school." Snitgen's name was engraved on the Support Person Plaque, to be displayed at his building for the next year, and a short video of the surprise visit was shown.

**Legislative CAP Students Report**
Students from the Legislative track of the Career Accelerator Program (CAP) reported on their engagement with the school board, the city, and state senators and representatives. Troy Center for Transition teacher Brynn Lawrence and International Academy East teacher Mark Chrzanowski were invited to the podium to introduce their students. Ava Pittman of IA-East and Nathan Kohnert of TCT described their experience and shared a brief video. CAP students who shared their experiences were Ayush Jaganath (Troy High), Tasnia Jannah (Athens), Sulayma Setiaarif (Athens), Aarshia Soni (Troy High), Amal Surti (IAE), Syeda Tarannum (IAE) and Harini Shrii Vengata Raghavan (Troy High).

**Schools of Character Recognition**
Hamilton Elementary School and Troy Union Elementary School were honored as National Schools of Character, two of just 72 schools nationwide to receive the distinction from Character.org. The designation recognizes schools that use character development to positively impact academics, student behavior and school culture. Schroeder Elementary School, Troy Union Elementary School and Boulan Park Middle School were named State Schools of Character, and Wattles Elementary School and Barnard Elementary School received Honorable Mention. Character.org also recognized Troy Union and Wattles as the only schools in Michigan to earn recognition for Promising Practices, highlighting innovative efforts that strengthen school culture, encourage student leadership and service, and promote goodness in action.

**Volunteer Appreciation**
April is Volunteer Appreciation Month, and the board thanked volunteers whose students graduate from TSD this year. Parents recognized and given a token of appreciation were: Athens - Kristin Kennaugh, Heather and Kevin Blum, and Samantha Zoll; IAE - Harj Deol, Minal Kulkarni, and Surya Saladi; Troy High - Cheri Armstrong and Sherry Gillespie.

**National Teacher Appreciation Week resolution**
Teacher Appreciation Week was celebrated Monday, May 4 through Friday, May 8, 2026. Moved by Mrs. Zendler and supported by Mrs. Potts, the resolution recited that teachers inspire and open children's minds, promote and strengthen the principles of democratic equality, develop leaders and encourage critical thinking, and that Troy teachers set the bar for excellence. It resolved that the Troy School District supports National Teacher Appreciation Week, May 4-8, 2026. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Mental Health Awareness Month resolution**
Introduced with reference to Oakland Community Health Network and its service provider network and to other school boards across Oakland County. Moved by Mrs. Potts and supported by Dr. Philippart, the resolution recited that one in five of all Americans, including children, experience mental health issues that could lead to school difficulties, physical problems and even suicide; that May 7, 2026 is designated National Children's Mental Health Awareness Day; and that May 3 through May 9, 2026 is designated Children's Mental Health Acceptance Week. It resolved that the Troy Board of Education recognizes May 2026 as Mental Health Awareness Month. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Procedural**
A five-minute recess followed the recognitions. There were no additions or deletions to the agenda and no public communication on agenda items.

**Consent agenda**
Moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Alic, the board approved items A through L: minutes of the April 7, 2026 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the April 7, 2026 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the April 14, 2026 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the April 21, 2026 Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the April 28, 2026 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the April 28, 2026 Closed Session Meeting; minutes of the April 28, 2026 Board of Education Workshop; the Treasurer's Report for March 2026; Approve Oakland Intermediate School District Budget; a Resolution to Hold a Public Hearing on the Proposed 2026/2027 School Year Budget; IA Budget Approval for the 2026/2027 School Year; and the K-8 Literacy Pilot Purchase. Vote: Yes 7, No 0. The Personnel and Curriculum sections contained no items.

**Business: Boulan Park Renovation Project (Recommendation 3 of 3)**
Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Zendler, the board resolved that the bid for a complete renovation of Boulan Park Middle School, including architectural, mechanical, electrical and structural work, be awarded as attached in the amount of $297,803.00, and that the amount be approved as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Business: Purchase of Replacement Vehicles for Food Service and Operations**
Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt, the board resolved that the bid for a Food Services vehicle and an Operations vehicle be awarded to Gorno Ford in the amount of $205,610.00, approved as an expenditure of the Food Services Fund and the Maintenance Improvement Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Public communication (non-agenda items)**
One community member addressed the board. No action was taken by the board.

**Other: Oakland Schools Biennial Election**
Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mr. Haupt. The resolution recited that Mich. Comp. Laws section 380.614 requires a constituent school board to designate its representative and identify the Intermediate School Board candidate it supports by a resolution adopted not earlier than 21 days prior to the election; that the statute prescribes consideration of the resolution at not less than one public meeting before adoption; and that the board previously considered the resolution at an open meeting conducted under the Open Meetings Act on May 19, 2026. The board designated Kendra Montante as its representative and a member of the Troy School District administration team as its alternate representative to serve on the 2026 electoral body responsible for electing members to the Oakland Schools Intermediate School District Board of Education. The board supported candidate Gary Hauff for the one position on that board for a term of six years ending June 30, 2032, and directed representative Kendra Montante to vote for Gary Hauff at least on the first ballot taken at the June 1, 2026 election. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Reports from high school student representatives**
Chloe Gentilini reported for Troy College and Career High School; Ahyoung Song for International Academy-East; Sara Graunstadt for Athens High School; and Bella Doss for Troy High School, each on events and activities at their schools.

**Board comments**
Topics raised included Troy Youth Assistance Recognition; the Troy Community Coalition Incredible Kid; a Troy Interfaith Group event and a Faith and Community Leaders breakfast; the TFEE Golf Outing on June 9; the Larson Celebration of Learning event; Operation Belonging at Athens; retirees recognition June 1 at Troy High; Teacher Appreciation Week; thanks to volunteers; an Oakland County Government Relations Committee legislative update by Mrs. Alic; the Oakland County Enhancement Millage; budget reductions in connection with a $12 million deficit; a salmon release at Riverbends Park; TSD and Robotics partnering to find a site for teams to work; the SSAB Middle School Leadership Conference; Mental Health Awareness and the Red Pillar; congratulations to graduating senior board representatives; Coffee with the Superintendent and Board on May 21 at 5:00 pm; and congratulations to the 2026 graduates.

**Upcoming meetings and adjournment**
The next board workshop was scheduled for Tuesday, June 1 at Troy High, and the next regular meeting for Tuesday, June 16 at the Services Building. The meeting was adjourned at 8:27 p.m.

**Meeting**
Troy Board of Education regular meeting, Tuesday, April 21, 2026, Service Center, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m.; adjournment at 8:35 p.m. Minutes submitted by Matt Haupt, Secretary (MH/jh).

**Attendance**
Board: Anne (President), Alic, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts, Zendler. Administration: Superintendent Machesky, plus DiPilato, Griffor, Smotherman, Brennan, Griffin, Algeier, Montante, Pagel and Trudel. Approximately 75 members of the audience.

**Recognitions**
More than 49 Troy School District educators were nominated for Outstanding Teacher of the Year; three were selected. Winners: Lindsey Maliepaard, Elementary Teacher of the Year, Costello Elementary School; Tammy Gilbert, Middle School Teacher of the Year, Boulan Park Middle School; Christina Rick, Troy High School, High School and Overall Teacher of the Year. Christina Rick was also named the 2026 Oakland County High School Teacher of the Year. A reception for all nominees was set for Wednesday, April 29 at Troy High School.

A TSD Mission Moment covered the Shamrock Shakedown, a basketball tradition of Troy Center for Transition partnered with International Academy East. Teachers Brynn Lawrence (TCT) and Mark Chrzanowski (IA East) presented with students Ava Pittman (IA-East) and Nathan Kohnert (TCT).

**Autism Acceptance Month resolution**
Moved by Dr. Philippart, supported by Mrs. Alic. Recitals note that Autism Spectrum Disorder affects more than five million people in the United States and that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention report 1 in 36 children may have autism. The resolution recognizes April 2026 as Autism Acceptance Month in the Troy School District. Yes: 7, No: 0. A five minute recess followed.

**Consent agenda (items A through M)**
Moved by Mr. Haupt, supported by Mrs. Alic; Yes: 7, No: 0. | Troy High, Baker, Barnard, Bemis renovations | Philippart / Haupt | $441,960.61 | Building Site & Sinking Fund |

All three carried Yes: 7, No: 0. **Other**
Personnel, Curriculum, Other and Additions/Deletions: none. One community member addressed the Board on agenda items and three on non-agenda items; no action taken. Student representatives reporting: Chloe Gentilini (Troy College and Career High School), Ahyoung Song (International Academy-East), Sara Graunstadt (Athens High School), Bella Doss (Troy High School). **Identification and attendance**
Regular meeting minutes of the Troy Board of Education, Tuesday, April 21, 2026, held at the Troy School District Services Building (Service Center), 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mrs. Anne, Board members Alic, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts and Zendler were present. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Smotherman, Brennan, Griffin, Algeier, Montante, Pagel and Trudel. Approximately 75 members of the audience attended. The Pledge of Allegiance opened the proceedings. The meeting was adjourned at 8:35 p.m. Minutes were respectfully submitted by Matt Haupt, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the typing reference MH/jh.

**Recognition: Outstanding Teachers of the Year**
The Board recognized the district's 2026 Outstanding Teachers of the Year. More than 49 Troy School District educators were nominated for the distinguished recognition, and from that group three educators were selected on the basis of passion, dedication, impact and excellence in teaching. A short video was shown capturing the administrative team surprising each winner in the classroom. A special reception for all nominees and winners was scheduled for Wednesday, April 29 at Troy High School, giving teachers an opportunity to connect with those who nominated them; each nominee was to receive a certificate, their nomination materials, and a small token of appreciation. Each of the three winners came to the podium as their name was called, shared remarks, and posed for a photo with members of the Board of Education.

The 2026 Outstanding Teachers of the Year are Lindsey Maliepaard, Elementary Teacher of the Year, Costello Elementary School; Tammy Gilbert, Middle School Teacher of the Year, Boulan Park Middle School; and Christina Rick, Troy High School, High School and Overall Teacher of the Year. All three winners were submitted to Oakland Schools to represent Troy in the countywide Outstanding Teacher Award program, and Christina Rick was named the 2026 Oakland County High School Teacher of the Year.

**TSD Mission Moment: Shamrock Shakedown**
The Mission Moment described the Shamrock Shakedown, which began as a shared passion for basketball between students and staff at Troy Center for Transition and grew into a school-wide tradition celebrating teamwork, inclusion and community. International Academy East (IA East) has been an essential partner, leading game-day setup and serving as master of ceremonies, with a soundtrack and halftime performances. Troy Center for Transition teacher Brynn Lawrence and International Academy East teacher Mark Chrzanowski were invited to the podium to introduce their students and describe the event. Ava Pittman from IA-East and Nathan Kohnert from TCT spoke about participating and shared a brief video.

**Autism Acceptance Month resolution**
April was designated Autism Acceptance Month. The resolution was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Alic. Its recitals state that Autism Spectrum Disorder affects more than five million people in the United States; that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention report that 1 in 36 children may have autism; that autism is a neurological and developmental disorder characterized by social impairment and restricted interactive and communication behaviors that can affect anyone regardless of race, ethnicity, gender or socioeconomic background; that symptoms may present in a variety of combinations and can result in significant, lifelong challenges affecting learning, daily living, employment, social-interactive behaviors, and understanding verbal and nonverbal communications; that physicians, psychologists, behavior analysts, speech and language pathologists, occupational therapists, vocational rehabilitation professionals and educators can assist persons with autism and their families through early identification, education, intervention and recreation; and that the Troy School District is committed to fostering acceptance and belonging. The resolution recognizes April 2026 as Autism Acceptance Month in the Troy School District. The vote was Yes: 7, No: 0. A five minute recess followed. There were no additions or deletions to the agenda.

**Public communication**
One community member addressed the Board during public communication on agenda items; no action was taken. Three community members addressed the Board during public communication on non-agenda items; no action was taken.

**General: consent agenda**
Moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Alic, the Board approved items A through M on the consent agenda: minutes of the March 3, 2026 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the March 7, 2026 Board of Education Winter Retreat; minutes of the March 17, 2026 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the March 17, 2026 Closed Session Meeting; minutes of the March 17, 2026 Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report for February 2026; Second Reading and Adoption of New/Revised Board Policies; E-Rate Voluntary Alternate 2; World Language Purchase for Spanish, French and German; Geometry Materials Purchase; SEAB Video for Elementary; Code of Conduct; and Athletics Handbook. Vote: Yes: 7, No: 0. There were no Personnel items and no Curriculum items.

Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Potts, the Board resolved that the bid for a complete renovation of Boulan Park Middle School, including architectural, mechanical, electrical and structural work, be awarded as attached in the amount of $7,293,050.00, approved as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund. Under the heading THS, Barnard, Bemis, Baker Renovation Projects, and moved by Dr. Philippart with support from Mrs. Potts, the Board resolved that the bid for the e-Rate bid pack be awarded as attached in the amount of $669,138.36, approved as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund. Chloe Gentilini, student representative for Troy College and Career High School; Ahyoung Song, student representative for International Academy-East; Sara Graunstadt, student representative for Athens High School; and Bella Doss, student representative for Troy High School, each reported on events and activities at their schools.

**Board comments**
Items raised included: Troy Youth Assistance needs a Treasurer; the TSD Board received a MASB Award of Distinction; the countywide enhancement millage; the TFEE Golf Outing on June 9th in need of golfers and sponsors, with information on the website; the Invest in My Kids ballot tabled pending more signatures; Les Miserables coming soon with tickets on sale; the end of the Ramadan season with wishes for Eid and Easter; CAP Day with 100 students participating; the IA-East Art Fair Reception on March 24 at 5:00 pm; the Love of Reading event on March 24 at 5:30 pm at Athens; the third of five SFEG meetings held, with a podcast of each meeting available on the website; congratulations to Teachers of the Year Lindsey Maliepaard, Tammy Gilbert and Christina Rick; surveys distributed to parents, students and teachers regarding middle school math; and budget discussion at the Board Retreat with all options under consideration.

**Business Services, item b: Declaration of necessity and condemnation authorization**
Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Alic. The Board declared it necessary to acquire permanent highway easements and sidewalk easements along Livernois Road for the new Smith Middle School project, noting that negotiations with the Owner had not been successful and that the District has power to acquire interests in real property by condemnation under the Uniform Condemnation Procedures Act.

Key elements of the resolution:
- Project: construction and operation of the new Smith Middle School on Livernois Road, City of Troy, Oakland County, including driveway approaches and a deceleration lane on the east side of Livernois Road, road widening, traffic signal and sidewalk improvements (the Livernois Road Improvements).

- Authorizations: the Superintendent, or in his absence the Deputy Superintendent of Business Affairs, may execute documents, record the Statement of Necessity and Declaration of Taking of Private Property, retain appraisers, make good faith written offers, negotiate just compensation, and initiate proceedings in the Oakland County Circuit Court.
- The Deputy Superintendent of Schools of Business Affairs is authorized to establish an escrow account with First American Title Company for amounts estimated to be just compensation, and to select a real estate appraiser or other consultants.
- Clark Hill PLC, or another firm selected by the Superintendent in the event of conflict, is retained to initiate condemnation proceedings.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: EL Education's Scope of Services Proposal to Troy School District sets out curriculum implementation professional development for an FY27 pilot of the EL Education 6-8 Language Arts curriculum. The package bundles strategic planning, a teacher pilot launch held as half days on August 19th and October 30th, virtual office hours, four in-person coaching days covering the four middle schools piloting the curriculum, and two virtual school-based coaching days. Every element except the teacher pilot launch is offered gratis, with foregone values shown as $6,000, $13,200, and $6,000. The proposal's stated Total Price is $5,000.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Provider and framing**

EL Education, described in the proposal as a leading K-12 education non-profit working to set a higher bar of achievement for America's public schools, offers multi-year partnerships to districts implementing its curriculum. Its portfolio includes a rigorous, intensive K-8 curriculum, classroom-tested teacher resources, professional learning, strategic planning, and coaching focused on leaders and teachers, aimed at meeting the higher bar of national standards, deepening student engagement, and transforming teaching and learning.

**Document title**

DISTRICT IMPLEMENTATION: Curriculum Implementation Professional Development Scope of Services Proposal FY27 Pilot.

**Services and pricing**

| Service | Detail | Price |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Strategic Planning | 2 days, facilitated in 60-90-minute collaborative planning sessions with the District Leadership Team; in-person meetings plus weekly phone/virtual touchpoints | gratis ($6,000 priced) |
| EL Education 6-8 Language Arts Curriculum: Teacher Pilot Launch | August 19th: 1/2 Day; October 30th: 1/2 Day | $5,000 (in person) |
| Virtual Office Hours w/Teachers + Coaches (Zoom Link) | 4-6 sessions scheduled around middle school schedules; a "Troy School District" landing page of resources | Gratis |
| 4 Coaching Days during Pilot | 1 day at each of the 4 Middle Schools piloting; in person | Gratis ($13,200 priced) |
| Virtual School-Based Coaching Days | 2 days, which can be broken down into 12 hours of support | Gratis ($6,000 priced) |
| **Total Price** | | **$5,000** |

**Delivery details**

Strategic planning sessions are customized, occur with expert EL Education staff members and school/district leadership teams, inform the design of the partnership plan, and occur at critical points in the year to monitor progress on implementation goals and adjust the plan for clarity and alignment with school/district needs.

The teacher pilot launch gives essential learning for those planning to implement the 6-8 ELA curriculum. Through virtual or in-person sessions, participants will describe the structure, design, and key features of the curriculum; identify specific ways it is designed to close the literacy achievement gap; analyze its components to begin planning for instruction; and plan to implement specific instructional practices and strategies that meet the needs of all learners (High Leverage Instructional Practices).

Virtual Office Hours provide structure and consistency, pairing a small professional learning segment with teacher questions. They are to be scheduled when teachers can be paid a stipend to stay after school and no substitute is needed.

During the in-person coaching days, teachers teach a half day and are then released for feedback, action steps, and PD for a half day. EL coaches work with school-based instructional leadership, the implementation team, and teachers on professional learning plans, professional learning development, data analysis, and other implementation supports, guiding partners through strategic planning and goal setting and progress monitoring using the Qualtrics data platform.

The virtual school-based coaching days are delivered to individual schools and designed in alignment with each school's goals and data; the EL Education coach supports building level leaders with data collection and analysis, observes teachers and conducts feedback conversations, and leads grade level planning sessions, with building leaders scheduling the delivery.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Nature of the item**

A Scope of Services Proposal from EL Education presented to the Troy School District Board of Education for its May 19, 2026 meeting. The proposal is headed DISTRICT IMPLEMENTATION: Curriculum Implementation Professional Development Scope of Services Proposal FY27 Pilot, and it prices the professional development wrapper around a pilot of the EL Education 6-8 Language Arts curriculum in the district's middle schools.

**Provider description**

EL Education is characterized as a leading K-12 education non-profit at the forefront of an ambitious movement to set a higher bar of achievement for America's public schools. Through multi-year partnerships, EL Education provides school districts implementing its curriculum with a coordinated set of resources and support intended to ensure sustained implementation and results. Developed from its work with schools, the portfolio of resources includes a rigorous, intensive K-8 curriculum, classroom-tested teacher resources, and practical, inspiring professional learning, strategic planning, and coaching that focus on leaders and teachers. The portfolio of professional services for districts focuses on meeting the higher bar of national standards, deepening student engagement, and transforming teaching and learning to lead to high student achievement.

**Line item 1 - Strategic Planning**

Two days, facilitated in 60-90-minute collaborative planning sessions with the District Leadership Team. The planning sessions are customized and occur with expert EL Education staff members and school/district leadership teams. Sessions inform the design of the partnership plan and occur at critical points in the year to monitor progress on implementation goals and adjust the plan to ensure clarity and alignment with school/district needs. The meetings are a combination of in-person meetings along with weekly phone/virtual touchpoints. Price: gratis ($6,000 priced).

**Line item 2 - EL Education 6-8 Language Arts Curriculum: Teacher Pilot Launch**

Scheduled as August 19th: 1/2 Day and October 30th: 1/2 Day. This comprehensive professional development offering provides essential learning for those planning to implement the 6-8 ELA curriculum. Participants will gain an understanding of the principles behind the curriculum, explain the structure, explore specific ways the curriculum meets all students' needs, and begin planning for instruction. Via engagement in a series of virtual or in-person sessions, participants will be able to: describe the structure, design, and key features of the curriculum; identify specific ways the curriculum is designed to close the literacy achievement gap; analyze the components of the curriculum to begin planning for instruction; and plan to implement specific instructional practices and strategies that meet the needs of all learners (High Leverage Instructional Practices). Price: $5,000 (in person).

**Line item 3 - Virtual Office Hours w/Teachers + Coaches**

Delivered by Zoom link. Virtual Office Hours provide a structure and consistency in which EL Education shares a small professional learning segment and answers questions for teachers. The proposal contemplates setting up 4-6 Virtual Office Hours to occur when best for the dynamic school schedules at the Middle Schools, on days when teachers can be paid a stipend to stay after but do not need a substitute. EL Education will also set up a "Troy School District" landing page for teachers with links to resources, videos, and supports for the curriculum. Price: Gratis.

**Line item 4 - 4 Coaching Days during Pilot**

One day at each of the 4 Middle Schools piloting during the pilot, delivered in person, to support teachers. Teachers will be teaching a half day and then released for feedback, action steps, and PD for a half day. During coaching sessions, EL coaches work with the school-based instructional leadership, implementation team, and teachers to support professional learning plans, professional learning development, data analysis, and additional components of curriculum implementation support. EL coaches guide partners through strategic planning and goal setting and progress monitoring using the Qualtrics data platform, and build the capacity of school-based leadership, teacher leaders, and teachers. Price: Gratis ($13,200 priced).

**Line item 5 - Virtual School-Based Coaching Days**

Two days, which can be broken down into 12 hours of support, delivered virtually, and usable for office hours, planning sessions, or as needed for the schools. These coaching days, delivered to individual schools in the district, will be designed in alignment with the individual school's goals and data. The EL Education coach will support building level leaders with data collection and analysis, observe teachers and conduct feedback conversations, and lead grade level planning sessions. The building leaders will work collaboratively with the EL Education coach to schedule these days for the delivery of ongoing coaching support. Price: Gratis ($6,000 priced).

**Pricing summary**

| Service | Price |
| --- | --- |
| Strategic Planning (2 days) | gratis ($6,000 priced) |
| Teacher Pilot Launch (Aug 19, Oct 30 half days) | $5,000 (in person) |
| Virtual Office Hours w/Teachers + Coaches | Gratis |
| 4 Coaching Days during Pilot | Gratis ($13,200 priced) |
| Virtual School-Based Coaching Days (2 days / 12 hours) | Gratis ($6,000 priced) |
| Total Price | $5,000 |

**Observations**

The only charged component is the in-person teacher pilot launch, and the Total Price line matches that single charge at $5,000. Three of the five services carry a stated priced value that EL Education is waiving, so the proposal documents substantial support offered at no cost alongside the billed launch. The proposal is paginated 1 through 4 and names no signatory, contract term, or purchase order number.
