https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Presentation Identification**
Middle School Math Update: Board Workshop - January 2026, prepared for the Troy School District Board of Education. The deck reviews the district's middle school mathematics program change, the evidence behind it, perception data collected in May 2025, and current honors enrollment trends.

**TSD Vision for Mathematics**
All students are doers of mathematics. The stated purpose of the mathematics program is to cultivate students' positive mathematical identities so that all students develop deep mathematical understandings, understand and critique the world through mathematics, and experience the wonder, joy, and beauty of mathematics. The vision is attributed to NCTM (2020), Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics.

**Findings (May 2023)**
Finding 1, explore curricular changes: program data from the last 5 years preceding COVID revealed that student performance was slightly decreasing or stagnant, and that cohort data showed a decrease in the number of students who achieved at advanced and proficient along with an increase in students who were not proficient. Finding 2, explore course sequencing: students are not able to, or do not, fluidly move between tracks in middle school. Finding 3, explore classroom pedagogy: explore task-based, inquiry-based instruction that builds procedural fluency through conceptual understanding.

**Recommendation: Illustrative Math (May 2023)**
The recommended resource was Illustrative Math, characterized as problem-based; grounded in Universal Design for Learning; with embedded supports for students with disabilities and English learners; extensions for students who are ready for more; built-in instructional routines that support teachers and students; activity and lesson structure that is predictable and purposeful; and practice problem sets with built-in cumulative review.

**Choosing Math 8 or Honors Algebra 1 (May 2023)**
Math 8 is described as a natural transition from a Math 7 experience, in which students explore ideas of linearity, functions, and geometry and establish a solid foundation for future work in Algebra 1 and Geometry. Honors Algebra 1 embeds Math 8 standards into Algebra 1, with students moving to formalizing and generalizing their understandings with a focus on efficiency and mastery. In the spring of 7th grade, buildings host information nights to discuss and illustrate the differences between Math 8 and Honors Algebra 1 so families can make informed decisions, and families engage with math teachers to discuss individual student needs. Student performance in problem solving skills, communication of mathematical thinking and ideas, math assessment feedback, and standardized test scores should be considered.

**Supporting All Students (May 2023)**
Supports listed include deep levels of learning; investing in staff through professional learning; enrichment materials embedded within Illustrative Math under the Are You Ready For More? feature; enrichment and enhancement opportunities such as Math Club and Robotics; and traditional test-out opportunities to move more quickly through grade levels.

**Monitoring Our Success (May 2023)**
Goal 1: see growth in the number of students who score advanced or proficient on the MSTEP math assessment, PSAT and SAT exams. Goal 2: increase enrollment in and successful completion of Honors Algebra 1 in 8th grade as measured through enrollment data and end of course summative exams. Goal 3: build student problem solving skills and communication of mathematical thinking as monitored through internal common assessment. Measurement of student achievement may include, reported annually, MSTEP/PSAT/SAT including cohort data and math benchmark assessments; and, studied with staff, unit assessments and common assessments, student enrollment in Algebra 1, and student success (grades) in higher levels of mathematics.

**2023 Reflections on Program Change**
The reflections state the intent to align course work with the district vision of deep learning for all students, noting the then-current system does not lend itself to that goal; that the district learned from the field that emphasis should be on depth and fluency, not speed; that the new curriculum provides additional instruction in number sense and procedural fluency and additional access to rich tasks that elicit meaningful discourse and deep understandings; that the new curriculum is designed to offer multiple entry points allowing true differentiation in the general education setting; and that students who desire to accelerate will have the opportunity to reach Algebra 1 by Grade 8 or before, with test-out continuing every spring.

**Student Perception Data (May 2025), n = 1,932**
Celebrations: 93% of students said their math class is a welcoming place for everyone; 87% said they had lots of opportunities to interact with each other; 88% agreed that in math class it is important to try rather than to get things right the first time; 90% agreed with the statement I know I can be good at math; 79% feel prepared for the next level of math; and 59% said the lessons are just right for them. Challenges: 34% of students would like to receive more specific feedback on how to improve their work; 45% of students do not enjoy learning math; 24% said the lessons are too easy; and 17% said the lessons are too hard.

**Student Voice (May 2025)**
Positive comments quoted include enjoyment of interactions with peers and being at a level where the math is not too easy or too hard; appreciation for a teacher who explains math equations with real life examples; appreciation that there are different ways to learn math; and a student who feels confident enough to raise a hand without being judged and enjoys working with friends, bouncing ideas off them or helping them. Suggestions quoted include adding a difficulty level to assignments to show improvement; more interactive projects or activities so class does not get too boring; a pre-test so the teacher can understand what students know; more repetitive practice per activity to aid retention before tests; and learning more things students will use in real life.

**Teacher Perception Data (May 2025), n = 19**
Celebrations: 95% of teachers say they are comfortable navigating the resource, and 79% say they have the tools they need to accurately measure student progress. Quoted teacher comments praise that there is not just one way to learn or know most of the content, material, skills or strategy and that the curriculum figures out the why; the conceptual content and the different ways of doing math, the Are You Ready For More feature, tasks that are good for students to work together on, and the effort put into getting students to talk and write math; and how the curriculum connects math to real-life situations along with a low floor approach that is inviting for students who may be struggling. Challenges: 37% of teachers need more resources for families and 42% of teachers are using the IM instructional routines that support student access. Quoted concerns include the need for more support for ELD students and students with low reading and comprehension skills, noting that reading a problem three times is not always doable and frequently does not help; requests for more supplemental practice, assessments that match the learning activities, and guidance on what can be combined or eliminated from lessons or units; and a wish for more at-home resources with more written-out examples beyond the online workbook and videos.

**Professional Learning for Middle School Teachers**
2024/25: monthly meetings with Honors Algebra 1, district release professional learning days covering PLCs, UDL, and NWEA learning, building-level PLCs, and support from Math Specialists. 2025/26: district release professional learning days covering PLCs, UDL, and NWEA learning, building-level PLCs, and support from Math Specialists.

**Honors Enrollment Goal and Data**
Under the goal to increase enrollment in and successful completion of Honors Algebra 1 in 8th grade as measured through enrollment data and end of course summative exams, the deck presents 8th Grade Enrollment Trends in Honors Math Courses (Algebra 1 and Above). The chart labels total students as 907, 961, 995, and 1023 across the periods shown. The summary states that the middle school math sequence change led to an increase in student enrollment in honors, and that the district will continue to monitor middle school honors math enrollments. A second chart, Representation of Federal Demographic Categories in Honors Math, carries the values 159, 451, 486, and 348, with population labels n = 1023 and n = 529; the extracted text does not preserve the category labels attached to those values.

**Data To Come**
Future reporting is to include successful completion of Honors Algebra I in 8th grade, measured by course enrollment fall/spring and course enrollment the following year as sequential data; achievement and growth data referencing the November 2025 Board presentation; MSTEP; and NWEA.

The Board accepted the District's audited 2025 financial statements from Plante Moran, which carried an unmodified opinion with no findings or questioned costs, and authorized issuance of the 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds in an amount not to exceed $220,000,000. Meeting and Attendance
Regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education, November 18, 2025, held at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Philippart called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Also present were Board members Alic, Anne, Haupt, Melton, Potts and Zendler; Superintendent Machesky; and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Pagel, Recker, Milanov, Pawlus, Crowe and Trudel. Approximately 30 members of the audience attended. The meeting adjourned at 9:08 p.m. Minutes submitted by Emina Alic, Secretary. Reference line EA/jh.

Recognitions
Wass Elementary School was honored for its designation as a National Blue-Ribbon School. Because the U.S. Department of Education discontinued the national program, the State of Michigan took over recognizing 2025 Blue Ribbon Schools; Wass was one of 13 public schools in Michigan named. Interim State Superintendent Dr. Sue C. Carnell and State Board President Dr. Pamela Pugh were quoted. Wass was recognized at a Lansing ceremony on November 13; Principal Kristin Crowe and staff came forward. The Communications Department was recognized for 17 National School and Public Relations Association (NSPRA) awards and 5 Michigan School and Public Relations Association (MSPRA) awards. Melissa Verduyn, Thomas Butcher, Adam Burns and Alison Hendry were thanked.

Consent Agenda
Moved by Mr. Haupt, supported by Mrs. Alic, to approve items A through D: minutes of the October 7, 2025 Board Workshop; minutes of the October 14, 2025 Board Meeting; Treasurer's Report for September 2025; and a garage door purchase for Troy High School. Yes 7, No 0. Additions and deletions, agenda-item public communication, personnel items, and other business were all recorded as None.

Curriculum
Assistant Superintendent of Elementary Instruction Kris Griffor and Assistant Superintendent of Secondary Instruction Christine DiPilato reported on state assessment performance over time, district-by-district comparisons and gaps between student groups, covering M-STEP, PSAT and SAT results in math, ELA, science and social studies, plus Seal of Biliteracy and AP enrollment and performance. Dr. Recker, Director of Teaching and Learning, previewed the District's new Data Dashboard.

Business Actions
| Item | Detail | Vote |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2024/2025 audit | Accept audited 2025 financial statements from Plante Moran; moved Anne, supported Alic | 7-0 |
| Series II bonds | Authorize 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds not to exceed $220,000,000; moved Zendler, supported Haupt | 7-0 |
| iPads | Purchase iPads and cases from Apple, $433,950.00, Capital Projects Fund; moved Haupt, supported Anne | 7-0 |
| Technology systems | Bid to TEL Systems, Inc., $384,610.17, 2023 Capital Projects Fund; moved Alic, supported Potts | 7-0 |
| Traffic signal, Smith MS | Bid to J. Ranck Electric, $494,694.00, 2023 Capital Projects Fund; moved Potts, supported Anne | 7-0 |
| ELD materials | Language Power ELD curriculum, $104,509.12, General Fund, with $82,681.38 funded through Title III; moved Alic, supported Potts | 7-0 |

Bond Detail
The $555,000,000 bond issue was passed by voters on November 8, 2022. The District proposed issuing the second series under that proposal in an amount not to exceed $193,000,000 and refunding the 2016 School Building and Site Bonds in an amount not to exceed $27,000,000, combined into a single series not to exceed $220,000,000 to reduce issuance and administration cost. Dr. Richard Machesky and Dan Trudel were authorized to accept a purchase offer.

Other
One community member addressed the Board during non-agenda public communication; no action was taken. Student representatives reporting were Chloe Gentilini (Troy College and Career High School), Ahyoung Song (International Academy-East), Sara Graunstadt (Athens High School) and Bella Doss (Troy High School). Dr. Philippart announced the next Board Workshop for December 9 at 6:00 p.m. and the next regular meeting for December 16 at 7:00 p.m., both at the Services Building.

Record of the regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education held Tuesday, November 18, 2025 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan. President Philippart called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Dr. Philippart, Board members Alic, Anne, Haupt, Melton, Potts and Zendler were present. Superintendent Machesky attended along with administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Pagel, Recker, Milanov, Pawlus, Crowe and Trudel. Approximately 30 members of the audience were present. The minutes carry the reference EA/jh and are respectfully submitted by Emina Alic, Secretary, Troy Board of Education.

RECOGNITION - NATIONAL BLUE-RIBBON AWARD, WASS ELEMENTARY SCHOOL. The Board recognized Wass Elementary School for its designation as a National Blue-Ribbon School, an award honoring the school as one of the very best in the United States. The minutes note that the U.S. Department of Education discontinued the national program, and that the State of Michigan therefore took over recognizing and designating 2025 Blue Ribbon Schools for exemplary high performance under the federal program. Wass was identified as one of 13 public schools in Michigan to receive the designation. Interim State Superintendent Dr. Sue C. Carnell was quoted saying students and parents, school staff and local communities deserve to be honored for outstanding achievement by Blue Ribbon Schools, and that such schools serve as an example to others while representing accomplishments and progress at schools around the state. State Board President Dr. Pamela Pugh was quoted saying MDE and the State Board of Education want to ensure these outstanding schools get the recognition they deserve. Wass was recognized by the Interim State Superintendent at a ceremony in Lansing on November 13. Principal Kristin Crowe and several Wass staff members came forward to receive congratulations from the Board.

RECOGNITION - MSPRA AND NSPRA AWARDS. The Board recognized the Troy School District Communications Department, which received 17 National School and Public Relations Association (NSPRA) awards and 5 Michigan School and Public Relations Association (MSPRA) awards. Melissa Verduyn, Thomas Butcher, Adam Burns and Alison Hendry were personally thanked for their service to OneTroy. The 17 national NSPRA awards comprised 6 Awards of Excellence, 6 Awards of Merit and 5 Honorable Mentions. Awards of Excellence: Financial Publication for the TSD 2024 Millage Renewal Guide; Marketing Materials for the 2025 IAE Postcard and the 2025 TSD Pre-K and K Info Night Booklet; Podcast for Attending IAE-The Best is Yet to Come; Special Purpose Publication for the 2025 MLK Day of Service Social Media Ad; and Video Series for Portraits. Awards of Merit: Excellence in Writing for the MLK 2025 Program Script; Infographic for Be Smart on Gun Safety; News Release for Turtle Woods Grant Approved; Podcast for Creativity - Rich Machesky's Educational Leadership; Video Series for TSD Alumni Profiles; and Video-Single for School Flood Creates Unique Opportunity for Collaboration. Honorable Mentions: Magazine for the OneTroy Voice Fall and Winter 2024 Issue; Photo for Alumnus Returns, A Full Circle Moment; and Video-Single entries Making Connections and Celebrating Community, Middle School Collaboration in the TSD, and Authentic Research with Bug Bacteria. The 5 MSPRA Michigan awards were an Award of Excellence for Marketing Materials (Athens High School Profile) and Awards of Merit for Video Series (TSD Alumni Profiles), Podcast (Smith Construction Update, June 2025), Photo (Athens Champion Powerlifting Team) and Infographic (Leonard Elementary Goals). The team was recognized for the national awards in July at the NSPRA conference and will be recognized at the MSPRA conference in March of 2026 for the Michigan awards.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS: None. PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (AGENDA ITEMS): None.

GENERAL - CONSENT AGENDA. Moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Alic that the Troy Board of Education approve items A, B, C and D on the consent agenda: minutes of the October 7, 2025 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the October 14, 2025 Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report for September 2025; and a Garage Door Purchase for Troy High School. Yes 7, No 0.

PERSONNEL: None.

CURRICULUM. Assistant Superintendent of Elementary Instruction Kris Griffor and Assistant Superintendent of Secondary Instruction Christine DiPilato provided a detailed report on student performance on state assessments and how performance has changed over time, addressing district-by-district performance and performance gaps between student groups. They shared strengths to build on and areas of focus for continuous improvement. M-STEP data, PSAT and SAT data were reviewed for math, ELA, science and social studies. The Seal of Biliteracy was discussed along with AP enrollment and student performance, followed by brief discussion. Dr. Recker, Director of Teaching and Learning, provided a brief look at the District's new Data Dashboard and invited community feedback.

BUSINESS - 2024/2025 AUDIT REPORT. Chris Geck, Audit Partner at Plante Moran, and Quinton Trudell, Assurance Manager at Plante Moran, presented on the audit of the 2024-2025 fiscal year. A draft copy of the District's Audit Report had been presented in detail to the Board at the November 11, 2025 Board of Education Workshop. Mr. Geck provided highlights and reported an unmodified opinion with no findings or questioned costs in the 2025 financial statement and in the 2025 federal program audit results, and mentioned the ASBO Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting for 2024. Governmental funds, revenue and expenditures were reviewed along with student population, foundation allowance and changes in federal funding. The audit partners and Board members recognized the Business Services team, Finance Director Aurel Malutan and Assistant Superintendent Dan Trudel, for their work managing the budget.

BUSINESS - 2024/2025 AUDIT. Moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mrs. Alic that the Board of Education accept and approve the Troy School District's audited 2025 financial statements as presented by Plante Moran. Yes 7, No 0.

BUSINESS - SERIES II BOND AUTHORIZATION RESOLUTION. The $555,000,000 bond issue was passed by the voters on November 8, 2022. The District sought to proceed with issuing the second series of bonds pursuant to the 2022 Bond Proposal in an amount not to exceed $193,000,000, and to refund the 2016 School Building and Site Bonds in an amount not to exceed $27,000,000. To reduce cost of issuance and administration, the new money and refunding issues were combined into a single series in an amount not to exceed $220,000,000. Dr. Richard Machesky, Superintendent, and Dan Trudel, Assistant Superintendent of Business Services, were named as the individuals authorized to accept a purchase offer on the bonds. Moved by Mrs. Zendler and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Board authorize the issuance of bonds designated the 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds in an amount not to exceed $220,000,000, with the attached resolution made part of the official minutes of the November 18, 2025 regular meeting. BUSINESS - IPAD PURCHASES. Moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Anne that the district purchase iPads and cases from Apple in the amount of $433,950.00, approved as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund. Yes 7, No 0.

BUSINESS - TRAFFIC IMPROVEMENT, SMITH MIDDLE SCHOOL. Moved by Mrs. Potts and supported by Mrs. Anne that the bid for the traffic signal and infrastructure be awarded to J. Ranck Electric in the amount of $494,694.00, approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Yes 7, No 0.

REPORTS FROM HIGH SCHOOL STUDENT REPRESENTATIVES. Chloe Gentilini reported for Troy College and Career High School, Ahyoung Song for International Academy-East, Sara Graunstadt for Athens High School, and Bella Doss for Troy High School, each on events and activities at their schools.

Members wished everyone a Happy Thanksgiving and a homework-free weekend, congratulated Wass staff on their award, praised the ELD program presentation, and referenced the MASB Conference in Traverse City, an NHS Induction Ceremony, the Data Dashboard, a visit to Athens classrooms with a Bemis visit upcoming, an OCSBA Government Relations Committee funding update, community support for the TCT Tina Houser Food Pantry with thanks to TYA and the Coalition team, Continuing the Conversation with Dr. Yancy on Wednesday at 5:30 p.m., CAP Parent Night with applications open for 100 students and over 50 business partnerships, the Hawk and Hornet Science Olympiad described as the largest in Michigan, 57 National Merit Semi-Finalists, board member professional learning and certification of the newest board members, and the TFEE Golf Outing on June 9, 2026.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Presentation to the Troy Board of Education workshop of December 9, 2025 recommending adoption of new AP Spanish and AP French resources from Vista Higher Learning. The current materials, Abriendo Paso (2014) for AP Spanish and T'es Branche (2014) for AP French, were adopted in 2017, lack current cultural content and AP test preparation, and in the French case are a Level 4 textbook rather than an AP text. Vista was selected over Wayside and Klett because its rigor matches the AP exam, its authors are College Board trainers, and it holds 80 percent of the AP World Languages market share.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
Purpose
AP Spanish and AP French resource adoption, presented at the 12/9/25 Board Workshop of the Troy School District.

Context and Rationale
The World Language sequence runs Level 1 through Level 5 AP, and the AP exams are written at the intermediate high and advanced levels. The TSD World Languages vision describes learners who can communicate in an ever-expanding global community, discover and experience the heritage of another culture, become resilient risk-takers able to adapt to new environments, improve memory and problem-solving skills, enhance college applications and professional marketability, and open themselves to world travel. AP World Language and Culture is described as equivalent to an intermediate-level college course, in which students apply interpersonal, interpretive and presentational modes of communication while exploring family and communities, personal and public identities, beauty and aesthetics, science and technology, contemporary life, and global challenges. The exam assesses both language and culture, but the resources adopted in 2017 do not represent current culture.

Current State
World Languages operates on a 7-year adoption cycle. Under the PLC structure, Troy AP World Language teachers want a common resource to build cohesion among programs. Current resources are Abriendo Paso (2014) for AP Spanish, with outdated readings that are not updated, no interpersonal speaking practice and no AP test prep; and T'es Branche (2014) for AP French, which is a Level 4 textbook with outdated readings and listening resources. Teachers currently pull materials from a wide variety of sources, some at their own cost.

Selection Process
Guided by Jen Howe, Oakland Schools Heritage and World Language Consultant. Timeline: exploration of resources during the 24-25 school year; 8/11 leadership planning; 8/20 department kickoff and visioning; 10/2 and 10/7 rubric creation and vendor presentations; 10/20 pilot planning; 11/11 and 11/18 PLC planning and check-ins; 12/2 pilot feedback and synthesis.

Vendors Considered
| Vendor | Assessment |
| --- | --- |
| Wayside | French and Spanish; relatable content with a variety of authentic resources, but does not represent the rigor of the AP assessment and is only a textbook without assessment practice |
| Klett | No AP resource for French; Spanish has many authentic resources and AP practice but does not represent AP rigor, has fewer resources than Vista, and less user-friendly technology |
| Vista Higher Learning | French and Spanish; matches the rigor of the AP exam, culturally relevant resources and a large resource bank; resources may need scaffolding at the start of the year |

Recommended Resource
Vista Higher Learning. Its authors are also College Board trainers, and Vista holds 80 percent of the AP World Languages market share. The 26-27 AP exam will be updated; Vista agreed to provide an updated crosswalk for launching the 26-27 school year and, when it updates its textbooks, to provide updated electronic and physical resources free of cost. The district will bank its professional learning credit to support the change in August. Sample features shown included AP French culturally relevant resources with student supports, an AP Spanish cultural comparison in which a student named Maya contrasts the role of grandparents in the United States and El Salvador, and AP Spanish simulated conversations, a free response task; interpersonal communication practice supports the Free Response AP tasks, which are 50 percent of the exam.

Stakeholder Support and Timeline
Student quotations praised the online textbook for offering more listening and speaking resources, easier navigation, iPad access and speaking practice that built confidence for the heavily weighted speaking sections of the AP test. Student and caretaker surveys were referenced, followed by a financial request slide. Anticipated timeline: December, order placed; January, physical materials inventoried and pilot licenses extended into June; August, 7-year licenses begin and are rostered, with PD from Vista covering College Board changes.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Board workshop presentation titled AP Spanish and AP French Resource Adoption, delivered at the 12/9/25 Troy School District Board Workshop, proposing replacement of the district's AP world language instructional materials.

CONTEXT AND RATIONALE. The presentation situates AP within the district's world language sequence of Level 1, Level 2, Level 3, Level 4 and Level 5 AP, noting that the AP exams are written at the intermediate high and advanced levels. The TSD World Languages vision states that world language learners can communicate in an ever-expanding global community; discover and experience the rich heritage of another culture; become resilient risk-takers with a greater capacity to adapt to new environments; improve their memory and problem-solving skills for better overall academic performance; enhance their college applications and increase their professional marketability; and open themselves to opportunities for world travel. The AP World Languages vision is quoted as describing AP World Language and Culture as equivalent to an intermediate-level college course in which students cultivate their understanding of language and culture by applying interpersonal, interpretive and presentational modes of communication in real-life situations while exploring concepts related to family and communities, personal and public identities, beauty and aesthetics, science and technology, contemporary life, and global challenges. The presentation stresses that the exam assesses both language and culture, but that the resources adopted in 2017 do not have current culture represented.

CURRENT STATE. World Languages follows a 7-year adoption cycle. With the PLC structure in place, Troy AP World Language teachers desire a common resource to help build cohesion among programs. The current resources are Abriendo Paso (2014) for AP Spanish, criticized for outdated readings that have not been updated, no interpersonal speaking practice and no AP test prep; and T'es Branche (2014) for AP French, which is identified as a Level 4 textbook with outdated readings and listening resources that have not been updated. The stated current reality is that teachers are doing their best to pull resources from a wide variety of sources, some even at their own cost.

PROCESS OF RESOURCE SELECTION. Jen Howe, Oakland Schools Heritage and World Language Consultant, supported the process. The AP resources timeline was: 24-25 school year, exploration of resources; 8/11, leadership planning; 8/20, department kickoff and visioning; 10/2 and 10/7, rubric creation and vendor presentations; 10/20, pilot planning; 11/11 and 11/18, PLC planning and check-ins; and 12/2, pilot feedback and synthesis.

AP VENDORS CONSIDERED, PROS AND CONS. Wayside was evaluated for both French and Spanish; while the resource has relatable content for students with a variety of authentic resources, it does not represent the rigor of the AP assessment and is only a textbook without assessment practice. Klett has no AP resource for French; for Spanish, while the resource has many authentic resources and AP practice, it does not represent the rigor of the AP assessment, does not have the number of resources that Vista has, and its technology was less user friendly. Vista Higher Learning was evaluated for both French and Spanish and was found to match the rigor of the AP exam, providing meaningful, culturally relevant resources as well as a large resource bank; because of that rigor, resources may need to be scaffolded at the start of the year. Additional points favoring Vista: the authors of Vista are also College Board trainers; Vista has 80 percent of the AP World Languages market share; the 26-27 AP exam will be updated and Vista has agreed to provide an updated crosswalk for launching the 26-27 school year; when Vista updates its textbooks it will provide the district updated electronic and physical resources free of cost; and the district will bank its professional learning credit to support this change in August.

FEATURES OF THE RECOMMENDED TEXTS. Illustrative slides covered AP French culturally relevant resources, and AP French culturally relevant resources with student supports. For AP Spanish, a cultural comparison example was shown: on the AP test students must compare the country they are studying with the United States, and in the sample a student named Maya shares how the role of grandparents differs in the United States versus El Salvador. Another example showed AP Spanish simulated conversations, described as a free response task on the AP exam. The presentation notes that this is an example of interpersonal communication that fosters student confidence and practice for the Free Response AP tasks, which constitute 50 percent of the exam.

ADDITIONAL STAKEHOLDER SUPPORT. Two student quotations were included. One student said they like an online textbook because it has more resources such as listening and speaking, they can navigate the pages better and faster, and it is easier to have the textbook on an iPad. A second student said they have used the ebook many times in class and the variety of resources has been really helpful; that the hardest part of learning Spanish at this level is being able to speak their thoughts; that the ebook gave them speaking practice that already allowed them to feel more confident about their speaking abilities; and that the speaking sections of the AP test are huge, very important to the overall score and heavily weighted, so having these resources builds confidence in trying to get a good score. Slides for a Student Survey and a Caretaker Survey followed.

FINANCIAL REQUEST AND TIMELINE. A financial request section was included in the deck. The anticipated timeline moving forward is: December, order placed; January, physical materials inventoried and pilot licenses extended into June; August, 7-year licenses begin and are rostered, with professional development from Vista covering the College Board changes. The presentation closes with a questions slide.

ATHLETIC DEPARTMENT COMMUNICATION. Meeting and Attendance
Regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education, October 14, 2025, held at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan. Vice President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mrs. Anne, Board members Alic, Haupt, Melton, Potts, and Zendler were present; Philippart was absent for all recorded votes. Superintendent Machesky attended along with administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Pagel, Zawislak, Cottone, Vasovski, and Trudel. Approximately 12 members of the audience were present. The meeting adjourned at 8:06 p.m. Minutes were submitted by Emina Alic, Secretary, Troy Board of Education (notation EA/jh).

Recognitions
The agenda opened with a TSD Mission Moment and presentation of the Apple Distinguished School Award to Troy Union Elementary and Larson Middle School, a designation held by fewer than a thousand schools worldwide.

Resolutions Adopted
- Learning Disabilities Awareness Month, October 2025: moved by Dr. Melton, supported by Mr. Haupt, noting that 1 in 5 individuals have a learning disability and joining Governor Gretchen Whitmer in commemorating October 2025 as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.
- Principal Appreciation Month: moved by Mrs. Zendler, supported by Mrs. Alic, recognizing October as Principal Appreciation Month in Troy. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.
- 2026 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists: moved by Mr. Haupt, supported by Mrs. Zendler, honoring fifty-seven Troy students. More than one million students from some 21,000 high schools entered the program nationally and approximately 16,000 seniors were selected as semifinalists, by scoring in the top one and one-half percent on the PSAT with comparable SAT scores. A reception was set for November 13th. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

Consent Agenda
Moved by Mr. Haupt, supported by Mrs. Alic, approving items A through D: minutes of the September 2, 2025 Board Workshop; minutes of the September 16, 2025 Board Meeting; Treasurer's Report for August 2025; and second reading and adoption of Board Policy Revisions. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

Personnel
Moved by Mrs. Potts, supported by Mr. Haupt, that the Board issue a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position to Mr. Saso Vasovski, beginning duties as Technology Director on October 15, 2025. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart. There were no curriculum items.

Business
- Administration Building furniture purchase, not to exceed $300,000, through pre-existing bid contracts (consortiums), as an expenditure of the 2023 Bond Fund; moved by Mrs. Alic, supported by Mrs. Potts. Yes 6, No 0.
- Cafeteria tables for Barnard Elementary awarded to School Specialty in the amount of $46,937.22 from the 2023 Capital Projects Fund; moved by Mrs. Zendler, supported by Mrs. Potts. Yes 6, No 0.
- Technology upgrades and access control bids, moved by Dr. Melton, supported by Mrs. Potts, as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Yes 6, No 0.

Official minutes of the regular meeting of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, held October 14, 2025 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. The minutes carry the notation EA/jh and are signed respectfully submitted by Emina Alic, Secretary, Troy Board of Education.

CALL TO ORDER AND ATTENDANCE
Vice President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mrs. Anne, Board members present were Alic, Haupt, Melton, Potts, and Zendler. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Pagel, Zawislak, Cottone, Vasovski, and Trudel. There were approximately 12 members of the audience. Board member Philippart was recorded absent on every roll call vote of the evening.

RECOGNITION - TSD MISSION MOMENT / APPLE DISTINGUISHED SCHOOLS AWARD
The Board recognized two schools for earning designation as Apple Distinguished Schools, described as a recognition awarded to schools that are centers of innovation, leadership, and educational excellence, demonstrating a clear vision for learning with technology, a culture that supports continuous innovation, and compelling evidence of academic achievement and student engagement. Fewer than a thousand schools worldwide have earned the distinction. The Apple Distinguished School Award was presented to Troy Union Elementary and Larson Middle School, with congratulations to principals, staff, and students.

RECOGNITION - LEARNING DISABILITIES AWARENESS MONTH, OCTOBER 2025
The introduction noted that several national associations dedicated to supporting individuals with learning differences have designated October as a month of awareness, including organizations focused on Dyslexia, Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), and Down Syndrome; that the U.S. Department of Education has recognized October as Learning Disabilities / Dyslexia / ADHD / Down Syndrome Awareness Month; and that Governor Whitmer declared October as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan. It was moved by Dr. Melton and supported by Mr. Haupt to adopt the resolution. The whereas clauses state that the term learning disabilities refers to differences in how brains work, which may affect the acquisition, organization, retention, understanding, or use of verbal or nonverbal information; that learning disabilities range in severity and may impact the acquisition and use of oral language, reading, written language, and mathematics; that 1 in 5 individuals have a learning disability; that learning disabilities may co-exist with other disabilities and conditions and can affect individuals regardless of race, gender, sexual orientation, or other intersecting factors; that disabilities are a natural part of human diversity though individuals may face discrimination or marginalization; that every person has strengths; that specialized assessments and interventions involving home, school, community, and workplace settings can significantly enhance quality of life; that appropriate supports and services allow individuals to achieve their goals and participate fully in society; and that understanding and celebrating unique abilities is essential to an inclusive society embracing the strengths of all Michigan residents. The resolving clause has the Troy School District Board of Education join Governor Gretchen Whitmer in commemorating October 2025 as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart. Resolution adopted.

RECOGNITION - 2025 PRINCIPALS APPRECIATION MONTH
The introduction noted that October has traditionally been celebrated statewide as Principal Appreciation Month in recognition of building-level educational leaders. It was moved by Mrs. Zendler and supported by Mrs. Alic. The whereas clauses cite that energetic and inspiring school leadership is essential if teachers, schools, and districts are to ensure all Troy students are college and career ready; that K-12 principals play a vital role in student success and act as liaison between school and community; that Troy School District principals are dedicated, quality educational professionals committed to sound leadership and guidance; and that the district joins educators, parents, and students throughout Michigan to raise awareness of educational leadership. The resolution officially recognizes October as Principal Appreciation Month in Troy. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart. Resolution adopted.

RECOGNITION - 2026 NATIONAL MERIT SCHOLARSHIP SEMIFINALISTS
The narrative states that more than one million students nationwide from some 21,000 high schools entered the National Merit Scholarship Program and approximately 16,000 seniors were selected as semifinalists. Troy's fifty-seven semifinalists were named: Hasmita Anil Kumar, Fatima Ateeq, Matthew Batke, Shrish Bhandarkar, Mason Chiew, Sumehra Darafzin, Aarush Das, Arnav Dighrasker, William Dong, Lana Fargaly, Atul Ganesh, Vihaan Gehlaut, Aryan Goswami, Aaroosh Guduguntla, Anusha Gupta, Yeonjoon Ha, Kashifah Hossain, Aafla Ibraheem, Raghav Karur, Ryeo-Won Kim, Shlagha Kompelli, Aarush Kulkarni, Iniya Kumar, Ria Lattupalli, Phuong Le, Seungheon Lee, Sophia Li, Abigail Losey, Jing-Yi Ma, Jeeva Maridass, Joel Matthew, Aasrith Modem, Michael Molenda, Pratyush Neelakantan, Sameer Pai, Aayushi Parab, Kanghee Park, Sanjana Prabhu, Kristin Prakash, Akshiithi Prithiviraj, Tejaaswin Raja, Hansini Ramini, Sahas Ravoor, Ashwin Shrivastav, Divya Sovani, Chinmay Sujith Nair, Saanvi Thippireddy, Julia Triculescu, Yunis Turk, Matthew Vijayasegar, Akein Weerakoon, Anthony Wu, Casey Xin, Jonathan Xu, Alice Yang, Angela Zhang, and Eric Zhou. Copies of the resolution were to be presented to the students at a reception on November 13th. It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Zendler. The resolution notes that National Merit students reach semifinalist status by scoring in the top one and one-half percent on the National Preliminary Scholastic Aptitude Test (PSAT) and earning comparable scores on the Scholastic Aptitude Test (SAT). Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart. Resolution adopted.

Board presentation to the Troy School District Board of Education dated November 2025, titled "Pieces of One Troy: Building Belonging Through Data and Action." The stated purposes for the evening were student performance on state assessments and how performance has changed over time, district-by-district performance, performance gaps between student groups, and areas of focus and celebrations.

ABOUT THESE DATA
The deck explains that state assessments are summative assessments designed to be a snapshot in time of student performance; that they are one part of a balanced assessment system that uses multiple and varied assessments to provide all users with information they need to support teaching and learning; that they help policy makers and decision makers understand overall levels of achievement and identify schools, groups, and students for support; and that they are not designed to be diagnostic or drive day-to-day teaching and learning.

M-STEP GRADES 3-7, PERCENT ADVANCED OR PROFICIENT
ELA by grade (3, 4, 5, 6, 7), 2025: 67.9, 66.3, 67.9, 64.5, 66.1. ELA 2024: 63.2, 66.8, 69.0, 64.4, 64.8. Math 2025: 77.9, 65.9, 65.5, 65.8, 68.4. Math 2024: 72.4, 68.9, 64.1, 66.3, 66.0.

ELA: TSD 74.0%, 69.1%, 65.9%, 63.2%, 67.9%; Oakland 53.3%, 51.4%, 52.0%, 50.2%, 49.8%; Statewide 45.1%, 41.6%, 40.9%, 39.6%, 38.9%. Math: TSD 75.0%, 74.6%, 73.1%, 72.4%, 77.9%; Oakland 57.3%, 53.6%, 54.8%, 55.9%, 55.4%; Statewide 46.7%, 41.5%, 42.9%, 43.4%, 42.7%. In both subjects the Troy line sits well above the Oakland County and statewide lines across every year shown.

M-STEP 3-7 COUNTY COMPARISON

ELA: TSD 87.1%, 81.0%, 85.6%, 84.2%, 83.5%; Oakland 72.5%, 69.5%, 71.4%, 74.4%, 74.5%; Statewide 61.9%, 59.7%, 59.7%, 64.5%, 65.3%. Math: TSD 75.1%, 67.5%, 69.1%, 64.3%, 64.3%; Oakland 55.1%, 47.6%, 49.0%, 45.9%, 42.4%; Statewide 41.4%, 36.2%, 36.3%, 32.6%, 30.4%.

2025 percent advanced or proficient: 51.0%, 68.1%, 56.9%. 2024 percent advanced or proficient: 34.9%, 47.5%, 46.6%. All three grades show marked increases from the prior year.

GAP ANALYSIS - IMPLICATIONS AND ACTIONS
The deck states that historically districts have struggled to raise the performance of students with disabilities, economically disadvantaged students, and English learners on par with countywide and statewide rates of performance, commonly known as the performance gap, and that some refer to this as an opportunity gap wherein certain student groups have not been afforded adequate opportunities and support to perform on par with statewide and countywide peers.

MULTI-TIERED SYSTEM OF SUPPORT
Listed elements: district commitment to building coherence, in process; focus on systems that support all students; commitment to Professional Learning Communities, in process at all schools; universal supports; review of progress monitoring for any student on a plan; development of a district handbook; interventions taught by content strong teachers; and focus on Tier 1 instruction.

PERFORMANCE GAPS 2025 - SPECIAL EDUCATION
Values shown by Grade 3, Grade 5, Grade 6, Grade 7, Grade 8, and Grade 11. ELA special education: 45.4, 49.4, 47.7, 49.8, 52.3, 53.1. Math special education: 39.1, 40.9, 46.7, 49.3, 54.1, 51.7.

ANALYSIS - STRENGTHS TO BUILD ON
TSD consistently outperforms county and state averages, demonstrating strong and effective instructional practices; all subgroups (economically disadvantaged, special education, English learners) are performing above their statewide peers, indicating effective support systems; performance stability over three years underscores the resilience and sustainability of current practices; and third grade ranked first in the county in ELA and math.

ANALYSIS - FOCUS AREAS FOR CONTINUOUS IMPROVEMENT
Special education represents the largest and most persistent achievement gap, with continued focus on inclusive practices and Tier 1 instruction and targeted interventions provided by content strong teachers. Economically disadvantaged students, while outperforming state and county peers, have fewer than half meeting proficiency and remain a critical area for support and targeted strategies and interventions. English learners show strong performance in comparison to county and state peers, yet a performance gap remains, and ongoing support for language acquisition and academic language development is described as essential.

Honors Algebra 2: 0.81%, 0.76%, 0.20%, 1.10%, 1.90%. Grades 6-8 combined: 21/22 16%, 22/23 15%, 23/24 14%, 24/25 22%, 25/26 22%. A spring 2025 third grade ELA proficiency ranking chart lists district values of 67.9%, 66.6%, 65.6%, 63.1%, 61.6%, 61.5%, 58.6%, 54.1%, 51.3%, 50.5%, 48.7%, 48.4%, 48.1%, 47.3%, 45.9%, 44.9%, 42.7%, 41.6%, 40.6%, 39.6%, 38.9%, 37.0%, 34.8%, 33.8%, and 21.0%. Counts by district: Detroit Public School Community District 162; Grand Rapids Public Schools 126; Portage Public Schools 112; Troy Public Schools 108; Forest Hills Public Schools 106; Lincoln Park, School District of the City of 99; Dearborn City School District 90; Utica Community Schools 70; West Ottawa Public Schools District 70; Hamtramck, School District of the City of 69. The deck explains the Seal of Biliteracy recognizes students who have achieved proficiency in English and at least one additional language and highlights strong communication skills, cultural awareness, and academic achievement. Reasons it matters: gives students a competitive edge for college admissions and scholarships; supports career readiness by validating bilingual skills valued in the global workforce; honors and celebrates the linguistic and cultural diversity of students; and encourages continued language learning and cultural competence.

AP students scoring 3 or higher: 82.5% in 2020-21, 84.6% in 2021-22, 87.3% in 2022-23, 86.6% in 2023-24, and 89.0% in 2024-25. The report is organized as Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 5-6), and Informational Items (pages 7-19). The auditors thank Mr. Dan Trudel, Mr. Aurel Malutan, and the business office. Key dates: engagement letter June 3, 2025; audit planning meeting June 18, 2025; auditor's report, management representation letter, and internal control/compliance letter all October 13, 2025.

**Results of the audit**

The Food Service Fund's fund balance continues to exceed the USDA maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures; the District should continue to monitor the spenddown plan entered into with the Michigan Department of Education.

**Selected state funding figures cited**

| Item | Figure |

Plante & Moran, PLLC issued this Report to the Board of Education of Troy School District in connection with the audit of the School District's basic financial statements as of and for the year ended June 30, 2025. The transmittal letter is dated October 13, 2025 and thanks Mr. Dan Trudel, Mr. Aurel Malutan, and the entire business office for their assistance and preparedness. The report is divided into Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 5-6), and Informational Items (pages 7-19). The Results of the Audit letter is signed by Plante & Moran, PLLC and Chris Geck, CPA.

RESPONSIBILITIES AND SCOPE. The engagement letter is dated June 3, 2025. The auditors' responsibility is to express an opinion on whether the financial statements prepared by management are fairly presented in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles, obtaining reasonable but not absolute assurance that the statements are free of material misstatement. Internal control was considered solely to determine audit procedures, not to provide assurance on internal control. The audit was also conducted in accordance with Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, and a separate letter dated October 13, 2025 addresses internal control over financial reporting and tests of compliance with laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements. The audit followed the scope and timing communicated at the planning meeting of June 18, 2025.

SIGNIFICANT AUDIT FINDINGS. For the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2024, the School District adopted the provisions of Governmental Accounting Standards Board Statement No. 101, Compensated Absences; the opinion is not modified with respect to this new accounting policy. Significant accounting policies are described in Note 2. No significant transactions were recognized in a different period than when they occurred. The most sensitive estimates were the District's share of the MPSERS net liability for pension and net asset for other postemployment benefits recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75; the District's estimates as of June 30, 2025 were $211.6 million for pension and $36.6 million for OPEB, based on data received from the Office of Retirement Services. Disclosures were described as neutral, consistent, and clear. No significant difficulties were encountered, no disagreements with management arose, and no misstatements were detected as a result of audit procedures. A management representation letter is dated October 13, 2025. There were no consultations with other independent accountants. The auditors read the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and nothing came to their attention suggesting material misstatement or inconsistency.

OTHER RECOMMENDATIONS AND OBSERVATIONS. The Food Service Fund's fund balance continues to exceed the U.S. Department of Agriculture's maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures. The School District should continue to monitor its spenddown plan, entered into with the Michigan Department of Education, for reducing the balance to an acceptable level.

MANAGING THE CHANGING LANDSCAPE. The State did not meet its self-imposed July 1 deadline to complete the school aid budget for fiscal year 2025/2026. The May 2025 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference produced upward revisions to short- and long-term revenue growth projections for the General Fund and School Aid Fund, with cautionary notes about macroeconomic events including evolving federal trade policies. The federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act was signed on July 4, 2025 and is estimated to significantly reduce State revenue and to make Medicaid changes affecting the State budget. The U.S. Department of Education is undergoing major changes in 2025 following an executive order to dismantle it; billions of dollars in education funding were initially frozen, primarily related to Title I, and the president's budget proposal eliminates funding for Title 1-C, Title III, Title II, and Title IV-A.

2024/2025 SCHOOL FUNDING. The target foundation allowance stayed at $9,608 per pupil for public schools, while public school academies received a 3.9 percent increase estimated at $9,983. The blended pupil count used 90 percent weighting for the October 2024 count and 10 percent for the February 2024 count, with a two-year blended count available under Section 29 for districts whose 2024 final membership was lower than 2023. Under Section 147a(4), state funding historically covering the OPEB UAAL was about $669 million statewide; the 2024/2025 School Aid Bill redirected about $598 million of savings back to districts through the 147a(4) categorical, representing approximately 5.75 percent of the District's 2024 MPSERS-related payroll. For fiscal year 2024/2025 the School District received $5,055,278 under 147a(4), approximately $411 on a per pupil basis. Section 147c(2) appropriated $250 million in additional one-time payments to the retirement system, with no fund balance impact because the District was invoiced for the same amount it received. Section 147g was new in 2024/2025 and reimbursed employees for their 3 percent employer contribution to the OPEB plan, providing no additional general operating resources. GSRP funding increased, with families below four times the federal poverty level eligible for free preschool. At-risk funding is now over $1 billion. Transportation, Future Educator Fellowship, Student Teacher Stipend, and ISD Operations support continued without substantive change. The most significant reduction was mental health and school safety under Section 31aa, cut from $328 million to initially only $26.5 million on an opt-in basis, later increased by a $125 million supplemental.

2025/2026 SCHOOL FUNDING. Michigan's Legislature, split between a Republican-led House and a Democratic-led Senate, missed the July 1 statutory deadline; negotiations continued past the July 1, 2025 start of the school fiscal year and past the State's October 1, 2025 fiscal year start, forcing an emergency one-week stopgap. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act was expected to shrink Michigan's 2026 revenue by roughly $677 million if the State adopted the federal tax rule changes. The school aid budget is $21.3 billion, about $0.5 billion higher than last year, while continuing to shift approximately $1.3 billion in 2026 from the School Aid Fund to colleges and universities. Key provisions: the per pupil foundation allowance rises to $10,050 from $9,608, approximately a 4.6 percent increase; the 147a(1) MPSERS cost offset of $100 million, roughly $75 per student statewide, was eliminated; 147a(4) was completely removed compared with the 2025 budget, equating to $598 million or approximately $400 per student, reflecting the statutory reduction in the MPSERS UAAL required contribution from 20.96 percent to 15.21 percent of covered payroll; Section 30d universal free school meals continues with about $200 million; Section 31a at-risk funding increased 25 percent, adding roughly $258 million, with a new parent reporting and feedback requirement; Section 41 English Language Learner grants received a 25 percent boost to approximately $62.7 million; Section 51e foundational special education grants grew about 4 percent, roughly $25 million statewide; $65 million in one-time funds was set aside for K-3 class size reduction; Section 31aa provides over $169 million, an increase from roughly $151.5 million allocated last year including supplemental funds; and $100 million in one-time infrastructure grant funding was allocated.

LOOKING FORWARD. The State's 2026 budget is approximately $81 billion, boosting road and bridge funding by approximately $1.1 billion per year through a new 24 percent wholesale tax on marijuana producing $420 million and by replacing the 6 percent sales tax on gasoline with a 20 cents per gallon fuel tax increase, aligning with Governor Gretchen Whitmer's "fix the roads" promise; the new tax measures are expected to generate over $1.5 billion per year once fully implemented. Statewide enrollment has historically been slightly under 1.5 million students, was declining by about 10,000 students per year before the pandemic, and decreased in excess of 50,000 students during the pandemic. On average it takes about 10 students to fully fund a teacher position. The next Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference occurs in January 2026. The federal government missed its October 1 deadline and is in a shutdown.

MICHIGAN SCHOOL MEALS. The state-funded free breakfast and lunch initiative launched in the 2023/2024 school year under State Aid Act amendments, with Section 30d funds allocated to the Food Service Fund. For 2024/2025 the School District received $3,719,300 in Section 30d state funding. Districts apply through the Coordinated Application in the State's NexSys system and must participate in the National School Lunch Program, serve breakfast and lunch at no cost to pre-K through 12th grade students, adopt the Community Eligibility Provision, collect family income information, and write off outstanding negative student balances using resources outside the Food Service Fund. Funding continued in the 2026 state budget with a new provision allowing MDE to withhold 5 percent of state aid payments for non-adherence to federal school meal rules or failure to require completion of the federal free and reduced-price meal application.

OTHER INFORMATIONAL ITEMS. Davis Bacon prevailing wage requirements apply when federal funding is used for remodeling, renovation, repair, or construction contracts over $2,000. MPSERS, which has a September 30 year end, had a net pension liability of approximately $24.5 billion at September 30, 2024, a decrease of approximately 24 percent from $32.4 billion at September 30, 2023, and a net OPEB asset of approximately $4.3 billion compared with $566 million at September 30, 2023, an increase of approximately 660 percent; the plan's annual investment rate of return was 15.5 percent for the year ended September 30, 2024 versus 8.3 percent for the prior year. During 2024/2025 the School District's General Fund expenditures exceeded revenue by approximately $3.1 million, reducing General Fund fund balance to approximately $33.7 million at June 30, 2025; the statewide average at June 30, 2024 was approximately 24.7 percent of operating expenditures excluding transfers, equal to about a 13-week period, while the School District's fund balance percentage is 17.4 percent, equal to approximately 9 weeks of operation. GASB Statement No. 103, Financial Reporting Model Improvements, and GASB Statement No. 104, Disclosure of Certain Capital Assets, are both effective for the District's June 30, 2026 year end. Sinking fund legislation effective August 6, 2023 allows sinking fund millages approved by voters after May 7, 2023 to be used for student transportation vehicles and related parts, supplies, and equipment, and for trucks and vans registered under the Michigan vehicle code, 1949 PA 300, MCL 257.1 to 257.923; sinking funds authorized prior to March 29, 2017, between March 29, 2017 and May 7, 2023, and after May 7, 2023 must be accounted for separately with annual independent audit. The District's arbitrage analysis determined an arbitrage liability of $6,989,263, reported in the government-wide statement of net position at June 30, 2025. The April 2024 OMB Uniform Guidance revisions increase the single audit threshold and the Type A threshold from $750,000 to $1 million, effective for fiscal year ends starting on or after October 1, 2024 and applicable for the District's fiscal year ending June 30, 2026, with new requirements beginning July 1, 2025; the equipment capitalization threshold rose from $5,000 to $10,000. Remaining items address cyber threats and the K-12 Cybersecurity Act of 2021 signed in October 2021, ERP marketplace changes including the sale of SchoolFinance to Linq and Skyward's marketing of Qmlative, hosting by Tyler Technologies, PowerSchool, Skyward, or an ISD, operations review and controls assessment, IT assessment and planning, artificial intelligence including Plante Moran's AI Readiness Workshops and Innovation Labs, and data analytics within K-12 districts.

Against a 2024-2025 baseline of 32 general education vehicles, 153 daily labor hours, and 1,161 daily miles, Scenario A would require 39 vehicles, Scenario B 43 vehicles, and Scenario C 56 vehicles under a 2-tier hybrid system. **Document and parties**
Bell Time Study executive summary from School Bus Logistics, LLC (SBL), dated 4/24/25, Version 1.0, prepared for Troy School District. The cover letter dated Thursday, April 24, 2025 is addressed to Dan Trudel, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, and signed by Timothy Micheals, Route Logistics Consultant, who can be reached at 331-575-2453 or tim.micheals@schoolbuslogistics.com. The letter also thanks Kathy for collaboration throughout the process.

**Objectives and methodology**
Objectives were to assess the current fleet schedule to establish a baseline, develop route packages aligned with bell time options for each scenario, and ensure each scenario incorporates a later high school start time. For each scenario SBL provides proposed bell times including AM arrivals and PM departures, analysis of vehicle requirements, daily driver hours, and daily vehicle mileage. SBL used Versatrans RP routing software focused on general education transportation, with all data housed on Troy School District servers and accessed via secure remote connection. Data verification and cleanup addressed anchor sit times, stop sit times, and student load times. Baseline documentation criteria were service windows at schools, total number of eligible riders, actual load counts provided by the district, and current route pairings.

**Baseline, SY 24-25**
Five-tier system. Tier 1 Athens HS and Troy HS: 7:20:00 AM bell, 2:08:00 PM bell, 06:48 instructional minutes, 2:17:00 PM departure, 9 and 20 buses. Tier 2 Larson MS and Boulan MS: 7:52:00 AM, 2:40:00 PM, 06:48, 2:45:00 PM, 9 and 14 buses. Tier 3 Baker MS and Smith MS: 8:17:00 AM, 3:05:00 PM, 06:48, 3:10:00 PM, 9 and 11 buses. Tier 4 Bemis, Hill, Martell, Troy Union, and Wattles elementaries: 8:39:00 AM, 3:37:00 PM, 06:58, 3:44:00 PM. Tier 5 Barnard, Costello, Morse, Hamilton, Schroeder, and Leonard elementaries: 9:09:00 AM, 4:07:00 PM, 06:58, 4:14:00 PM. Baseline totals: 32 vehicles for Gen Ed routing on the current 5-tier system, daily labor hours of 153, daily mileage of 1161.

**Scenario results**

| Scenario | Description | Vehicles | Daily labor hours | Daily mileage |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline | Current 5-tier | 32 | 153 | 1161 |
| A (Task 1) | High school time shift, 7:00 AM to 8:00 AM arrival | 39 (7 additional) | 197 | 1161 |
| B (Task 2) | Elementary and middle school switch | 43 (11 additional) | 215 | 1161 |
| C (Task 3) | Middle/high school combination, 2-tier hybrid | 56 (24 additional) | 181 | 1387 |
| D (Task 4) | Node stops variation of Scenario A | estimated 37-39 (5-7 additional) | estimated 197 | estimated 1161 |

**Scenario notes**
In Scenario A, Boulan Park and Larson move to a 7:00 AM arrival and Baker and Smith shift to 7:30 AM, with elementary arrivals unchanged. Scenario B reversed the middle school and elementary tiers and was determined not feasible because of the required increase in vehicle count and the potential for creating latchkey situations for elementary students. In Scenario C, Larsen and Baker Middle School students were paired with Athens High School students and Boulan Park and Smith Middle School students with Troy High School students; a 4-tier hybrid option that could reduce the fleet to an estimated 37-39 buses was briefly explored, but the school board decided not to proceed with combining middle and high school students on the same bus. Scenario D consolidated stops using Troy and Athens High Schools as a sample, showing 50 stops being removed from those routes; savings would be in mileage and fuel reductions, labor time would have minimal reductions due to driver guarantees, and route time savings would be in deadhead time between runs. Because it did not reduce the number of vehicles required, Scenario D was not pursued further.

OVERVIEW. School Bus Logistics, LLC (SBL) produced this Bell Time Study executive summary for Troy School District, dated 4/24/25 and marked Version 1.0. The transmittal letter, dated Thursday, April 24, 2025, is addressed to Dan Trudel, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, and signed by Timothy Micheals, Route Logistics Consultant, who lists a contact number of 331-575-2453 and an email address of tim.micheals@schoolbuslogistics.com. The letter thanks Mr. Trudel and Kathy for their collaboration and states that the report provides a comprehensive analysis of four distinct scenarios focusing on the impact of each scenario and the additional vehicle requirements.

STUDY OVERVIEW AND OBJECTIVES. SBL was selected to conduct a bell time study evaluating four distinct scenarios. At the request of the school board, each scenario includes a later start time for all high school students. Project objectives were to assess the current fleet schedule to establish a baseline, develop route packages aligned with bell time options for each scenario, and ensure each scenario incorporates a later high school start time. For each scenario, SBL provides proposed bell times including AM arrivals and PM departures, an analysis of vehicle requirements, daily driver hours associated with each route package, and daily vehicle mileage for each route package.

METHODOLOGY. SBL used Versatrans RP routing software to develop route sets for each scenario, focusing on general education transportation. All data was housed on Troy School District's servers, and SBL accessed it via a secure remote connection to compile and analyze results within Versatrans RP. SBL first established a baseline reflecting the current routing structure and configuration of route packages. Data verification and cleanup were required before in-depth analysis, addressing elements such as anchor sit times, stop sit times, and student load times. The finalized baseline data was documented using service windows at schools for unloading and loading, total number of eligible riders reflecting utilization of seat capacity, actual load counts provided by Troy School District, and current route pairings.

BASELINE DATA, SY 24-25. The analysis is based on data from the 2024-2025 school year. The baseline bell time table lists tier, school, AM arrival, AM bell time, PM bell time, instructional minutes in HH:MM, PM departure, and number of buses. Tier 1: Athens HS, arrival 6:48 to 7:10, bell 7:20:00 AM, PM bell 2:08:00 PM, 06:48 instructional minutes, departure 2:17:00 PM, 9 buses; Troy HS, arrival 6:55 to 7:05, bell 7:20:00 AM, 2:08:00 PM, 06:48, 2:17:00 PM, 20 buses. Tier 2: Larson MS, arrival 7:25 to 7:50, bell 7:52:00 AM, 2:40:00 PM, 06:48, 2:45:00 PM, 9 buses; Boulan MS, arrival 7:19 to 7:45, same bells, 14 buses. Tier 3: Baker MS, arrival 7:50 to 8:10, bell 8:17:00 AM, 3:05:00 PM, 06:48, 3:10:00 PM, 9 buses; Smith MS, arrival 7:51 to 8:10, same bells, 11 buses. Tier 4: Bemis ES arrival 8:20:00 AM (7 buses), Hill ES 8:35:00 AM (1 bus), Martell ES 8:24:00 AM (7 AM/8 PM), Troy Union ES 8:25:00 AM (7 buses), and Wattles ES 8:24:00 AM (7 buses), all with an 8:39:00 AM bell, 3:37:00 PM PM bell, 06:58 instructional minutes, and 3:44:00 PM departure. Tier 5: Barnard ES 9:00:00 AM (4 buses), Costello ES 8:55:00 AM (3 buses, 4:17:00 PM departure), Morse ES 9:00:00 AM (5 buses), Hamilton ES 9:03:00 AM (6 AM/5 PM), Schroeder ES 9:05:00 AM (7 buses), and Leonard ES 8:52:00 AM (5 buses), all with a 9:09:00 AM bell, 4:07:00 PM PM bell, 06:58 instructional minutes, and 4:14:00 PM departure. Baseline results: 32 vehicles are required for Gen Ed routing utilizing the current 5-tier system, with daily labor hours of 153 and daily mileage of 1161.

TASK 1 - SCENARIO A (HIGH SCHOOL TIME SHIFT). SBL explored shifting the current high school arrival time from 7:00 AM to 8:00 AM. Under this scenario, Boulan Park and Larson would move to a 7:00 AM arrival while Baker and Smith would shift to 7:30 AM, and elementary school arrival times would remain unchanged. Fleet schedule pairings were modified while maintaining the existing routing structure. The Scenario A bell time table places Larson MS and Boulan MS in Tier 1 with a 7:00:00 AM arrival, 7:20:00 AM bell, 2:08:00 PM PM bell, 6:48:00 instructional minutes, and 2:17:00 PM departure, at 9 and 14 buses; Baker MS and Smith MS in Tier 2 with a 7:30:00 AM arrival, 7:52:00 AM bell, 2:40:00 PM, 6:48:00, and 2:47:00 PM departure, at 9 and 11 buses; Athens HS and Troy HS in Tier 3 with an 8:00:00 AM arrival, 8:17:00 AM bell, 3:05:00 PM, 6:48:00, and 3:10:00 PM departure, at 9 and 20 buses; and the Tier 4 and Tier 5 elementary schedules unchanged from baseline. Results: 39 vehicles are required for Gen Ed routing utilizing the 5-tier system, described as 7 additional vehicles, with daily labor hours of 197 and daily mileage of 1161.

TASK 2 - SCENARIO B (ELEMENTARY AND MIDDLE SCHOOL SWITCH). Scenario B used the route set from Scenario A with the primary adjustment being the reversal of the middle school and elementary school tiers. After review and discussion between SBL and the Troy School District, it was determined that this scenario was not feasible; the required increase in vehicle count and the potential for creating latchkey situations for elementary students presented significant challenges. Fleet schedule pairings were modified to reflect the proposed tier shift while the existing routing remained unchanged. The Scenario B table puts Barnard, Costello, Morse, Hamilton, Schroeder, and Leonard elementaries in Tier 1 with a 7:00:00 AM arrival, 7:10:00 AM bell, 2:08:00 PM PM bell, 6:58:00 instructional minutes, and 2:17:00 PM departure; Bemis, Hill, Martell, Troy Union, and Wattles in Tier 2 with a 7:30:00 AM arrival, 7:42:00 AM bell, 2:40:00 PM, 6:58:00, and 2:47:00 PM departure; Athens HS and Troy HS in Tier 3 with an 8:00:00 AM arrival, 8:17:00 AM bell, 3:05:00 PM, 6:48:00, and 3:10:00 PM departure at 9 and 20 buses; Larson MS and Boulan MS in Tier 4 with an 8:30:00 AM arrival, 8:49:00 AM bell, 3:37:00 PM, 6:48:00, and 3:44:00 PM departure at 9 and 14 buses; and Baker MS and Smith MS in Tier 5 with a 9:00:00 AM arrival, 9:19:00 AM bell, 4:07:00 PM, 6:48:00, and 4:14:00 PM departure at 9 and 11 buses. Results: 43 vehicles are required for Gen Ed routing utilizing the 5-tier system, described as 11 additional vehicles, with daily labor hours of 215 and daily mileage of 1161.

TASK 3 - SCENARIO C (MIDDLE / HIGH SCHOOL COMBINATION). Scenario C was developed in response to feedback from the Troy School District and involved combining middle and high school students on the same bus routes, increasing the eligible rider load per vehicle. Larsen and Baker Middle School students were paired with Athens High School students, while Boulan Park and Smith Middle School students were paired with Troy High School students. New route sets were created and routing criteria adjusted to accommodate the combined student populations, with new routes developed to transport students to and from multiple schools on a single bus. In the Scenario C table, Tier 1 includes Larson MS, Baker MS, and Athens HS marked "Shared / 24" and Boulan MS, Smith MS, and Troy HS marked "Shared / 37"; the middle schools have a 7:30:00 AM arrival, 7:52:00 AM bell, 2:40:00 PM PM bell, 6:48:00 instructional minutes, and 2:47:00 PM departure, while the high schools have an 8:00:00 AM arrival, 8:17:00 AM bell, 3:05:00 PM, 6:48:00, and 3:10:00 PM departure. Tier 2 places all eleven elementaries (Bemis, Hill, Martell, Troy Union, Wattles, Barnard, Costello, Morse, Hamilton, Schroeder, and Leonard) at an 8:30:00 AM arrival, 8:39:00 AM bell, 3:37:00 PM, 6:58:00, and 3:44:00 PM departure. Results: 56 vehicles are required for Gen Ed routing utilizing the 2-tier hybrid system, described as 24 additional vehicles, with daily labor hours of 181 and daily mileage of 1387. An option to implement a 4-tier hybrid system that would stagger drop-off and pickup times was briefly explored and had the potential to reduce the number of vehicles needed to an estimated 37-39 buses; however, when this scenario was presented to the school board, a decision was made not to proceed with combining middle and high school students on the same bus, and the option was set aside.

TASK 4 - SCENARIO D (NODE STOPS). Scenario D was developed as a variation of Scenario A focused on a node-based stop system using strategically placed neighborhood-based stops, aiming to consolidate bus stops and increase walking distances for high school students to reduce the number of individual stops. The node-based consolidation reduced total mileage but did not decrease driver labor hours, and similar outcomes would be expected if applied to the elementary and middle school tiers. Because the option did not reduce the number of vehicles required, it was not pursued further. SBL used Troy and Athens High Schools as a sample for node-based stop consolidation, counting only stops with assigned students. Sample route data includes AHS AM 01 with 62 assigned students, 5 total stops, 2 removed, 3 remaining; AHS AM 03 with 104 students, 10 stops, 2 removed, 8 remaining; AHS AM 11 with 58 students, 6 stops, 1 removed, 5 remaining; AHS AM 12 with 78 students, 7 stops, 1 removed, 6 remaining; AHS AM 17 with 65 students, 11 stops, 4 removed, 7 remaining; AHS AM 22 with 99 students, 9 stops, 3 removed, 6 remaining; AHS AM 25 with 72 students, 10 stops, 4 removed, 6 remaining; AHS AM 26 with 59 students, 7 stops, 1 removed, 6 remaining; and AHS AM 49 with 75 students, 5 stops, 0 removed, 5 remaining. Troy High routes include THS AM 04 (65 students, 6 stops, 3 removed, 3 remaining), THS AM 05 (72 students, 7 stops, 2 removed, 5 remaining, order changed), THS AM 07 (43 students, 10 stops, 1 removed, 9 remaining), THS AM 08 (55 students, 5 stops, 1 removed, 4 remaining, two stops combined at MOR), THS AM 09 (79 students, 5 stops, 1 removed, 4 remaining), THS AM 10 (46 students, 7 stops, 0 removed, 7 remaining, hazard stops that cannot be consolidated due to safety), THS AM 14 (91 students, 6 stops, 0 removed, 6 remaining, could consolidate 2), THS AM 16 (87 students, 10 stops, 3 removed, 7 remaining), THS AM 19 (47 students, 2 stops, 0 removed, 2 remaining, MOR overflow), THS AM 20 (88 students, 7 stops, 3 removed, 4 remaining), THS AM 23 (64 students, 13 stops, 1 removed, 12 remaining), THS AM 24 (73 students, 8 stops, 2 removed, 6 remaining), THS AM 28 (94 students, 9 stops, 4 removed, 5 remaining), THS AM 31 (57 students, 5 stops, 0 removed, 5 remaining), THS AM 32 (111 students, 11 stops, 2 removed, 9 remaining), THS AM 34 (60 students, 6 stops, 1 removed, 5 remaining), THS AM 35 (91 students, 10 stops, 4 removed, 6 remaining), THS AM 46 (72 students, 7 stops, 1 removed, 6 remaining), THS AM 52 (82 students, 9 stops, 1 removed, 8 remaining), and THS AM 53 (68 students, 8 stops, 2 removed, 6 remaining). The Task 4 summary shows 50 stops being removed from Athens and Troy High School routes; savings would be in the form of mileage and fuel reductions, labor time would have minimal reductions due to driver guarantees, and route time savings would be in the form of deadhead time between runs. Scenario D is summarized as an estimated 37-39 vehicles required for Gen Ed routing utilizing the 5-tier system (5-7 additional vehicles), with estimated daily labor hours of 197 and estimated daily mileage of 1161.

CONCLUSION. The report states that all scenarios explore later start times for high school students but each carries distinct trade-offs in fleet utilization, driver hours, and overall efficiency. School Bus Logistics states its commitment to supporting Troy School District in balancing student well-being, operational feasibility, and community needs while focusing on safety, and invites follow-up questions or further analysis.
