Elementary Writing Materials Adoption, dated May 2025 and submitted by Natalie Haezebrouck and Lisa McDonald, is the Troy School District's recommendation document for a K-5 writing curriculum adoption.

RATIONALE. The district regularly reviews curricular materials and has updated its philosophy since the last curricular adoption, concluding that a comprehensive look at programming — instructional practices, intervention, assessment, and current data — is essential rather than simply seeking new materials. Troy states a commitment to a high-quality writing curriculum aligned with Michigan's writing standards. While CORE ELA programs have supported the five pillars of literacy (phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension), they have historically offered limited support for writing instruction; to address that gap and ensure full rigor with state standards, the district has consistently implemented an additional writing curriculum alongside whatever reading program it has used. The district views writing instruction as equally critical to student success as reading, and is evaluating comprehensive writing programs that function independently of any reading curriculum. The last writing adoption was in 2016.

COMPREHENSIVE LITERACY SYSTEM BACKGROUND. Strong Leadership Team: the elementary literacy leadership team was created with representation of all grade levels, buildings, and departments, and meets regularly to engage in shared learning, review data, reflect on culture, conditions and competencies, and create goals and action plans. Vital Professional Learning Community: changes included utilizing common prep time for teachers, opportunities for teachers to observe grade-level peers, creating vertical observations, providing district job-embedded lab days multiple times a year for each grade level, principal and teaching-and-learning collaborative walk-throughs, administration positioning themselves as co-learners, continuous support from literacy specialists at each building, lab classroom experiences, learning and training at district, county and national levels, and learning partnerships with universities. High Quality Classroom Instruction: support for teacher expertise through professional learning communities and on-site support, close observation and monitoring of student progress, immediate action and effective intervention when students are not progressing, new teacher onboarding in literacy, assessment and MTSS, district PD around handwriting, phonics, and upper-grade word work/spelling, vertical alignment learning and resource development around writing genres, Summer Homegrown Institutes, and small group intervention training with emphasis on writing support. System for Assessing and Monitoring Programs: the assessment system is rooted in teachers' close observation of students' literacy behaviors with progress monitoring, using both formative and summative assessments, citing Afflerbach, 2007. Effective and Timely Literacy Intervention: early identification and early intervention within the MTSS system, with intervention supplementary to Tier One instruction, short-term, and continuously progress monitored. Family and Community Involvement and Access to High Quality Preschool round out the system, the latter including a streamlined kindergarten transition process, shared learning around early literacy processing with preschool and kindergarten teachers, and instructional coaching.

PROCESS AND SELECTION FOR THE 2024-2025 WRITING CURRICULUM REVIEW. The review began in September 2024 with the Literacy Leadership Team, an interdepartmental, established team with representation from all grade levels and roles. In Fall 2024 the district held a preschool-to-12th-grade literacy leadership meeting to study an overview of the system and future goals, gathered feedback from the K-5 team, expanded job-embedded learning around writing instruction with an additional project school, and continued district professional learning in upper-grades word study/spelling, K-2 handwriting, norming and scoring of writing samples and thin slicing, unpacking writing units and studying student work, and job-embedded learning around writing and phonics assessment and small group instruction. Training also ran for literacy specialists and a cohort of teacher consultants and resource room teachers focused on writing intervention, and all K-5 teachers were updated on the review process. In Spring 2025 the literacy leadership team expanded to over 100 members, made up of representatives from all grade levels in each building, principals, literacy specialists, ELD specialists, special education, media specialists, and Teaching and Learning. Meeting outcomes were reflecting on the current state in writing, reviewing student writing samples from the current year and progressions over time K-5, and shared learning around best practice.

RESEARCH BASE AND REVIEW TOOLS. Texts and sources studied included "Creating a Classroom Vision for Teaching Writing" by Steve Graham, a professor/researcher of 30-plus years published by the International Literacy Association; "Why Writing Workshops Work" by Zaner-Bloser, with underpinnings from researchers over the last 30 years; "Writing for Life: The Evidence Base for Powerful Writing Instruction" by Marisa Stukey, PhD and Elyse Eidman-Asdahl, PhD of the National Writing Project, described as the nation's largest network of teacher-leaders working for almost 50 years; and "Teaching Elementary School Students to Be Effective Writers," a What Works Clearinghouse practice guide from the Institute of Education Sciences, the statistics, research, and evaluation arm of the U.S. Department of Education, offering four recommendations for improving elementary students' writing. The team created its own rubric around its values in writing instruction matched to the Troy vision and district pillars, and reviewed additional curriculum score cards and rubrics: EdReports, an independent nonprofit reviewing K-12 instructional materials for alignment to standards and usability; the NYU Culturally Responsive Curriculum Score Card, developed by the Education Justice Research and Organizing Collaborative at NYU's Metro Center; The Reading League tool for alignment with the science of reading; and Knowledge Matters for knowledge-building instruction. Michigan Writing and Language Standards were used to match alignment. Data studied included demographic data (current numbers of students served K-5), process data (leadership team and early adopter feedback), perception data (family and staff survey), and academic data (M-STEP target analysis and student writing samples), with a note referencing "Beyond Testing" by Deborah Meier and its seven alternative forms of assessment.

PROGRAMS EXCLUDED AND REVIEWED. Excluded from review for lack of a cohesive K-5 program or limited rigor in writing instruction were Wit and Wisdom, Heggerty Bridge to Writing (K-3), and i-Ready Ready Writing (2-5). Programs reviewed and scored, with the share of the team choosing each as top choice: Writing by Design, 0% — criticized for lacking instructional support, being heavy with worksheets and graphic organizers, focusing primarily on 6 traits, not being robust enough to meet state standards, lacking volume of writing, poor and outdated mentor texts, weak assessments, and lack of professional development. Step-Up to Writing, 0% — a writing process approach with multiple genres not taught until upper grades, students learning within workbooks, students told what to write, weak assessments, no use of mentor texts, and professional development limited to online videos. Being a Writer, 4% — multiple genres taught though lacking literary essay, diverse mentor texts, some grammar and spelling, but workbook-based, lacking teacher resources and differentiation support, with professional learning mostly webinars or study guides. Benchmark Education Writing Workshop, 6% — a workshop model with less time for actual student writing, multiple genres, a grammar component, mentor texts lacking diversity, slower pacing, student workbooks, limited assessment, and no job-embedded professional learning. Writing Units of Study, 90% — a K-5 cohesive curriculum meeting Michigan State Standards, covering narrative, opinion/argumentative, informational, and literary essay genres, with teacher implementation supports, parent communication resources, digital features, an assessment system, access and support for all learners, high-leverage small groups and conferences, built-in professional development, culturally relevant and engaging materials, more support for phonics, spelling, grammar and writing conventions, volume in writing, explicit instruction, responsive teaching and in-the-moment feedback, diverse mentor texts, writing trajectories, writing for real audiences, and leveraging AI as a tool.

FINDINGS FROM THE LEADERSHIP TEAM, K-5 STAFF AND FAMILIES. What is going well and valued: the workshop model providing explicit and responsive teaching; student voice, identity, critical thinking, choice, volume, and variety of genres; alignment to Michigan writing standards; student outcomes in organization, elaboration, and supporting evidence; and real-world connections. Areas for improvement considered during review: grammar, spelling, handwriting, learning for families about the writing process and progression, and deep learning opportunities for special education and support staff. Families were engaged through a feedback survey, information at building PTO meetings, and a family Writing Review Information Night.

MATERIALS RECOMMENDATION. The Writing Units of Study 2024, 2025 are recommended to move forward, with publisher quotes included at the end of the document. Currently 24 teachers with representation in all 12 buildings and all grade levels are early adopting parts of the updated writing Units of Study, and all K-2 teachers have early adopted at least one updated writing unit. Early adoption team feedback reports that 100% of the teachers felt the updated Units of Study were helpful to them as teachers and responsive in their instruction, and 100% felt the updated units had a positive impact on their students' learning. Teacher testimonials praise the grammar lessons, simplified and explicit mini lessons, short and manageable spelling and grammar lessons, spelling charts, digital access and E-books, shorter and more student-friendly writing checklists, more engaging mentor texts, the literary essay unit, the color layout of the books, the purposeful integration of grammar and phonics, and the "Supporting All Writers" small group book.

IMPLEMENTATION PLAN. All resources will be available for instruction on the first day of school for the 2025-26 academic year. Teachers may receive training on the updated changes in June and/or August through the Homegrown Institute, and all teachers will participate in a kick-off during back-to-school PD in August 2025 focused on the writing curriculum. Teachers will participate in job-embedded professional learning with literacy specialist support at each building. Professional learning will focus on newer grammar and spelling components in grades 3-5, AI and digital writing in grades 3-5, unpacking new units to grade levels, embedding phonics assessments and spelling inventory in the K-5 assessment calendar, continued thin slicing of writing on-demands with adjusted writing rubrics, ongoing review of PD around handwriting, balance of writing on paper and digital writing, more family engagement nights, and continuous learning for support staff around writing intervention.

**Document**
Attendance Area Review Community Feedback, Troy School District, presented for the May 6, 2025 Board of Education workshop (PDF version).

**Phases**
Phase 1 Discovery — committee formed; research, analysis and planning; potential recommendations developed. Phase 2 Recommendation (January) — committee provides the Board with options; Board determines whether to proceed. Phase 3 Feedback (March-April) — four listening sessions for families, one at each middle school, plus a community survey. Phase 4 Determination (May) — TSD provides the Board a summary of feedback and the Board determines any future changes.

**AARC goals**
Goal 1: right-size middle schools, equal student ratios. Goal 2: resolve double splits. Goal 3: no impact on high schools.

**Community meetings**
Five community meetings were held, one at each middle school with two at Larson due to spring break. Feedback themes: preferred time to split students (ES to MS or MS to HS), moving high school boundaries, reducing middle school splits another way, managing Somerset Apartments other than having them attend six schools, the duration of legacy status, mental health and social/emotional impact of an MS-to-HS split under Option C, and open enrollment for Larson, Smith and others.

**Feedback form (5 community meetings)**
31 responses; 74% of respondents from Troy Union. Open-ended tallies: TU to Larson 6; TU to Troy High 3; TU to Smith 3; consider other options 8; mental health impacts from splits 5; move HS boundaries 3; remove all splits 3; no MS to HS splits 5.

**Adult survey — 1,777 responses**
90.7% were a parent/guardian of a current student. Highest respondent student attendance: Troy High 328, Larson 327, Athens 297, Boulan Park 266, Hamilton 240; live in Somerset Apartments 53. 60.8% were familiar with the AARC process, most having read about it on the website and/or weekly newsletter. 70.1% favored some version of Option C, with Option C at 31.8%; 76.1% did not have an opinion or did not want the Board to consider any other option. Additional unlabeled percentage callouts: 73% and 52.3% important; 80.7% and 76% important; 81.3% and 76.5% important; ES to MS 72.7% and Yes & No Preference 51.5%; increase SOC 53% and allow open enrollment 63.2%.

**Student survey — 1,229 responses**
Optional for middle and high school students. Highest respondent attendance: Baker 344, Boulan Park 309, IA East 284, Larson 216. 547 students experienced a split after 5th grade, with 70% feeling neutral about the experience (Yes 44.5%, Neutral 31.3%). 300 students experienced a split after 8th grade, with 88% feeling neutral (Yes 24.4%, Neutral 21.4%). Further callouts: ES to MS 54.5% and Important 61.2%; Important 63.5% and Not Important or Don't Know 54.1%; Important 70.5% and Important 82.2%; Important 53.2%.

**Enrollment outcomes by scenario**

| Scenario | Baker | Boulan Park | Larson | Smith |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Existing Boundary (2024) | 631 | 847 | 863 | 599 |
| Maintain Existing Boundary/Policy (2027) | 517 | 793 | 750 | 466 |
| Option C | 616 | 603 | 625 | 682 |
| Option C — ONLY TU | 517 | 793 | 625 | 591 |
| Option C — ONLY SA | 616 | 603 | 750 | 557 |
| Option C — TU to Larson | 616 | 603 | 830 | 477 |

The four middle schools held 2,940 pupils in December 2024 and are projected at 2,526 pupils in 2027 (a 2027 reduction of 400+ students).

**Timeline and assumptions**
2025/2026 prepare for adjustments; 2026/2027 changes implemented. Students continue to have access to advanced programming; siblings enrolled in middle school at the same time may stay together; students currently in 5th, 6th, 7th or 8th grade (classes of 2032, 2031, 2030, 2029) are not impacted; current 5th or 6th graders slotted for a new school may move in 2025/2026. Curriculum and athletics are consistent across the four middle schools. Next steps in May: Board consideration and decision.

Attendance Area Review Community Feedback is a Troy School District presentation prepared for the May 6, 2025 Board of Education workshop summarizing community input on middle school attendance boundary options and presenting projected building enrollments under each scenario.

PHASES. Phase 1, Discovery: the committee was formed and research, analysis, and planning commenced, with the committee developing potential recommendations. Phase 2, Recommendation (January): the committee provided the Board of Education with a recommendation in the form of options, and the Board determined whether the district should move forward with the work. Phase 3, Feedback (March-April): TSD held four listening sessions for all families, one at each middle school, and sent out a community survey for additional feedback. Phase 4, Determination (May): TSD provides the Board with a summary of feedback and the Board determines any future changes.

ATTENDANCE AREA REVIEW COMMITTEE GOALS. Goal 1 is to right-size middle schools with equal student ratios. Goal 2 is to resolve double splits. Goal 3 is no impact on high schools.

AARC COMMUNITY MEETINGS. Five community meetings were held, one at each middle school, with two held at Larson due to spring break. Feedback questions and themes raised included: the preferred time to split students, if needed, whether elementary-to-middle school or middle-to-high school; whether to consider moving high school boundaries; whether the district could reduce middle school splits any other way; whether the district could manage Somerset Apartments some other way instead of having them attend six schools; how long the district would provide legacy status for a family and whether elementary students would be considered; whether other options could be considered; the mental health and social/emotional impact of the middle-to-high school split caused by Option C; and whether open enrollment could be offered for Larson, Smith and other buildings.

AARC FEEDBACK FORM. Feedback forms collected from the five community meetings yielded 31 responses, with 74% of respondents from Troy Union and the majority of open-ended feedback coming from Troy Union families. The tallied open-ended comments were: TU to Larson, 6; TU to Troy High, 3; TU to Smith, 3; consider other options, 8; mental health impacts from splits, 5; move HS boundaries, 3; remove all splits, 3; and no MS to HS splits, 5.

AARC ADULT SURVEY. The adult survey drew 1,777 responses. 90.7% of respondents were a parent or guardian of a current student. The highest numbers of respondents' students attended or had attended Troy High (328), Larson (327), Athens (297), Boulan Park (266), and Hamilton (240); 53 respondents live in Somerset Apartments. 60.8% of respondents were familiar with the AARC process, and most individuals read about it on the district website and/or in the weekly newsletter. The presentation notes that all collected data was shared with the Board of Education for review. On options, 70.1% of people were in favor of some version of Option C, with a callout of 31.8% for Option C itself, and a majority of respondents — 76.1% — either did not have an opinion or did not want the Board of Education to consider any other option. Several further adult survey slides display paired percentage callouts without the underlying question text: "Important 73%" with "Important 52.3%"; "Important 80.7%" with "Important 76%"; "Important 81.3%" with "Important 76.5%"; "ES to MS 72.7%" with "Yes & No Preference 51.5%"; and "Increase SOC 53%" with "Allow Open Enrollment 63.2%."

AARC STUDENT SURVEY. The student survey drew 1,229 responses and was optional for middle school and high school students. The highest numbers of respondents attended or had attended Baker (344), Boulan Park (309), IA East (284), and Larson (216). All collected data was shared with the Board of Education for review. On the experience of a split after 5th grade, the slide shows Yes 44.5% and Neutral 31.3%, with the note that 547 students experienced a split after 5th grade and 70% of students felt neutral about this experience. On a split after 8th grade, the slide shows Yes 24.4% and Neutral 21.4%, with the note that 300 students experienced a split after 8th grade and 88% of students felt neutral about this experience. Additional student survey callouts, again without accompanying question text, are: "ES to MS 54.5%" with "Important 61.2%"; "Important 63.5%" with "Not Important or Don't Know 54.1%"; "Important 70.5%" with "Important 82.2%"; and "Important 53.2%."

NEXT STEPS. In May the Board of Education takes the matter under consideration and a decision is determined.

AARC OUTCOMES — NO CHANGE. Under this scenario all Somerset Apartment students go to Boulan Park. The four middle schools held 2,940 pupils in December 2024, projected at 2,526 pupils in 2027, described as a 2027 reduction of 400+ students. Existing Boundary (2024) enrollments: Baker (Blue) 631 students, Boulan (Orange) 847 students, Larson (Green) 863 students, and Smith (Yellow) 599 students. Maintaining the existing boundary and policy in 2027 yields: Baker (Blue) 517 students, Boulan (Orange) 793 students, Larson (Green) 750 students, and Smith (Yellow) 466 students.

AARC OUTCOMES — OPTION C. Projected enrollments are Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 625, and Smith 682. This option was updated after the AARC concluded, based on questions asked by the group. Under it, all Troy Union students go to Smith; all students living in community housing follow their currently assigned elementary school to that elementary school's assigned middle school; and Somerset Apartments' 319 students go to Boulan Park from six elementary schools.

TROY UNION ELEMENTARY DETAIL. For Fall 2027, Troy Union Elementary is projected at 205 students. Middle school students from Troy Union total 205: Troy Union assigned to Smith, 100; Troy Union assigned to Larson, 105; Troy Union open enrolled from Smith to Larson, 20. Actual students from Troy Union to Smith would be 80, and actual students from Troy Union to Larson would be 125.

AARC OUTCOMES — OPTION C, ONLY TU. Projected enrollments are Baker 517, Boulan Park 793, Larson 625, and Smith 591. This option was updated after the Board of Education workshop on 1/14/25. All Troy Union students go to Smith; all students living in community housing go to Boulan Park Middle School under current policy; and Somerset Apartments' 319 students go to Boulan Park from six elementary schools.

SOMERSET APARTMENTS — ELEMENTARY. For Fall 2027, 319 students from Somerset Apartments are distributed across elementary schools as follows: Hamilton 0, Schroeder 60, Bemis 69, Martell 39, Leonard 52, Wattles 52, Morse 47, Troy Union 0, Costello 0, Wass 0, Hill 0, and Barnard 0. All Somerset Apartments students go to Boulan Park Middle School.

AARC OUTCOMES — OPTION C, ONLY SA. Projected enrollments are Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 750, and Smith 557. Updated after the Board of Education workshop on 1/14/25, this variant makes no changes for Troy Union; all students living in community housing follow their currently assigned elementary school to that elementary school's assigned middle school; and Somerset Apartments' 319 students go to Boulan Park from six elementary schools currently.

AARC OUTCOMES — OPTION C, TU TO LARSON. Projected enrollments are Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 830, and Smith 477. Also updated after the Board of Education workshop on 1/14/25, this variant sends all Troy Union students to Larson; all students living in community housing follow their currently assigned elementary school to that elementary school's assigned middle school; and Somerset Apartments' 319 students go to Boulan Park from six elementary schools.

TIMELINE AND ASSUMPTIONS. The 2025/2026 school year would be used to prepare for adjustments, with changes implemented in 2026/2027. Assumptions stated: Advanced Programming — students will continue to have access to advanced programming. Siblings — TSD will ensure that families with multiple middle school students enrolled at the same time will have the option to stay together, with siblings able to attend the same middle school. MS Legacy — students currently enrolled in 5th, 6th, 7th or 8th grade will not be impacted (classes of 2032, 2031, 2030, and 2029), and these students will have the option to continue in the building they are in during the Fall of 2025. Option to Move — a current 5th or 6th grader slotted to attend a new school may do so in the 2025/2026 school year, ahead of the proposed changes. Curriculum — the curriculum offered at all four middle schools is consistent across the district, and athletics are also uniform. The presentation closes with a Questions slide.

Feedback captured: preferred time to split students, if needed, elementary-to-middle school or middle-to-high school; consider moving high school boundaries; whether middle school splits can be reduced any other way; whether the district can manage Somerset Apartments another way instead of having them attend six schools; how long the district will provide legacy for a family and whether elementary students would be considered; consider other options; consider mental health and social/emotional impact on the middle-to-high school split caused by Option C; and whether open enrollment could be offered for Larson, Smith, and others.

SLIDE 5 — FEEDBACK FORM. From the five community meetings, 31 responses were received, with 74% of respondents from Troy Union and the majority of open-ended feedback coming from Troy Union families. Counts: TU to Larson 6; TU to Troy High 3; TU to Smith 3; consider other options 8; mental health impacts from splits 5; move HS boundaries 3; remove all splits 3; no MS to HS splits 5.

SLIDE 6 — ADULT SURVEY RESULTS. 1,777 responses. 90.7% of respondents are a parent or guardian of a current student. The highest numbers of respondents' students attend or attended Troy High (328), Larson (327), Athens (297), Boulan Park (266), and Hamilton (240); 53 respondents live in Somerset Apartments. 60.8% of respondents are familiar with the AARC process, and most read about it on the district website and/or in the weekly newsletter. A footnote states that all collected data was shared with the Board of Education for review.

SLIDE 7 — OPTION SUPPORT. 70.1% of people are in favor of some version of Option C, with a separate callout of 31.8% labeled Option C. A majority of respondents — 76.1% — do not have an opinion or do not want the Board of Education to consider any other option.

SLIDES 8-12 — ADULT SURVEY CALLOUTS. These slides carry paired percentage callouts without the underlying question text in the extracted deck: Slide 8, Important 73% and Important 52.3%. Slide 9, Important 80.7% and Important 76%. Slide 10, Important 81.3% and Important 76.5%. Slide 11, ES to MS 72.7% and Yes & No Preference 51.5%. Slide 12, Increase SOC 53% and Allow Open Enrollment 63.2%. Slide 13 is a further adult survey slide without extractable text.

SLIDE 14 — STUDENT SURVEY RESULTS. 1,229 responses. The survey was optional for middle school and high school students. The highest numbers of respondents attend or attended Baker (344), Boulan Park (309), IA East (284), and Larson (216). All collected data was shared with the Board of Education for review.

SLIDES 15-21 — STUDENT SURVEY DETAIL. Slide 15 shows Yes 44.5% and Neutral 31.3%, with the note that 547 students experienced a split after 5th grade and 70% of students felt neutral about this experience. Slide 16 shows Yes 24.4% and Neutral 21.4%, with the note that 300 students experienced a split after 8th grade and 88% of students felt neutral about this experience. Slide 17 shows ES to MS 54.5% and Important 61.2%. Slide 18 shows Important 63.5% and Not Important or Don't Know 54.1%. Slide 19 shows Important 70.5% and Important 82.2%. Slide 20 shows Important 53.2%. Slide 21 is an additional student survey slide without extractable text.

SLIDE 22 — NEXT STEPS. In May, Board of Education consideration takes place and a decision is determined.

SLIDE 23 — OUTCOMES, NO CHANGE. Under a no-change scenario all Somerset Apartment students go to Boulan Park. The four middle schools held 2,940 pupils in December 2024 and are projected at 2,526 pupils in 2027, described as a 2027 reduction of 400+ students. Existing Boundary (2024): Baker (Blue) 631 students, Boulan (Orange) 847 students, Larson (Green) 863 students, Smith (Yellow) 599 students. Maintain Existing Boundary/Policy (2027): Baker (Blue) 517 students, Boulan (Orange) 793 students, Larson (Green) 750 students, Smith (Yellow) 466 students.

SLIDE 24 — OUTCOMES, OPTION C. Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 625, Smith 682. The option was updated after the AARC concluded, based on questions asked by the group. All Troy Union students go to Smith; all students living in community housing follow their currently assigned elementary school to that elementary school's assigned middle school; Somerset Apartments' 319 students go to Boulan Park from six elementary schools.

SLIDE 25 — TROY UNION ELEMENTARY. Fall 2027: 205 students. Middle school students from Troy Union total 205; Troy Union assigned to Smith 100; Troy Union assigned to Larson 105; Troy Union open enrolled from Smith to Larson 20. Actual students Troy Union to Smith 80; actual students Troy Union to Larson 125.

SLIDE 26 — OUTCOMES, OPTION C, ONLY TU. Baker 517, Boulan Park 793, Larson 625, Smith 591. Updated after the Board of Education workshop on 1/14/25. All Troy Union students go to Smith; all students living in community housing go to Boulan Park Middle School under current policy; Somerset Apartments' 319 students go to Boulan Park from six elementary schools.

SLIDE 27 — SOMERSET APARTMENTS, ELEMENTARY. Fall 2027: 319 students, distributed as Hamilton 0, Schroeder 60, Bemis 69, Martell 39, Leonard 52, Wattles 52, Morse 47, Troy Union 0, Costello 0, Wass 0, Hill 0, Barnard 0. All Somerset Apartments students go to Boulan Park Middle School.

SLIDE 28 — OUTCOMES, OPTION C, ONLY SA. Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 750, Smith 557. Updated after the Board of Education workshop on 1/14/25. Troy Union sees no changes; all students living in community housing follow their currently assigned elementary school to that elementary school's assigned middle school; Somerset Apartments' 319 students go to Boulan Park from six elementary schools currently.

SLIDE 29 — OUTCOMES, OPTION C, TU TO LARSON. Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 830, Smith 477. Updated after the Board of Education workshop on 1/14/25. Troy Union students all go to Larson; all students living in community housing follow their currently assigned elementary school to that elementary school's assigned middle school; Somerset Apartments' 319 students go to Boulan Park from six elementary schools.

SLIDE 30 — TIMELINE AND ASSUMPTIONS. 2025/2026 is for preparing for adjustments; 2026/2027 is when changes are implemented. Advanced Programming: students will continue to have access to advanced programming. Siblings: TSD will ensure families with multiple middle school students enrolled at the same time will have the option to stay together, with siblings able to attend the same middle school. MS Legacy: students currently enrolled in 5th, 6th, 7th or 8th grade will not be impacted (classes of 2032, 2031, 2030, and 2029), and will have the option to continue in the building they are in during the Fall of 2025. Option to Move: a current 5th or 6th grader slotted to attend a new school can do so in the 2025/2026 school year, ahead of the proposed changes. Curriculum: the curriculum offered at all four middle schools is consistent across the district, and athletics are also uniform.

SLIDE 31 — Questions.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A Troy School District secondary mathematics update presented to the Board of Education on May 6, 2025, covering the district's math vision, professional learning supports for Illustrative Mathematics implementation, Honors Algebra 1 enrollment trends, NWEA MAP Growth assessment, and student and teacher perception survey results. Honors Algebra 1 enrollment reached 8% of grade 7 and 50% of grade 8 in 2024-2025. Student perception data from 1,932 respondents shows 93% saying their math class is a welcoming place for everyone, while 45% said they do not enjoy learning math.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Presentation**
Secondary Math Updates, Troy School District, May 6, 2025.

**Vision for mathematics**
All students are doers of mathematics; the program's purpose is to cultivate students' positive mathematical identities so that all students develop deep mathematical understandings, understand and critique the world through mathematics, and experience the wonder, joy, and beauty of mathematics. Sourced to NCTM (2020), Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics.

**Professional learning**
The 2024 Math Summer Institute; back-to-school professional learning days; onsite learning with Illustrative Math and NWEA; monthly job-embedded professional learning with Honors Algebra 1; full days of learning during October, January, and March district professional learning; Math Specialists attending the IM coaching institute; and a full-time Math Specialist in each building to unpack units, co-plan, co-teach, coach teachers, and do intervention with struggling students.

**Support for families**
Every IM unit includes Family Support Materials describing the big ideas in plain language, with an overview of the mathematics, what to expect as learning deepens, and conversation-prompting questions. Every IM lesson includes a lesson summary in student-friendly language, useful for absences and for families. A Family Math Night was held for families with students in Math 7.

**Honors Algebra 1 enrollment**

| Course | 2021-2022 | 2022-2023 | 2023-2024 | 2024-2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Honors Algebra 1, Grade 7 | 2% | 1% | 1% | 8% |
| Honors Algebra 1, Grade 8 | 36% | 37% | 35% | 50% |

**NWEA MAP Growth**
MAP Growth is a computer-adaptive assessment used in K-12 schools by over 16 million students, nationally normed and standards aligned; MAP stands for Measures of Academic Progress. In 2024/25 all students in grades 6-8 and students enrolled in Algebra 1 took MAP Growth in the Fall and Spring, with Math 7 students also testing in Winter to provide an additional data point when choosing Math 8 or Honors Algebra 1. In 2025/26 all students in grades 6-8 and students in all levels of Algebra 1, Geometry, and Algebra 2 will test in Fall, Winter, and Spring. MAP Growth provides RIT (Rasch Unit) scores indicating instructional level, growth over time, projected growth against national norms, and disaggregated data. Next steps: use as a screener for intervention and extension, establish cohort data, compare Fall to Spring, use district data with teachers in late summer, hold a Summer 2025 Data Retreat with administrators, and continue professional learning in 2025-26.

**Student perception data (1,932 respondents)**
Celebrations: 93% said their math class is a welcoming place for everyone; 87% said they had lots of opportunities to interact with each other; 88% agreed it is important to try rather than to get things right the first time; 90% agreed with "I know I can be good at math"; 79% feel prepared for the next level of math; 59% said the lessons are "just right for them." Challenges: 34% would like more specific feedback on how to improve their work; 45% do not enjoy learning math; 24% said the lessons are too easy; 17% said the lessons are too hard.

**Teacher perception data (19 respondents)**
Celebrations: 95% say they are comfortable navigating the resource; 79% say they have the tools they need to accurately measure student progress. Challenges: 37% need more resources for families; 42% are using the IM Instructional Routines that support student access. Written comments request more support for ELD students and students with low reading/comprehension skills, more supplemental practice, closer alignment between assessments and learning activities, guidance on what can be combined or eliminated, and more at-home written examples.

**Distinguished math students**
In the 2025-26 school year a committee including a variety of stakeholders will be formed to investigate how to recognize distinguished middle school math students, considering extensions in and outside the classroom; information will be posted on the district website and communicated through the Troy Newsletter.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Secondary Math Updates is a Troy School District presentation delivered to the Board of Education on May 6, 2025.

VISION FOR MATHEMATICS. The presentation states that all students are doers of mathematics, and that the purpose of the mathematics program is to cultivate students' positive mathematical identities so that all students develop deep mathematical understandings, understand and critique the world through mathematics, and experience the wonder, joy, and beauty of mathematics. The vision is attributed to NCTM (2020), Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics.

SUPPORTING IMPLEMENTATION THROUGH PROFESSIONAL LEARNING. Supports listed are the 2024 Math Summer Institute and, for the 2024/25 school year, back-to-school professional learning days; onsite learning with Illustrative Math and NWEA; monthly job-embedded professional learning with Honors Algebra 1; a full day of learning during October, January, and March district professional learning; Math Specialists attending the IM coaching institute; and a full-time Math Specialist in each building to unpack units, co-plan, co-teach, and coach teachers as well as do intervention with struggling students.

SUPPORT FOR FAMILIES. Every Illustrative Mathematics unit includes a section called Family Support Materials, which describes in plain language the big ideas students will encounter, provides an overview of the mathematics students are learning, gives details about what to expect as the learning deepens, and includes questions that promote conversation about the mathematics. Every IM lesson includes a lesson summary written to summarize the main mathematical points of a lesson, including any new vocabulary, in student-friendly language; these are meant for students to read on their own time or to catch up on a day they were absent, and are useful for families who want to understand in more detail what their student is learning. The district also held a Family Math Night for families with students in Math 7.

COHORT SLIDES. The deck includes slides for current 9th grade students, Class of 2028; current 8th grade students, Class of 2029; and current 7th grade students, Class of 2030.

ENROLLMENT IN HONORS ALGEBRA 1. The presentation reports the share of students enrolled in Honors Algebra 1 across four school years, 2021-2022, 2022-2023, 2023-2024, and 2024-2025. For Honors Algebra 1 in Grade 7, the figures are 2%, 1%, 1%, and 8%. For Honors Algebra 1 in Grade 8, the figures are 36%, 37%, 35%, and 50%.

ASSESSMENT AND NWEA MAP GROWTH. MAP Growth is described as a computer-adaptive assessment used in K-12 schools by over 16 million students to measure student performance and growth over time; it is nationally normed and standards aligned, and MAP stands for Measures of Academic Progress. In the 2024/25 school year, all students in grades 6-8 and students enrolled in Algebra 1 took the NWEA MAP Growth assessment in the Fall and Spring. Math 7 students also took MAP Growth in the Winter to provide an additional data point when choosing Math 8 or Honors Algebra 1 as their next math course. In the 2025/26 school year, all students in grades 6-8 and students enrolled in all levels of Algebra 1, Geometry, and Algebra 2 will take the NWEA MAP Growth assessment in the Fall, Winter, and Spring.

WHAT MAP GROWTH PROVIDES. RIT Scores (Rasch Unit Score): a RIT score indicates a student's instructional level, not tied to grade level but to a continuum of learning. Growth Over Time: MAP Growth can track how much a student has grown from fall to winter to spring, or year over year, supporting the study of learning trends and evaluation of the impact of instruction or interventions. Projected Growth: each student receives a growth projection based on national norms. Disaggregated Data: MAP Growth data can be analyzed by demographic subgroups, achievement levels, or custom student groups. The deck includes three slides headed NWEA Fall 2024-25 Achievement Data whose charts are not represented in the extracted text.

NEXT STEPS WITH NWEA. MAP Growth is established as a screener to identify students who may need intervention and students who may need extension; the district will establish cohort data to identify grade-level growth; comparisons from Fall to Spring will be made, with spring testing happening at the time of the presentation; the aim is maintaining high levels of performance and growing student performance; district data will be used late summer with teachers; a Data Retreat with administrators is planned for Summer 2025; and continued professional learning with teachers is planned for the 2025-26 school year.

STUDENT PERCEPTION DATA (1,932). Celebrations reported: 93% of students said their math class is a welcoming place for everyone; 87% of students said they had lots of opportunities to interact with each other; 88% agreed that in their math class it is important to try rather than to get things right the first time; 90% of students agreed with the statement "I know I can be good at math"; 79% of students feel prepared for the next level of math; and 59% said the lessons are "just right for them." Challenges reported: 34% of students would like to receive more specific feedback on how to improve their work; 45% of students do not enjoy learning math; 24% of students said the lessons are too easy; and 17% of students said the lessons are too hard.

STUDENT VOICE. Quoted student comments include enjoying interactions with peers and being at a level where "the math isn't too easy or too hard"; a teacher explaining math equations with real-life examples; appreciation that there are different ways to learn math; and feeling confident enough to raise a hand without being judged and working with friends. Suggestions from students include adding a difficulty level to assignments to show improvement, more interactive projects or activities so class does not get boring, a pre-test so the teacher understands what students know, more repetitive practice per activity to aid retention before tests, and learning more things that will be used in real life.

TEACHER PERCEPTION DATA (19). Celebrations: 95% of teachers say they are comfortable navigating the resource, and 79% of teachers say they have the tools they need to accurately measure student progress. Quoted teacher comments praise that there is not just one way to learn most content, that the curriculum figures out the "why," the conceptual content, the "are you ready for more" tasks, the collaborative tasks, the emphasis on getting students to talk and write math, the connection of math to real-life situations, and the low-floor approach that is inviting for struggling students. Challenges: 37% of teachers need more resources for families, and 42% of teachers are using the IM Instructional Routines that support student access. Teacher comments request more support for ELD students and students with low reading and comprehension skills, noting that reading a problem three times is not always doable or helpful; more supplemental practice to solidify concepts; assessments that match more of what the learning activities look like throughout lessons; more guidance on what can be combined or eliminated from lessons or units; and more at-home resources with written-out examples beyond the online workbook and videos.

RECOGNIZING DISTINGUISHED MATH STUDENTS. In the 2025-26 school year the district will form a committee that includes a variety of stakeholders to investigate how it might recognize distinguished middle school math students. As extensions are considered, the district will look to include opportunities in and outside of the classroom. Information will be posted on the district website and communicated through the Troy Newsletter.

**Identification**
- Title: TSD PEPS Report - March 2025
- Board meeting date: April 1, 2025
- Format: PDF
- Subject: the district's PEPS report, i.e. its pupil enrollment projection study

**Extraction status**
The PDF's embedded fonts are subset fonts with no usable character mapping, so the text extraction produced glyph indices instead of letters and digits. Each line of the supplied source appears as a run of slash-delimited numbers with a repeating token standing in for the space character. The numbering restarts and is reassigned from one embedded font to the next, so the same index refers to different characters on different pages.

**What can be stated**
The file is long and page-structured, with a running header repeated at the top of many pages and with the bulk of the body consisting of dense tabular material - long rows of uniform-width numeric tokens, consistent with enrollment counts, grade-level breakdowns, and multi-year projection grids - interspersed with shorter caption and section-label lines and with graphic-heavy pages carrying little text. Section-heading structure and district map or figure pages are discernible from the layout alone.

**Caveat**
No figure from this report is reproduced here. Any enrollment count, birth count, projection year, grade cohort, building name, or percentage that a reader might expect from a pupil enrollment projection study is present in the original PDF but absent from the extracted text, and none has been inferred or supplied from other sources. A summary with substantive content will require re-extracting this PDF with optical character recognition or with a glyph-mapping decoder rather than the standard text layer.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Agenda item for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of April 1, 2025, filed under the title "TSD PEPS Report - March 2025" and attached as a PDF. PEPS is the district's pupil enrollment projection study, the periodic demographic and enrollment forecast used to inform capacity, staffing, boundary, and facilities planning.

The controlling fact for this summary is a technical one. The PDF supplied for re-summarization does not carry a readable text layer. Its embedded fonts are subsetted without a ToUnicode mapping, and the extraction step therefore emitted raw glyph indices rather than characters. Every content line in the source arrives as a run of slash-delimited integers, with a single repeated token occupying the position of each space. The index-to-character assignment is local to each embedded font subset and is reassigned as new fonts are introduced, so the mapping changes from page to page and even between typefaces on the same page. Nothing in the extracted stream is legible as English text or as Arabic numerals.

Consequently no substantive content of the report is transcribed here. That includes, and is not limited to: total district enrollment, enrollment by building, enrollment by grade, kindergarten entry counts, resident live-birth counts, cohort-survival ratios, housing or development counts, Schools of Choice or non-resident counts, capacity or utilization figures, and every projected year in the forecast horizon. None of these were legible, none have been carried over from any other Troy School District document, and none have been reconstructed by inference. Writing any such figure would be fabrication rather than summarization, which is precisely the failure mode this re-summarization effort exists to eliminate.

What the source does permit is a description of the document's physical shape. It is a multi-page, page-formatted report. A short running header line repeats at the top of the majority of pages, and a second, shorter line beneath it varies from page to page in the manner of a section or figure label. The body is dominated by tabular material: long lines composed of many uniform-length numeric tokens arranged in regular columns, with left-hand label tokens of consistent length, which is the signature of grade-by-year or building-by-year projection grids. Several pages consist of only a handful of short lines, consistent with map, chart, or full-page graphic content whose labels sit outside the text layer. Other pages carry short stacked single-token lines of the sort used for chart axis tick labels and legends. Toward the end of the file the density of numeric tokens falls and short label-style lines predominate, consistent with summary or methodology pages.

For downstream use, this item should be treated as an unindexed attachment. Full-text search against it will return nothing, and the tiered summaries stored for it should not be relied on for any enrollment number. Recovering the content requires re-processing the original PDF - either by rendering the pages and running optical character recognition, or by reconstructing the per-font glyph-index tables and decoding the existing stream. Until one of those is done, the record for this document is limited to its title, its format, its identification as the district's pupil enrollment projection study report for March 2025, and its placement on the April 1, 2025 Board of Education agenda.

Minutes of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, for the Board Meeting of February 25, 2025, held at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Philippart called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Dr. Philippart, present were Board members Alic, Anne, Haupt, Melton, Potts, and Zendler. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Montante, Griffor, Griffin, Jansen, and Trudel. There were approximately 75 members of the audience. The minutes close "Respectfully submitted, Emina Alic, Secretary, Troy Board of Education," with the notation EA/jh.

RECOGNITION - ALL-STATE ATHLETES FALL 2024. Mr. Matt Jansen, Director of Athletics, recognized students named All-State Athletes in their respective sports: Graham Bauman (Boys' Soccer, 2nd Team), Marc Delikat (Boys' Soccer, 3rd Team), Dhruv Gupta (Boys' Tennis, 1st Team), Audrey Hamilton (Girls' Cross Country), Jesse Hao (Boys' Tennis, 1st Team), Prabath Inturi (Boys' Tennis, 1st Team), Daniel Kadiu (Boys' Soccer, 1st Team), Nick Kamugunga (Boys' Soccer, 3rd Team), Derrick Kim (Boys' Tennis, 1st Team), Nahuel Larroquette (Boys' Soccer, 2nd Team), Madie Miller (Girls' Cross Country), Neel Nagappala (Boys' Tennis, 1st Team), Ishan Patel (Boys' Tennis, 1st Team), Kian Schneeweis (Boys' Cross Country), Varun Shetty (Boys' Tennis, 1st Team), and Anthony Wu (Boys' Tennis, 1st Team). Coaches Adam Spinks, Kevin McConnell, Mike Messina, Andrew Shipp, and Brian Miska were also recognized. The students came up to receive a certificate and congratulations from the Board.

TSD MISSION MOMENT - IA-EAST CAPSTONE EXPERIENCE, IB MIDDLE YEARS PROGRAMME. The Board recognized Thyra Foronda, a sophomore at the International Academy East, for excellence in her MYP Personal Project, the capstone experience of the IB Middle Years Programme, in which all sophomores spend a semester investigating a topic of their choice. Foronda is the founder of YPLA (Youth Peace & Language Association), a nonprofit focused on English language learning for people in the Middle East, with multiple departments offering internships and volunteer opportunities. Her passion for languages, particularly Arabic, inspired the initiative, which also explores the impact of globalization and combines language learning with cultural understanding and leadership development.

TSD MISSION MOMENT - SSAB EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE MLK DAY OF SERVICE. The Board recognized the Superintendent Student Advisory Board Executive Committee, which leads the 56-member SSAB meetings by planning, setting agendas, running meetings, and orchestrating activities and events. The minutes note this is the second year the group has had an executive board, refer to "these eight students" and later to "these six individuals," and record that the committee organized and executed the MLK Citywide Celebration and Day of Service, which hundreds of families attended; photos were shared on the district Facebook page and were to appear in the Friday newsletter. The executive board members called forward for recognition and a token of appreciation were Nurayda Albeez, Elyse Lazrado, Maaz Ali, Vihaan Gehlaut, Angelina Matti, and Reah Pawar.

STUDENT SPOTLIGHT. The Board recognized creative achievement in the TSD Creative Guild, welcoming Student Board Representative from IA-East Nurayda Albeez; Mr. Thomas Butcher, Creative Guild advisor, was invited up to speak about her accomplishments.

ADDITIONS & DELETIONS: None. PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (AGENDA ITEMS): None.

GENERAL - CONSENT AGENDA. It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Anne that the Troy Board of Education approve items A, B, C, D, E, and F on the consent agenda: minutes of the January 14, 2025 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the January 21, 2025 Board of Education Organizational & Regular Meeting; Treasurer's Report - December 2024; Schools Closed to Open Enrollment; Schools of Choice 105 & 105c; and Secondary Course Description Book Adoption. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

PERSONNEL: None. CURRICULUM: None.

BUSINESS - ATHLETICS PHASE 2. It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mrs. Alic that the bid for the high school athletic renovations be awarded as follows and that the amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund: Cortis Bros Trucking & Excavating, Site Work, $8,315,200.00; E&L Construction Group, General Trades, 1,414,000.00; Great Lakes Hotel Supply, Food Service Equipment, 80,766.00; CSM Mechanical, Mechanical, 348,185.00; Innovated Energy Controls, Electrical, 803,307.00; Shaw Integrated & Turf Solutions, Inc., Synthetic Turf, 978,545.00; Contingency (8%), $955,200.00; TOTAL, $12,895,203.00. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

BUSINESS - MOVING SERVICES. It was moved by Dr. Melton and supported by Mr. Haupt that the bid for professional moving services be awarded to Premier Relocations, LLC in the amount of $246,180.00 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

BUSINESS - NETWORK AND WIRELESS PROJECT. It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Anne that the purchase and implementation of a network and wireless solution from Cisco Networks be awarded to People Driven Technology in the amount of $2,154,355.01 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Board members inquired about E-rate funding; Mr. Trudel said the district would be eligible for E-rate funding after April 1st. The minutes as extracted do not print a vote tally for this item.

BUSINESS - EPIC PA, BELL, AND SECURITY SYSTEM. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt that the purchase of the EPIC System be awarded to VSC, Inc. in the amount of $1,826,553.30 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

BUSINESS - MARTELL CAFETERIA TABLES. It was moved by Mrs. Zendler and supported by Mrs. Anne that the purchase of cafeteria tables be awarded to School Specialty in the amount of $39,786.15 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (NON-AGENDA ITEMS). Dr. Philippart provided the opportunity for community members to address the Board on non-agenda items. Four community members addressed the Board during public communication. No action was taken by the Board.

OTHER - IDEA FULL FUNDING ACT RESOLUTION. Background recorded in the minutes: the K-12 Alliance of Michigan held a press conference to launch efforts both to celebrate the success of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) on the 50th anniversary of its passage and to press the federal government to fund it adequately; Congress has never funded the program higher than 18%, and this year funding has dropped all the way back to 10.3%, costing Michigan roughly $650 million this year alone. School boards in Michigan were asked to pass a resolution in support of the IDEA Full Funding Act, with signed resolutions to be shared with members of Congress at the K-12 Alliance symposium in April. It was moved by Dr. Melton and supported by Mrs. Alic. The whereas clauses state that public education is the cornerstone of democracy; that in the decade following the Great Recession students across the U.S. lost nearly $600 billion from the states' disinvestment in their public schools; that prior to the COVID-19 pandemic both state and federal funding for public schools was already failing to meet critical student needs; that since the pandemic students have needed additional academic, social, emotional, and mental health supports through targeted programming, additional personnel, enhanced professional development, new technology, and critical facility updates; that research consistently shows increased education funding positively affects academic performance, increases graduation rates, and future earnings; that when IDEA was passed in 1975 the federal government committed to pay 40 percent of the average per pupil expenditure for special education; that the financial pledge has never been met and is currently funded at approximately 10.7 percent, leaving a gap of billions of dollars; that Troy School District serves a student population that includes 10.69 percent of students with disabilities; that unfunded IDEA costs require the district to reallocate money from other programs; and that federal underfunding has negatively impacted the academic opportunities of all students for generations. The resolution calls on Congress to immediately pass the IDEA Full Funding Act (S.2217/H.R. 4519), which would create a 10-year mandatory path to fully fund IDEA, and calls on the state legislature to provide adequate, equitable, and sustainable funding increases to districts. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

OTHER - MASB BOARD OF DIRECTORS' ELECTION, REGION 8. It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Troy Board of Education cast its ballot for the following candidate to serve on the 2025 Michigan Association of School Boards' Board of Directors: Randel Meisner, Region 8, three-year term. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

REPORTS FROM HIGH SCHOOL STUDENT REPRESENTATIVES. Kristian Vitanovich, student representative for Troy College and Career High School, shared a report on events and activities at his school. Nurayda Albeez, student representative for International Academy-East, shared a report on events and activities at her school. Adam McManus, student representative for Troy High School, was not in attendance. Diana D'Aloisio, student representative for Athens High School, shared a report on events and activities at her school.

BOARD MEMBER COMMENTS/ANNOUNCEMENTS. Topics listed: Ramadan; NSBA Advocacy Institute; Career & Technical Education Month; TSD Inclusive Newsletter; Oakland County Grant Program; THS Activist Week & AHS Charity Week; TCCHS College & Career Fair; Schools of Choice addition of 70 students; AARC meetings on 3/6 Baker, 3/10 Boulan, 3/11 Smith, and 3/20 Larson; CAP Match Day; March is Reading Month; and Orchestra Teacher of the Year Wendy Stuart. Dr. Philippart announced that the next Board Workshop will be held Tuesday, March 4th at 6:00 pm at the Administration Building, the Board Winter Retreat Saturday, March 8th at 8:30 am in the Administration Building, and the March 18th Board Meeting at 7:00 pm in the Services Building.

ADJOURNMENT. The meeting adjourned at 8:55 p.m.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Career Readiness and Technical Education is a slide presentation delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education on March 4, 2025, laying out a K-12 career-readiness continuum tied to the district's Portrait of a Learner: career awareness in grades K-5 built around Michigan's six Career Zones, career exploration in grades 6-8 organized around Michigan's 17 Career Clusters, and career preparation in grades 9-12 through pathway-specific programs. The deck reports five years of CTE enrollment by program cluster, with Marketing the largest at 548 students in 2023-2024 and 287 concentrators reported for that year.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Overview**
Presentation titled "Career Readiness and Technical Education" given to the Troy School District Board of Education on March 4, 2025. It maps a K-12 progression -- awareness (K-5), exploration (6-8), preparation (9-12) -- anchored to the district's Portrait of a Learner, then details career programs and CTE enrollment.

**Career Awareness (K-5): "Let the Journey Begin"**
Elementary awareness is described as helping students develop a sense of self, discover personal interests and strengths, and explore work beyond jobs held by family members. Best practices center on the six Michigan Career Zones, embedding them across the curriculum, and family engagement. Current practices: EDPs initiated in 1st grade and revised annually through Media; Talent Portfolios begun in 3rd grade; a STEMi Mobile field trip for 4th and 5th grade students; parent nights; and grade-level events with guest speakers and assemblies.

**Career Exploration (6-8): "The Journey Continues"**
Middle school is framed as a bridge for self-discovery rather than locking in a career choice. Best practices introduce Michigan's 17 Career Clusters to students and families and continue the EDP and Talent Portfolio. Current practices include an 8th grade parent night on the middle-to-high-school transition, career readiness activities in general education courses, career exploration electives, and a culminating 8th grade interview. Future growth: pacing plans to transition from Zones to Clusters, cluster-specific field trips, industry tours and job shadows, visits to high school CTE programs, and adding EDP and Portrait of a Learner components to the 8th grade interview.

**Career Preparation (9-12): "Multiple Pathways Ahead"**
Students update self-assessments, research labor market demand and postsecondary options, and build pathway-specific and employability skills while cultivating a Talent Portfolio. The EDP is revised annually into a 4-year plan. Counselors and the Career Facilitator assist students; programs cited include CTE, OSTC, Dual Enrollment, LTU EMC and CAP, plus an annual College and Career Fair. Future growth: staff work time to insert career components into lessons, a senior exit experience, career-related professional development, and further exploration of CAPS.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Career Readiness and Technical Education is a 32-slide presentation prepared for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of March 4, 2025 (file title "TSDCareerBOE3_4 - Read-Only (003)"). It presents the district's Career Readiness Pathway as a K-12 continuum grounded in the district's Portrait of a Learner, moving from career awareness in the elementary grades, to career exploration in middle school, to career preparation in high school, and closes with a program-by-program accounting of the district's career offerings and five years of Career and Technical Education enrollment data.

**Career Awareness, Grades K-5 ("Let the Journey Begin")**

The rationale slide, "Why Start Early?", states that career awareness at the elementary level helps students develop a sense of self, discover an awareness of personal interests and strengths, and explore the world of work beyond jobs held by family members. The stated goal is to provide students with a wide range of experiences that build confidence, challenge job stereotypes, and expand their view of the immense possibilities.

Best practices for K-5 are to familiarize students and families with the six Michigan Career Zones and provide opportunities for career discovery; to connect academic content to those zones and embed it across the curriculum; and to provide family engagement opportunities. Supporting resources referenced include K-1 Career Zone Slides, a Career Zone Coloring Example, 2-5 Career Zone Slides, and Career Zone Videos.

Current K-5 practices listed are: students initiate Educational Development Plans (EDPs) in 1st grade and revise them annually through Media; students initiate Talent Portfolios in 3rd grade; intentional Career Readiness projects and activities delivered through Media; a STEMi Mobile Field Trip for 4th and 5th grade students; parent nights; and grade-level career awareness events including guest speakers and assemblies.

Future growth for K-5 is organized under Career Zones (increase ways of familiarizing students and parents with the six Michigan Career Zones), Career Awareness (increase intentional and targeted activities providing awareness of career zones), and Family Engagement (additional activities supporting career awareness).

**Career Exploration, Grades 6-8 ("The Journey Continues")**

The "Career Exploration: The Bridge" slide states that middle school is the perfect time for career exploration, self-discovery, experiential learning, and seeing the relevancy between learning and future careers, and that rather than locking in a specific career choice, exploration allows students to consider possible roles for their future selves. A transition slide is labeled "Awareness to Exploration."

Best practices for grades 6-8: introduce Michigan's 17 Career Clusters to students and families; connect academic content in all classes to the Michigan career clusters and embed it across the curriculum; acquire career, postsecondary, and employment knowledge; provide family engagement opportunities to support career exploration; and continue and revise the Educational Development Plan (EDP) and Talent Portfolio.

Current practices for grades 6-8: continuation of EDPs and Talent Portfolios; an 8th grade parent night covering the transition from middle to high school; career readiness activities embedded in general education courses; career exploration electives; and a culminating 8th grade interview.

Future growth for grades 6-8 is grouped under Career Clusters, Career Exploration, and Family Engagement. Under Career Clusters: increase ways of familiarizing students and parents with the seventeen Michigan Career Clusters; develop pacing plans to transition from Zones to Clusters; and organize cluster-specific events such as field trips, industry tours, or job shadows. Under Career Exploration: engage with guest speakers and visit high school CTE programs; review current career electives to ensure alignment with future pathways provided in high school; and add components to the 8th grade interviews to include EDP information and the Portrait of a Learner. Under Family Engagement: provide additional family engagement activities supporting career awareness.

**Career Preparation, Grades 9-12 ("Multiple Pathways Ahead!")**

The career preparation narrative states that in high school students update self-assessments, refine evolving career goals, and engage in deeper career exploration; that students shift to a more focused pathway aligned with their career aspirations and increase their knowledge by researching labor market demand and postsecondary opportunities; and that this is the time for building pathway-specific skills and employability skills and cultivating a Talent Portfolio showcasing proficiencies, certifications, experiences, and accomplishments. A transition slide is labeled "Exploration to Preparation."

Best practices for grades 9-12: in-depth exploration of the Michigan career clusters and related career pathways; connecting academic content in all classes to those clusters and pathways to establish relevancy; increasing student knowledge about career options, job outlooks, training, and education opportunities and demonstrating career-ready practices (also referred to as employability skills or soft skills); providing family engagement opportunities; revising the EDP annually to help create a 4-year plan aligned with student goals; and recording information in a Talent Portfolio to demonstrate marketable skills to a prospective employer or admissions committee.

Current practices for grades 9-12: students review and revise their EDP each year; counselors and the Career Facilitator assist students in making informed choices about education, careers, and lifestyle options; various career-ready programs are available including but not limited to CTE Programs, OSTC, Dual Enrollment, LTU EMC, and CAP; general education teachers include Career Readiness lessons to show the relevancy of their content; and a College and Career Fair is open to all high school students on an annual basis.

Future growth for grades 9-12 is grouped under Building Target, Academic Connections, and Family Engagement: provide work time for staff to insert a career component in current lessons; create a senior exit experience; encourage teachers to connect content area curriculum to careers by participating in career-related professional development; further exploration of the CAPS program; and provide additional family engagement activities supporting career readiness.

**Career and Technical Education**

CTE is defined as an innovative approach to learning that combines academic instruction with hands-on, real-world experiences to prepare students for success in college, careers, and life, focusing on the knowledge and skills students need to excel in specific industries or fields while fostering 21st-century skills such as problem-solving, teamwork, communication, and adaptability. A subsequent slide addresses the components of CTE, followed by a slide headed "CTE Programs in TSD."

The CTE Enrollment 2019-2024 table reports enrollment by program cluster for five school years. Architecture & Construction: 16 (2019-20), 33 (2020-2021), 24 (2021-2022), 30 (2022-2023), 34 (2023-2024). Arts, AV Technology & Communication: 48, 65, 29, 46, 41. Education & Training: 46, 71, 56, 50, 45. Finance: 74, 88, 134, 62**, 62**. Hospitality & Tourism: 54, 65, 66, 83, 85. Information Technology: 172, 124, 101, 76**, 113. Manufacturing: ** for the first two years, then 15, 32, 30. Marketing: 383, 449, 336, 419, 548. Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics: 170, 187, 168, 138, 52**. Transportation, Distribution, Logistics: 95, 73, 77, 70, 71. A footnote explains that the double-asterisk numbers do not reflect total enrollment for the course, and that those numbers reflect the number of students enrolled in a CTE program taught by a CTE Certified Instructor. The slide is captioned "287 Concentrators in 2023-2024!"

**Dual Enrollment**

Dual enrollment is described as a program that allows students to take college courses while still in high school, with the courses counting for both high school and college credit, saving time and money and giving students a jump start on their college education. Enrollment is listed as 66 students at Troy High and 54 students at Athens.

**Oakland Schools Technical Campus (OSTC)**

OSTC is described as designed for any student who wants to graduate high school with industry certifications, on-the-job experiences, business connections, and college credits, seeking students who want a head start on their careers and desire cutting-edge, hands-on learning. Troy High enrollment is 22 students; Athens enrollment is 73 students, with an asterisk noting that 9 students are enrolled in OSTC and OCC EMC.

**Early Middle College with Lawrence Technological University (LTU)**

The LTU Early Middle College is a partnership between TSD and LTU in which a student earns a high school diploma with TSD, a certification in Cybersecurity with LTU, and an Associate's degree in Computer Science with LTU over a 5-year program. Five students are currently enrolled.

The five-year course sequence spans Year 1 (9th grade), Year 2 (10th grade), Year 3 (11th grade), Year 4 (12th grade), and Year 5 ("Superior"), each with fall and spring terms. High school courses in the grid include English 9A/9B, English 10A/10B, English 11A/11B, English 12A/12B, Algebra 1A/1B, Geometry A/B, Algebra 2A/2B, Biology A/B, Physics, Chemistry, World History A/B, US History A/B, Government, Economics, Health, Physical Education, and World Language 1. LTU courses listed include MCS 1142 Intro to Computers, MCS 1514 Computer Science 1, MCS 1111 Coding Club (Python and Java), MCS1003 Intro to Computer Applications, MCS 1243 Foundations of Computer Science, MCS 2513 Engineering 1, MCS 2514 Computer Science 2, MCS 5013 Web Server Programming, MCS 5813 Computer Security, INT 4023 Cybersecurity, COM 1103 College Composition, COM 2103 Tech and Professional Communication, COM1002 Pathways to Research Careers, HUM1213 Engaging Ancient Text, HUM1223 Engaging Modern Texts, LLT 2xx3 LLT 2000 Elective, SSC 2xx3 Elective, and NSC natural science elective lecture and lab options. Summer offerings MCS0054 and COM0094 are marked as courses a student may test out of. LTU credits by term are listed as 0, 0, 2, 5, 8, 8, 10, 10, 10, and 9, with a stated total of 60 LTU Credits.

**Career Accelerator Program (CAP)**

The Career Accelerator Program is described as designed for high school juniors and seniors to bridge the gap between education and the professional world by providing mentorship and exposure to various career opportunities for students within the community. The program consists of two parts: the Career Accelerator classes and the pre-internship.

**CAPS Program**

The Center of Advanced Professional Studies (CAPS) is described as offering high school students the opportunity to explore career paths and gain hands-on experience in a professional setting through real-world projects, collaboration with industry experts, and development of the skills needed to thrive in their chosen field. Further exploration of CAPS is listed among the district's high school future growth targets.
