POLICY OF NONDISCRIMINATION (Revised August 2023). Addressed to students, parents, and citizens of the Troy School District, the policy statement cites Title IX of the Educational Amendments of 1972, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, and the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). Troy School District states that it does not discriminate on the basis of sex or handicap in admission or access to, treatment or employment in, its programs and activities, and periodically reviews its educational and employment programs for compliance. A grievance procedure is available through any school office or through the Title IX and Section 504/ADA Coordinator; bargaining-unit employees may alternatively use the grievance procedure in their collective bargaining agreement. In accordance with Federal regulations, the district has appointed Jordan M. Harris, J.D., Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, as Title IX and Section 504/ADA Coordinator for employment and personnel matters, and the District's Director of Special Education as Section 504/ADA Coordinator for handicapped and suspected handicapped students. Questions, suggestions, or concerns are directed to John Pagel, Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, Title IX and Section 504/ADA Coordinator, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, MI 48098-4799, (248)823-4000.

DIPLOMA AND CREDIT REQUIREMENTS. All students attending TCCHS must earn 19.5 credits to be eligible for a Troy School District high school diploma. Students interested in earning a diploma from Troy High School or Athens High School must meet the credit requirements in the THS and AHS course description book, totaling 22.5 credits. In alignment with the needs of alternative education students, TCCHS offers students with demonstrated need the opportunity to deviate from the 19.5-credit requirement; any TCCHS student may request a meeting with a counselor or administrator. All students enrolled at TCCHS must complete 8 semesters/4 years of high school and the 18 credits required by the Michigan Department of Education.

GRADUATION REQUIREMENT FLEXIBILITY OPTIONS (Updated 9.2015; MCL 380.1278a and MCL 380.1278b). Personal Curriculum allows students to earn additional credits in some core academic areas in lieu of requirements in other areas. Physical Education credit may be earned through athletics, extracurricular activities, or a counselor-approved PE class. The World Language requirement of 2.0 credits carries flexibility for non-English heritage language proficiency, international study and residence world language proficiency, and substitution of Career & Technical Education or Visual & Performing or Applied Arts credits. Students completing a Career & Technical Education program of study may exchange credits earned on a 1:1 basis for required credits in science or world language, or satisfy the Algebra 2 requirement by completing a CTE program with Algebra 2 content embedded.

GRADUATION REQUIREMENTS BEGINNING WITH THE CLASS OF 2023. English 4.0 credits, covering Literature, Informational Reading and Writing, Communications, and other English electives. Science 3.0 credits: Biology 1.0, Chemistry 0.5, Physics 0.5, Science Elective 1.0. Mathematics 4.0 credits: Algebra 1 1.0, Geometry 1.0, Algebra 2 1.0 (which may be met through CTE program completion, e.g., OSTC), plus a math elective or math-related course during the final year of high school. Social Studies 3.0 credits: World History/Geography 1.0, American History/Geography 1.0, Economics 0.5, Government and Civics 0.5. Personal Finance 0.5 credit, embedded into Economics and a graduation requirement for all students beginning with the class of 2028; students must take a TSD Economics or AP Economics course to be eligible. Physical Education/Health 1.0 credit (Physical Education 0.5, which may be earned through approved extracurricular athletics or activities, and Health 0.5). World Language 2.0 credits, satisfied by formal coursework or an equivalent K-12 learning experience, accepting 2.0 credits of world language (non-sequential accepted) or 1.0 credit of world language plus either 1.0 credit of CTE or 1.0 credit of Visual, Performing, or Applied Arts. Visual, Performing, Applied Arts & Electives 2.0 credits (1.0 VPAA, 1.0 elective). TCCHS Program Requirements 0.5 credit (Careers). Online Learning Experience 0.0 credits, a 20-hour non-credit online learning experience embedded in Troy classroom experiences throughout middle and high school. State Assessments 0.0 credits, requiring completion of State of Michigan required assessments as administered during high school. Total Credits 19.5.

CAREER TECHNICAL EDUCATION. Woodworking Design & Fabrication 1 (1/2 credit per semester, no prerequisite; satisfies 1 credit of the math-related graduation requirement during the 12th grade year) introduces designing, drawing, and manufacturing using CAD software, hand and power tools, power machines, and automation (CNC and 3D printing). Woodworking Design & Fabrication 2 (prerequisite Woodworking Design 1) emphasizes CAD and CNC design and production and advanced furniture and cabinet projects. Woodworking Design & Fabrication 3 (prerequisite Woodworking Design 2) continues the curriculum with heavy industry influence. Each carries 1/2 credit per semester and the same math-related credit provision.

ENGLISH DEPARTMENT. Literature (1/2 credit per semester, 4 semesters required, 2.0 credits total) uses a competency-based skill framework covering short stories, poetry, and novels, American literary eras, world literature, and forms of prose and verse. Informational Reading and Writing (1/2 credit per semester, 2 semesters required, 1.0 credit total) covers non-fiction and informational texts, data mining, note taking, synthesis, summarizing, and research. Communications (1/2 credit per semester, 1 semester required) covers non-verbal, verbal, visual, written, and communal styles, elements of journalism, debate, and public speaking. Creative Writing 1 (1 semester, 1/2 credit) is an elective for grades 10-12. Creative Writing 2 (prerequisite Creative Writing 1) covers poetry, essays, flash fiction, and short stories. Film and Literature covers film vocabulary, genre, film-making techniques, and film history. Literature of Suspense investigates authors including Edgar Allan Poe, Mary Shelley, and Stephen King. Short Stories emphasizes the American tradition. Music Literature examines music's role in culture and introduces Pro Tools recording software concepts. Science Fiction covers speculative literature. Classical Mythology and Drama explores myth and the origin of plays. Several English electives require successful completion of freshman year English.

FINE ARTS DEPARTMENT. Drawing 1; Advanced Drawing (prerequisite Drawing 1, with color as a focus); Painting 1 (water-soluble media); Advanced Painting (prerequisite Painting 1); Studio Art, with portfolio preparation as the goal and the option to be scheduled during Advanced Placement Art; Applied Arts and Design; Computer Graphics 1, teaching Photoshop along with art history and art theory; Principles of Photography 1, covering framing, composition, rule of thirds, light, texture, pattern lines, symmetry, depth of field, distance, perspective, culture, space, balance, color, and black and white photography; and Intro to Music Technology and Recording, using ProTools in a recording studio setting. Each is 1 semester, 1/2 credit.

HEALTH DEPARTMENT. Health (1 semester, 1/2 credit) covers healthy lifestyles, violence, sexual harassment, nutrition, fitness and weight control including steroids and eating disorders, alcohol and drug abuse, tobacco, human sexuality, birth control, and sexually transmitted diseases including HIV/AIDS. The course is required for graduation and is taken online through the Edgenuity platform.

MATHEMATICS DEPARTMENT. Business Math in Algebra A/B (Algebra 1 students)/Business Math A/B (Algebra 2 students), 4 semesters at 1/2 credit per semester, has students operate a business running an advanced fabrication lab customizing textile products and manufacturing items of wood, metal, and/or plastic, with proceeds self-funding the venture and supporting community service or monetary gifts to local charities; skills include sublimation, CNC operations, rapid prototyping, composite technologies, alternative energies, and automation robotics. Geometry by Design (2 semesters, 1/2 credit per semester) integrates geometry with building and construction trades. Personal Finance/Financial Well-Being (2 semesters, 1/2 credit per semester) is based on Michigan Personal Finance Competencies. Algebra 1 (2 semesters) covers linear, absolute value, quadratic, rational, polynomial, power, and exponential functions. Algebra 2 (prerequisite Algebra 1 and Geometry) covers the real number system, quadratics, sequences and series, polynomials, radicals, exponentials and logarithms, rational expressions, and introductory trigonometry and statistics. Geometry (prerequisite Algebra 1) covers triangles, quadrilaterals, circles, areas and volumes, trigonometry, similarity, congruence, and coordinate geometry. Trigonometry (1 semester, prerequisite Geometry and Algebra 2) covers radians and degrees, the unit circle, and trigonometric graphs. Financial Management (1 semester, 1/2 credit; satisfies 1/2 credit of the math-related graduation requirement during the 12th grade year) includes a stock market game simulation and a budget challenge. School-Based Enterprise (2 semesters, 1/2 credit per semester; satisfies 1 credit of the math-related graduation requirement during the 12th grade year) has students manage and operate a school store. Introduction to Probability and Statistics (2 semesters, 1/2 credit per semester) covers probability, sampling, data distributions, linear and exponential relationships, and systems of linear equations.

MULTI-DEPARTMENTAL. Innovation Exploration (1 semester, 1/2 credit) covers job research, resume writing, interviewing, career portfolios, and mentor connections. Innovation Learning (1 semester, 1/2 credit) and Innovation Lab (prerequisite Innovation Learning) reference creatinginnovators.com and dschool.stanford.edu and are influenced by the D school at Stanford University, with the second semester devoted to a personal innovative project. Careers (1 semester, 1/2 credit) prepares students for the transition to post-secondary education and the workforce through cover letters, resumes, self-assessment profiles, and portfolios. Design & Innovation Studio (1 semester, 1/2 credit) uses design thinking and includes career and technical student organization (CTSO) activities and work-based learning (HQWBL) with local businesses. Computer Science (1 semester, 1/2 credit) teaches Python and earns 0.5 mathematics-related credit. Work Based Learning requires students to hold a job and work at least 8 hours weekly, with teacher worksite visits and supervisor goal-setting. Not all listed courses are offered each year.

PHYSICAL EDUCATION DEPARTMENT. 1 semester, 1/2 credit; Lifetime Fitness is taken online through the Edgenuity platform.

SCIENCE DEPARTMENT. Introductory Biology (2 semesters, 1/2 credit per semester). Active Chemistry/Earth Science (2 semesters) covers matter and atoms, chemistry of art, food chemistry, and chemistry of cleaning products. Chemistry 1 (2 semesters, prerequisite Algebra 1; satisfies 1 credit of the math-related graduation requirement during the 12th grade year). Organic Chemistry (1 semester, prerequisite Chemistry 1) includes melting point determination, distillation, and fermentation labs. Introductory Physics (2 semesters, prerequisite Introductory Biology and Algebra 1; satisfies 1 credit of the math-related requirement during the 12th grade year) fulfills the one-year chemistry-or-physics requirement under State of Michigan graduation requirements and aligns with the Michigan High School Content Standards and Expectations. Physics 1 (2 semesters) recommends completion of Geometry and enrollment in Algebra 2 and covers mechanics, waves, and electricity. Forensic Science A/B (2 semesters) covers crime scene procedures, evidence types, bone identification, entomology, pathology, fingerprinting, DNA, blood typing and blood spatter analysis, hair and fiber analysis, and handwriting analysis. Environmental Science (1 semester) includes field studies and water quality tests. Human Impact on the Earth A/B (2 semesters) covers weather, climate, geography, human cities, and climate change.

SOCIAL STUDIES DEPARTMENT. Advanced Placement Art History (2 semesters, 1/2 credit per semester). World History/Geography 1 (1 semester) runs from the collapse of Rome to the French Revolution and the defeat of Napoleon. World History/Geography 2 (1 semester) runs from the Industrial Revolution to current issues. American History/Geography 1 and 2 (2 semesters, 1/2 credit per semester) cover the development of the United States from 1877. Economics (1 semester) covers economic systems, demand, supply, consumers and savers, trade, and the role of government. Government and Civics (1 semester) covers the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution, and the federal system. Conflicts of the 20th & 21st Centuries (1 semester, 1/2 credit) examines total war, civil war, and limited war.

WORLD LANGUAGE DEPARTMENT. Spanish 1, 2, 3, and 4 and Spanish AP, each 2 semesters at 1/2 credit per semester with sequential prerequisites and teacher recommendation, all completed on the Edgenuity online platform. Spanish 1 targets Novice-mid to Novice-high proficiency on the ACTFL Proficiency Guidelines. Spanish AP follows College Board AP Spanish Language and Culture guidelines across the Interpretive, Interpersonal, and Presentational modes.

ONLINE PROGRAMS. The Inspire Online Program runs classes on the Edgenuity platform and the Intersect Online Program runs classes through the Pearson Connexus platform. The associated high school course list includes Advertising and Sales Promotion, African American Studies (Black History), Algebra 1 A/B, Algebra 2 variants, Algebra with Finance A/B, Animation 1 A/B, AP Biology A/B, AP Calculus AB A/B, AP English Language & Composition A/B, AP English Literature & Composition A/B, AP Environmental Science A/B, AP Human Geography A/B, AP Macroeconomics, AP Microeconomics, AP Psychology, AP Spanish A/B, AP Statistics A/B, AP U.S. Government and Politics, AP U.S. History A/B, Art History A/B, Art in World Cultures A/B, Astronomy A/B, Biology A/B, Business Applications, Calculus A/B, Chemistry A/B or Physics A/B, Coding 1 A/B, Consumer Math A/B, Digital Photography 1 A/B and 2, Earth Science A/B (Honors Available), Economics, English 9 through 12 A/B, Entrepreneurship A/B, Environmental Science A/B, Explorations in Math A/B, French 1-4 A/B, Fundamentals of English Composition, Game Design A/B, Game Design for Chromebooks A/B, Geography and Society, Geometry A/B, German 1-3 A/B, Gothic Literature, Government, Health, Health Fitness and Nutrition A/B, History of the Holocaust, Human Geography, International Business, Introduction to Drawing, Introduction to Grammar and Composition, Introduction to Graphic Design A/B, Living Music I & II, Marine Science A/B, Music Appreciation, Mythology and Folklore, Nutrition and Wellness, Personal Fitness, Personal Health and Safety with Sex Education, Physical Education and Physical Education II and III A/B, Physical Science A/B (Honors Available), Pre-Calculus A/B (Honors Available), Principles of Business & Finance A/B, Principles of Marketing A/B, Psychology A/B, Sociology 1 & 2, Spanish 1-4 A/B, Statistics A/B, U.S. History A/B, World Geography, and World History A/B.

OAKLAND SCHOOLS TECHNICAL CAMPUS. OSTC-SE is described as an extension of the home high school, with students attending their high school half the day and the technical campus the other half. Programs are organized into clusters staffed by instructors holding both a Michigan Teaching Certificate and Vocational Authorization. Several programs qualify students for advanced standing or college credit; students may attend for one or two years, with the second year providing advanced work, specialization, and a certificate of completion. Programs are offered to juniors and seniors on a selective basis, with OSTC recommending high school credit based on local district requirements, generally 1.5 credits per semester. If regular students carry six (6) credits, OSTC students must carry three (3) credits at their home high school in addition to three (3) credits at OSTC. Two sessions operate: Morning Session classes begin 7:50 AM and are dismissed 10:20 AM; Afternoon Session classes begin 12:00 PM and are dismissed 2:30 PM. Students apply online at www.ostconline.com by the end of February, with exploration tours for current sophomores and juniors in the fall. The Southeast Campus is at 5055 Delemere Street, Royal Oak, MI, north of 14 Mile between Crooks and Coolidge, serving grades 11-12, with course codes 08101 Session 1 AM and 08102 Session 2 PM. Southeast Campus programs listed are Automotive Technology (must begin in 11th grade), Collision Repair and Refinishing, Computer Programming, Computer Networking, Construction Technology, Culinary Arts/Hospitality, Electrical and Energy Technologies, Entrepreneurship & Advanced Marketing, Health Sciences, Machining, Mechatronics, Visual Imaging Technology, Welding, and Homeland Security (Criminal Justice or Cyber Security). The Northeast Campus in Pontiac, MI offers Cosmetology, which must begin in 11th grade. Credits offered at OSTC are not NCAA approved. A bus transports students to OSTC-SE and back; afternoon session students must provide their own transportation home from OSTC-SE or the high schools.

ANTIDISCRIMINATION GRIEVANCE PROCEDURE. Any student or employee who believes he or she has been discriminated against, denied a benefit, or excluded from participation based on sex (including sexual harassment), race, color, religion, national origin, age (employees only), height, weight, marital status, or handicap files a written grievance with the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, the designated compliance administrator; forms are available in the Employee Services Department. Step 1 requires a written grievance form to the immediate supervisor or administrator within 10 workdays of the incident; the administrator must send a copy to the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services not later than the next workday; the supervisor or administrator meets with the grievant within 5 workdays of the filing date and gives a written answer within 3 workdays of the meeting. Step 2 requires appeal to the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services within 3 workdays of receipt of the answer; that official (or the Deputy Superintendent, if appropriate) meets with the grievant within 10 workdays of receipt of the appeal and gives a written answer within 5 workdays of the meeting. Step 3 requires appeal to the Superintendent within 3 workdays of receipt of the answer; the Superintendent meets with the grievant within 10 workdays of the appeal and gives a written answer within 5 workdays of the meeting, a decision that is final and binding on all parties. The Superintendent, Deputy Superintendent, and Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services may designate representatives. A grievance not filed or appealed within the specified time limits is conclusively deemed abandoned; failure of an administrator to hold a meeting or render a decision allows automatic appeal to the next level; time limits may be extended only by mutual written agreement. All records concerning a grievance are treated confidentially, and no record is kept in a staff member's personnel file if the final decision is that there was no reasonable basis for the grievance.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: New Solutions K12 delivered a February 2025 board update to the Troy School District titled Improving Outcomes and Equity for Students with Disabilities and Other Students Who Struggle. The presentation lays out four project goals, the firm's credentials and those of Nate Levenson, a three-phase Phase 1 project plan, five commendations, five opportunity areas, and the district's current implementation efforts. The central recommendation set is to expand elementary reading specialists' reach, build general education teacher capacity, build coherent elementary schedules with time for tier 1, tier 2, and intervention, implement best-practice extra-time intervention at the secondary level, and further align what is 'loose' and what is 'tight' across schools.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Presentation**
Improving Outcomes and Equity for Students with Disabilities & Other Students Who Struggle - Troy School District Board Update, February 2025, prepared by New Solutions K12 (www.newsolutionsk12.com).

**Project goals**
Develop an understanding of current practices related to special education and supporting all students who struggle; explore alignment of current practice with best practices; identify opportunities to raise student achievement and improve work-life balance for teachers and staff; craft a plan for implementing prioritized opportunities.

**About the firm and presenter**
New Solutions K12 describes serving over 300 districts in over 30 states, acting as lead partner for state departments of education in LA, CT, MD, VA, and VT, and staffing engagements with a former Superintendent, Special Ed Director, Principal, Instructional Coach, and teachers. Nate Levenson is described as a superintendent who closed the achievement gap in Arlington, MA, a consultant of over 15 years, and author of 6 books and 50+ whitepapers and articles. The firm states its best practices have been recommended by the U.S. Department of Education, cites a 66% reduction in achievement gap, and reports Louisiana results in which early adopters had the highest growth rates for students with disabilities on LEAP scores, all early adopters outpaced state average growth for students with disabilities by at least two-fold, some by three-fold and one by five-fold, nearly two thirds of high growth districts had top growth two years in a row, and one district's schools identified for low performance for students with disabilities dropped from 10 to 3.

**Phase 1 project plan**
Kickoff and engagement (assemble Guiding Coalition, share research on best practices, gather data on current practices); analysis (interviews and focus groups, analyze district data against benchmarks, develop key findings); share findings (highlight strengths and preliminary opportunities, discuss with the Guiding Coalition, prioritize and plan for implementation).

**Commendations**
Teachers are hardworking, dedicated, and caring; the district has the faith and confidence of parents and the community; the district has a deep understanding of reading best practices, particularly at the elementary level; the elementary Multi-Tiered System of Support (MTSS) process is well defined and consistently implemented; the district has the desire and ability to serve students with severe needs in district.

**Opportunities**
1. Expand the reach of elementary reading specialists. 2. Build general education teacher capacity, including 2A ensuring students with mild to moderate disabilities work toward the same standards and curriculum, 2B expanding instructional coaching, and 2C improving integration of Special Education, ELD, and General Education by shifting responsibility to the general education teaching and learning team (with new teaching and learning and special education organizational charts). 3. Create comprehensive and coherent elementary schedules with sufficient time for tier 1, tier 2, and intervention, using staggered intervention. 4. Implement best-practice secondary interventions, including 4A extra-time intervention from content strong teachers and 4B creating a sense of urgency for change. 5. Further align what is 'loose' and what is 'tight' across schools.

**Best-practice intervention course criteria**
Extra time in addition to core; content strong teachers; graded/pass fail; credit bearing in high school; subject specific direct instruction targeted to specific skill gaps; approximately 15 students to a class; 40 plus minutes a day, five days a week; during the school day.

**Current implementation efforts**
Three key focus areas: re-organizing special education and general education leadership responsibilities (decision-making rights codified); defining and rolling out elementary 'non-negotiables' (two schools piloting); and expanding extra-learning time from content strong staff at the middle and high school levels, including sections/FTE needs, staffing and budgeting plans, and IEP change processes.

**Metrics**
Students with mild to moderate disabilities receive 100% of core instruction; equal access to extra-time intervention from content strong teachers; reading proficiency increases; secondary math and ELA proficiency increases. An appendix lists best-practice research and selected publications of Nate Levenson.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Board update presentation delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education in February 2025 by New Solutions K12, titled Improving Outcomes and Equity for Students with Disabilities & Other Students Who Struggle.

PROJECT GOALS. Four goals are listed: (1) develop an understanding of current practices related to special education and supporting all students who struggle; (2) explore alignment of current practice with best practices; (3) identify opportunities to help raise achievement of students and improve work-life balance for teachers and staff; and (4) craft a plan for implementing prioritized opportunities.

ABOUT NEW SOLUTIONS K12. The firm describes an experienced team that has served over 300 districts in over 30 states; being trusted by state departments as lead partner for state departments of education in LA, CT, MD, VA, and VT; being bold yet practical, staffed by a former Superintendent, Special Ed Director, Principal, Instructional Coach, and teachers; and being evidence based, constantly conducting primary and secondary research. Nate Levenson is profiled as a superintendent who closed the achievement gap in Arlington, MA; a consultant of over 15 years and millions of miles; and an author of 6 books and 50+ whitepapers and articles. The presentation states that the firm's best practices have been recommended by the U.S. Department of Education and that the gains can be dramatic, citing a 66% reduction in achievement gap.

LOUISIANA RESULTS. The deck reports that early adopters had the highest growth rates for students with disabilities based on LEAP scores combining all grades and subjects; that all early adopters outpaced the state average growth for students with disabilities by at least two-fold (2X State Average); that some early adopters outpaced the state average by three-fold (3X State Average) and one early adopter by five-fold (5X State Average); that nearly two thirds of the high growth districts had top growth two years in a row; and that in one district the number of schools identified for low performance for students with disabilities dropped from 10 to 3.

PHASE 1 PROJECT PLAN. Three stages are described. Stage 1, Kickoff & Engagement: assemble a Guiding Coalition, share research on best practices, and gather data on current practices. Stage 2, Analysis: interviews and focus groups to build understanding, analyze district data and compare to benchmarks, and develop key findings. Stage 3, Share Findings: share findings that highlight strengths and preliminary areas of opportunity, discuss findings with the Guiding Coalition, and prioritize findings and plan for implementation.

SUMMARY OF COMMENDATIONS. Teachers are hardworking, dedicated, and caring. The district has the faith and confidence of its parents and the community. The district has a deep understanding of reading best practices, particularly at the elementary level. The elementary Multi-Tiered System of Support (MTSS) process is well defined and consistently implemented. The district has the desire and ability to serve students with severe needs in district with its broad range of supports and services.

SUMMARY OF OPPORTUNITIES. (1) Expand the reach of elementary reading specialists to support more students who struggle. (2) Build general education teacher capacity to take greater responsibility for all students' success, with sub-items 2A ensure students with mild to moderate disabilities are working toward the same standards and utilize the same curriculum; 2B expand instructional coaching to reach a greater number of teachers; and 2C improve integration of Special Education, ELD, and General Education by shifting responsibility for programming and support for nearly all students to the general education teaching and learning team. (3) Create comprehensive and coherent schedules at the elementary level to define and include sufficient time for tier 1, tier 2, and intervention. (4) Implement best-practice interventions at the secondary level for nearly all students, with 4A embrace extra time intervention from content strong teachers for students with disabilities and 4B create a sense of urgency for change. (5) Further align what is 'loose' and what is 'tight' across schools in the district to accelerate implementation of recommended best practices.

OPPORTUNITY 1 DETAIL. The deck states that students with disabilities are not yet achieving at high levels, that this is common even in high performing districts, and that the district is proactively addressing the challenges. It urges that students with disabilities not be excluded from best practice interventions. An illustration shows that across four classrooms, five students are struggling with phonics, and argues that interventionists should group all five students with common needs, since grouping by area of need makes intervention easier for staff and more impactful for students.

OPPORTUNITY 2 DETAIL. Under 2b, expanding instructional coaching, the deck lists elements of good teaching: begin a lesson with a short review of previous learning; present new material in small steps with student practice after each step; ask many questions and incorporate multiple opportunities for student response; think aloud and provide models; guide students as they begin to practice; check for understanding and provide systematic feedback and corrections; provide scaffolds for difficult tasks; have students express their ideas verbally as scaffolding for writing; provide ongoing opportunities for review and practice; and teach skills and strategies that increase self-determination so students achieve their goals with greater independence, under the heading Good Teaching Is Good Teaching. Under 2C, the deck presents a new Teaching and Learning organizational chart and a new Special Education organizational chart.

OPPORTUNITY 3 DETAIL. Creating comprehensive and coherent elementary schedules is illustrated with the point that staggering intervention expands the reach of teachers.

OPPORTUNITY 4 DETAIL. Implementing best-practice interventions at the secondary level for all students who struggle academically is framed as Core Instruction plus Extra Time to Learn equaling Mastery, with the observation that most of the widely used current supports do not provide students with extra-time intervention from content strong staff. Best practice intervention courses are defined as including extra time in addition to core; content strong teachers; graded/pass fail; credit bearing in high school; subject specific, direct instruction targeted to specific skill gaps; approximately 15 students to a class; 40 plus minutes a day, five days a week; and during the school day.

OPPORTUNITY 5 DETAIL. District wide expectations might be established for who receives intervention; who provides intervention instruction; how intervention fits into the master schedule; when special education intervention should differ from general education intervention; expectations for work load, use of time, group size, and total students served for literacy specialists and other interventionists; and expectations for workload, use of time, and total teachers supported for instructional coaches.

CURRENT IMPLEMENTATION EFFORTS. Three identified key focus areas are: (1) defining and re-organizing the responsibilities of the special education and general education leadership teams, for which clear decision-making rights have been codified; (2) clearly defining and rolling out non-negotiables at the elementary level; and (3) expanding extra-learning time from content strong staff at the middle and high school levels. The elementary non-negotiables defined and agreed to are: all students receive 100% of core reading and math; interventions and supports are taught by teachers with content expertise; intervention is grouped by student area of need; interventions are aligned to high quality tier 1 core curriculum; students with mild to moderate disabilities have full access to best practice interventions; and IEPs will be updated to reflect best practice interventions. Two schools are piloting, and continued support is underway to detail a roll-out plan. For the secondary work, continued support is underway to finalize what extra-time intervention at the secondary level will look like; identify how many sections and FTE will be needed for intervention at each school; create a staffing and budgeting plan to adequately staff intervention; create a plan to ensure all students who need it, including students with mild to moderate disabilities, access these intervention classes next year; document a process for changing IEPs as needed; and support building strategic schedules that support extra-time intervention.

END STATE AND METRICS. The stated end state is that all elementary students will receive reading best practice core and intervention; all secondary students will receive best practice intervention including extra time from content strong staff; and the district will have a means to monitor both implementation and outcomes. The metrics identified as mattering most are: students with mild to moderate disabilities receive 100% of core instruction; students with disabilities have equal access to extra time intervention from content strong teachers; reading proficiency scores increase for students with and without disabilities; and math and ELA proficiency scores at the secondary level increase for students with and without disabilities.

APPENDIX - BEST PRACTICE RESEARCH. Broad theory of action and strategies sources include the American Psychological Association (2015) Top 20 Principles from Psychology to PreK-12 Teaching and Learning; John Hattie, Visible Learning (Routledge, 2013); Hehir, Grindal, and Eidelman (April 2012) Review of Special Education in the Commonwealth of Massachusetts; Levenson (2011) Something Has Got to Change: Rethinking Special Education (AEI); Levenson, Six Shifts to Improve Special Education and Other Interventions (Harvard Education Press, 2020); Louisiana Department of Education (September 2023) Special Education Playbook for System Leaders; New Jersey School Boards Association (March 2014) Special Education: A Service, not a Place; Nordengren (November 2023) in The 74; O'Keeffe (2009), Northern Arizona University; and the Rennie Center for Education Research & Policy (Spring 2009). Sources on the importance of core instruction include Boser, Wilhelm, and Hanna (2014) Center for American Progress; Najarro (2022) Education Week; Napolitano (2023) on Dallas ISD's opt-out policy; Douglas B. Reeves, Making Standards Work (Lead+ Learn Press, 2002); and Rosenthal and Jacobsen, Pygmalion in the Classroom (Holt, Rinehart and Winston, 1968). Sources on the need for extra time interventions include Abott and Wills (2011); Allington (2006); Cortes, Goodman, and Nomi (April 2013) Harvard Kennedy School working paper RWP13-09 on Double Dose Algebra; DuFour, DuFour, Eaker, and Karhanek, Whatever It Takes (2004); the Florida Center for Reading Research; Grossman (2021) EdWeek; Harn, University of Oregon; Harlacher, Sanford, and Walker (2015) RTI Action Network; Gersten et al. (2008) NCEE 2009-4045 What Works Clearinghouse; Gertsen et al. (April 2009) IES Practice Guide; Guryan et al. (March 2021) NBER; Jones, Vaughn, and Fuchs (June 2020) EdResearch for Recovery Brief 2; King, Lemons, and Hill (2012) NASSP Bulletin 2012 96:5; District Management Council (June 2015) Reading Intervention Group Sizes; Pashler et al. (September 2007) IES Practice Guide; Rich (2014) NYT; Scammacca et al. (2007) Center on Instruction; Schmoker (September 2010) Education Week; Shanahan, Chapter 5; Sparks (October 2023) Education Week; Stiggins and DuFour (2009) Phi Delta Kappan 90.9: 640-644; Vaughn, Wanzek, Murray, and Roberts (2012) RMC Research Corporation; Vaughn, Denton, and Fletcher (May 2010) NIH Public Access 47(5): 432-444; and White, Groom-Thomas, and Loeb (August 2023) EdWorking Paper No. 22-652, Annenburg Institute at Brown University. Sources on content strong teachers include Darling-Hammond et al. (2009); District Management Council (2015); Hehir (2002) Harvard Educational Review Vol. 72 No. 1; Ingraham (September 2021) AEI; Jones, Vaughn, and Fuchs (June 2020); Kane (2013) MET Project; Mathews (2009) Washington Post; and Weisberg et al. (2009) The Widget Effect. Sources on instructional coaching include Booker and Russell (January 2022); District Management Council (2015); Joyce and Showers (2002); REL West (March 2019); and Killion and Harrison (2006).

APPENDIX - SELECTED PUBLICATIONS OF NATE LEVENSON. Books: It's Time for Strategic Scheduling, co-authored with David James (ASCD, 2023); Smarter Budgets, Smarter Schools, Second Edition (Harvard Educational Press, available 2022); Six Shifts to Improve Special Education and Other Interventions (Harvard Educational Press, 2020); A Better Way to Budget (Harvard Educational Press, 2015); Spending Money Wisely (District Management Journal, 2014); and Smarter Budgets, Smarter Schools (Harvard Educational Press, 2012). White papers include Maximizing the Impact of Intervention Time (2024); Are SEAS Working Hard to Solve the Wrong Problem in Special Education (2024); Maximizing Funding Impact (Excellence In Education, 2021); Maintenance of Effort (MOE) for IDEA Funds (District Management Group, September 2020); Assessing the Adequacy and Means of Funding Services for Students with Disabilities in Wyoming (2020); Addressing Inequities in District Budgets (May 2019); Expanding and Strengthening Best-Practice Supports for Students Who Struggle in Vermont (2017); Intervention Group Size Research Brief: Smaller Isn't Better (June 2015); The Promise of Education Information Systems (Center for American Progress, June 2014); Boosting the Quality and Efficiency of Special Education (Thomas B. Fordham Institute, September 2012); Applying Systems Thinking to Improve Special Education in Ohio (Thomas B. Fordham Institute, September 2012); Something Has Got to Change (American Enterprise Institute, January 2011); and Special Education Benchmarks: A Statewide Perspective (MA), unpublished, December 2010. Best practice guides include the Special Education Playbook for System Leaders (Louisiana Department of Education, Fall 2024); Staffing and Scheduling Best Practices Guidance (District Management Group and the Louisiana Department of Education, September 27, 2021); COVID-19 School Restart Research Briefs (Summer & Fall 2020); Managing Special Education During School Closures (April 2020); Building Great Elementary School Schedules (2019); Building Better Secondary School Schedules to Raise Achievement (2019); Partnering with Skilled Community Based Specialists (2019); and Best Practices in School Budgeting (GFOA, 2017).

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: The Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) 2025 Board of Directors election booklet, carried in the Troy School District Board of Education's February 11, 2025 materials, sets out MASB membership bylaws, the mechanics of the 2025 election, and statements from thirteen candidates. Eight seats were up: Regions 1 (two-year term), 3, 4, 6 (open seat, one-year term), 7, 8 (open seat), and Groups V and VI. Five were uncontested and those candidates were declared elected without ballots, leaving online voting only in Regions 6, 7 and 8, with ballots due by 1 p.m. on Wednesday, March 5, 2025.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**What it is**
The Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) 2025 Board of Directors election booklet, informational material for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of Feb. 11, 2025. It reprints MASB Bylaws Article IV on membership, explains the election and email voting procedures, and prints election statements for thirteen candidates on pages 5-17, closing with MASB's mission and vision on page 18.

**Board composition**
The MASB Board of Directors is comprised of 23 members, including three at-large directors. Sixteen directors are elected from the eight regions, two from each region, and one director per group is elected from Groups V, VI and VII. The MASB President nominates an at-large director, subject to Board approval. Article VIII, Section 6 permits only one director from any one local or intermediate school district board; Article VIII, Section 8 declares an unopposed nominee elected without an election.

**Seats up in 2025** (one seat each, three-year terms unless noted)

| Seat | Term | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Region 1 | two-year | Unopposed - Kristen Cambensy, Marquette Area Public Schools |
| Region 3 | three-year | Unopposed - Rick Dernberger, Zeeland Public Schools and Ottawa Area ISD |
| Region 4 | three-year | Unopposed - John Tramontana, DeWitt Public Schools |
| Region 6 | one-year, open seat | Contested, online ballot |
| Region 7 | three-year | Contested, online ballot |
| Region 8 | three-year, open seat | Contested, online ballot |
| Group V | three-year | Unopposed - Stephen Hyer, Clarkston Community Schools |
| Group VI | three-year | Unopposed - Marc Siegler, Walled Lake Consolidated Schools |

**Voting procedure**
Each district received ONE ballot, emailed to its superintendent secretary of record on Friday, Jan. 24, 2025, and not forwardable. Ballots had to be cast and confirmed by 1 p.m. on Wednesday, March 5, 2025. Unofficial results were to be posted on the voicemail at 517.327.5915 generally after 2 p.m. that day and emailed that afternoon; official results were to be approved at the March 14, 2025, Board of Directors' meeting. The Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) 2025 Board of Directors election booklet, included in the Troy School District Board of Education's Feb. 11, 2025 materials. A note on the candidate list states that incumbents are bolded.

**Membership structure (Bylaws Article IV, Section 2)**
The board of education of any public school district in Michigan may become an active member. Active members are divided into eight regions designated by intermediate school district boundaries:
- Region 1: Copper Country ISD, Delta-Schoolcraft ISD, Dickinson-Iron ISD, Eastern Upper Peninsula ISD, Gogebic-Ontonagon ISD, Marquette-Alger RESA, Menominee County ISD.
- Region 2: Alpena-Montmorency-Alcona ESD, Charlevoix-Emmet ISD, Cheboygan-Otsego-Presque Isle ESD, COOR ISD, Iosco RESA, Manistee ISD, Northwest Education Services, Wexford-Missaukee ISD.
- Region 3: Ionia County ISD, Kent ISD, Mecosta-Osceola ISD, Montcalm Area ISD, Muskegon Area ISD, Newaygo County RESA, Ottawa Area ISD, West Shore ESD.
- Region 4: Bay-Arenac ISD, Clare-Gladwin RESD, Clinton County RESA, Gratiot-Isabella RESD, Midland County ESA, Saginaw ISD, Shiawassee RESD.
- Region 5: Genesee ISD, Huron ISD, Lapeer County ISD, Sanilac ISD, St. Clair County RESA, Tuscola ISD.
- Region 6: Allegan Area ESA, Barry ISD, Berrien RESA, Branch ISD, Calhoun ISD, Heritage Southwest ISD, Kalamazoo RESA, St. Joseph County ISD, Van Buren ISD.
- Region 7: Eaton RESA, Hillsdale County ISD, Ingham ISD, Jackson County ISD, Lenawee ISD, Livingston ESA, Monroe County ISD, Washtenaw ISD.
- Region 8: Macomb ISD, Oakland Schools, Wayne RESA.
Members are also divided into seven groups by pupil membership: Group I, all intermediate districts; Group II, 0 to 1,400; Group III, 1,401 to 2,500; Group IV, 2,501 to 5,000; Group V, 5,001 to 11,000; Group VI, 11,001 to 40,000; Group VII, more than 40,000.

**Board composition and limitations**
The Board of Directors is comprised of 23 members, including three at-large directors. Sixteen directors are elected from the eight regions, two from each region, and one director per group is elected from Groups V, VI and VII; the MASB President nominates a member as an at-large director, subject to Board approval. Article VIII, Section 6 permits only one director from any one local or intermediate school district board, and Article VIII, Section 8 declares an unopposed nomination elected without an election for that group or region.

**Seats up and unopposed outcomes**
Eight seats were up, one seat each and three-year terms unless otherwise noted: Regions 1 (two-year term), 3, 4, 6 (open seat, one-year term), 7, 8 (open seat), and Groups V and VI. Five drew no opposition and no ballots were sent: Region 1, Kristen Cambensy, Marquette Area Public Schools; Region 3, Rick Dernberger, Zeeland Public Schools and Ottawa Area Intermediate School District; Region 4, John Tramontana, DeWitt Public Schools; Group V, Stephen Hyer, Clarkston Community Schools; Group VI, Marc Siegler, Walled Lake Consolidated Schools. Voting in Regions 6, 7 and 8 took place via online ballot.

**Voting procedures and deadlines**
Each district received ONE ballot, emailed to the superintendent secretary on record with MASB on Friday, Jan. 24, 2025; ballots cannot be forwarded. Completed ballots had to be cast and confirmed by the superintendent secretary by 1 p.m. on Wednesday, March 5, 2025. Unofficial results were to be available on the voicemail recording at 517.327.5915 generally after 2 p.m. on the deadline date and emailed that afternoon. Official results were to be approved at the March 14, 2025, Board of Directors' meeting, which newly elected directors should plan to attend. Questions went to Cheryl Huffman at 517.327.5915 or chuffman@masb.org.

**Campaign rules**
No local district or ISD funds can be used to campaign, and a candidate may not use a school district email account to message other school board members, so a personal account must be used. Questions on what constitutes an expenditure of school district funds go to MASB Legal Counsel Brad Banasik, J.D., at bbanasik@masb.org or 517.327.5929. Each candidate receives an electronic file of physical and email addresses for the voting group or region under a revokable license limited to contacting school board members about the election.

**Item.** Attendance Area Review Committee (AARC) proposal presentation to the Troy School District Board of Education, January 21, 2025. It revises the January 14 deck by replacing Options A through E with Option C and three Option C variants developed after the 1/14/25 Board workshop.

**Background.** Prior AARC groups convened in 2015 and 2018, and a 62-member Facilities Review Committee ran a 6-month process in 2021/22 producing recommendations for the 2022 bond proposal. Middle school enrollment ranges from 590 to 870 per building. Plante Moran was hired as demographers. The 2024 AARC had 25 members (15 administrators, 10 community members) and met October 14, October 28, November 11, November 25 and December 9; cabinet discussions have been weekly since August 2024.

**Optimal size model.** Learning Community size of 125 students; average class size 25; full-time teachers teach 5 sections (5x25 = 125); two learning communities per grade level (250 in grade 6); grades 6-8 totaling 750 students, flexing up to 900. The new Smith Middle School was built for an optimal enrollment of 750, and all four middle schools rank in Metro Parent's Top 6 in Michigan.

**Goals.** Goal 1 - right-size middle schools with equal student ratios. Goal 2 - resolve double splits. Goal 3 - no impact on high schools.

**Baseline enrollment.**

| Middle school | Existing boundary (Dec 2024) | Maintain existing boundary (2027) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Baker (Blue) | 631 | 556 |
| Boulan (Orange) | 847 | 721 |
| Larson (Green) | 863 | 713 |
| Smith (Yellow) | 599 | 536 |

Four middle schools total 2,940 pupils (2024) and a projected 2,526 pupils (2027).

**Options presented.**

| Option | Baker | Boulan Park | Larson | Smith | Schools affected | Students moved | Goals met |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Option C | 616 | 603 | 625 | 682 | 5 | ~630 | 3 |
| Option C - ONLY TU | 517 | 793 | 625 | 591 | 3 | ~250 | 2 |
| Option C - ONLY SA | 616 | 603 | 750 | 557 | 3 | ~380 | 2 |
| Option C - TU to Larson | 616 | 603 | 830 | 477 | 6 | ~380 | 2 |
| No Change | 517 | 793 | 750 | 466 | 0 | n/a | 1 |

**Driver populations.** Troy Union Elementary is projected at 205 students for Fall 2027: 100 assigned to Smith, 105 assigned to Larson, with 20 open-enrolled from Smith to Larson, yielding actual counts of 80 to Smith and 125 to Larson. Somerset Apartments is projected at 319 elementary students for Fall 2027, all of whom attend Boulan Park Middle School under current policy.

**Impacts.** Each option notes potential special education staffing effects, continued building-by-building staffing for special education and English learners, and transportation in which routes and bus numbers may shift while keeping driver numbers consistent and the longest route at 30 minutes or less.

**Timeline and next steps.** 2025/2026 prepare for adjustments; 2026/2027 changes implemented. Students in grades 5-8 (classes of 2032, 2031, 2030, 2029) are not impacted and may continue in their Fall 2025 building; current 5th and 6th graders slotted for a new school may move in 2025/2026. Community meetings at the four middle schools in February/March, a community survey in March/April, and Board consideration and decision in April/May.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Document and setting.** Attendance Area Review Committee (AARC) Proposal presentation, Troy School District, delivered to the Board of Education on January 21, 2025. It is a revision of the AARC deck given at the January 14, 2025 Board workshop: the earlier Options A through E are removed and replaced with Option C plus three Option C variants built in response to Board and committee questions.

**Why the review.** Historic district practice is to review enrollment patterns and challenges every 5-10 years. Previous AARC groups convened in 2015 and 2018, and a 62-member Facilities Review Committee ran a 6-month process in 2021/22 to create recommendations for the 2022 bond proposal with staff, student, cabinet and Board of Education feedback. Challenges include enrollment 'splits' as students transition from elementary to middle school or middle to high school, a double split at Troy Union, single splits at Smith, Baker, Wattles and Hamilton, and current ratios at each middle school, where enrollment ranges from 590 to 870 per building. Additional factors listed are enrollment projections, birth rate and schools of choice, the new Smith Middle School built for an optimal enrollment of 750, and Metro Parent rankings placing all four middle schools in the Top 6 in Michigan.

**Optimal middle school size.** Ideal parameters are a Learning Community size of 125 students, an average class size of 25 students, full-time teachers teaching 5 sections (5 x 25 = 125), two Learning Communities per grade level (250 in grade 6), and grades 6-8 totaling 750 students. Learning Communities can flex up to 900 students as class size increases above an average of 25, and to fewer than 750 students as class size dips below 25, which increases costs. Cited benefits include more full-time elective staff and 3 lunch periods aligned with grade levels.

A smaller school risks more partial staff, impact on school culture, limited course availability (example: only 2 sections of art offered), increased costs from lower class sizes, staff split across two content areas, and too few students for extracurriculars such as jazz band, theatre and yearbook. A larger school may require staffing 'overages' (example: more than a 1.0 orchestra teacher), teachers giving up prep periods, congestion in classrooms, hallways and cafeteria, saturated club and athletic opportunities, and limited ability to support new or move-in families.

**Process to date.** The district hired Plante Moran as demographers for yearly and future enrollment projections. The AARC group was formed in 2024 with 25 members representing each elementary and middle school - 15 administrators and 10 community members - drawn from applications requested in September. The 3-month process met on October 14, October 28, November 11, November 25 and December 9, and cabinet discussions have occurred weekly since August 2024. Criteria and data used included enrollment, grade cohorts and boundaries, birth rates, resident/non-resident/employee feeder paths, current maps, demographic data (ethnicity, English learners, students with disabilities, economics, content area performance), transportation implications, historical cohort data, and previous AARC information. Historical enrollment data slides are labeled January 2024. TSD directed the committee to focus on a four middle school future; committee feedback gave the district pause regarding community priorities and values such as programmatic experience, location and community schools, enrollment size, and duration of bus ride.

**Surrounding districts.** Rochester Community School District, Utica Community Schools, Walled Lake Consolidated Schools, Huron Valley Schools, West Bloomfield School District and Chippewa Valley Schools are described as considering or moving through the same process.

**Goals.** Goal 1: right-size middle schools, equal student ratios. Goal 2: resolve double splits. Goal 3: no impact on high schools.

**Current pathways.** Troy Union to Smith/Larson to Athens/Troy; Wass, Hill and Costello to Larson to Athens; Barnard to Baker to Athens; Morse and Wattles to Baker to Athens/Troy; Martell and Leonard to Smith to Troy; Hamilton to Smith/Boulan to Troy; Schroeder and Bemis to Boulan to Troy. The double split is Troy Union Elementary students splitting between Smith and Larson middle schools, with Smith students splitting again between Athens and Troy High. The elementary single split is Wattles and Morse students attending Baker MS splitting between Troy HS and Athens HS. The middle school single split is Hamilton students splitting between Smith and Boulan Park MS, with both feeding Troy HS.

**Current and future student counts.** All prior options presented assumed Somerset Apartment students would follow the feeder pattern. Four middle schools hold 2,940 pupils (2024) and a projected 2,526 pupils (2027). Existing Boundary (December 2024): Baker (Blue) 631 students, Boulan (Orange) 847 students, Larson (Green) 863 students, Smith (Yellow) 599 students. Maintain Existing Boundary (2027): Baker (Blue) 556, Boulan (Orange) 721, Larson (Green) 713, Smith (Yellow) 536.

**Fall 2027 projected middle school feeder enrollment (2,526 students).** Hamilton 226, Schroeder 216, Bemis 237, Martell 189, Leonard 212, Wattles 205, Morse 204, Troy Union 205, Costello 219, Wass 219, Hill 187, Barnard 207. All options are based on the Fall 2027 projected enrollment.

**Troy Union Elementary detail.** Fall 2027 projection of 205 students. Middle school students from Troy Union: 205. Troy Union assigned to Smith: 100. Troy Union assigned to Larson: 105. Troy Union open enrolled from Smith to Larson: 20. Actual students Troy Union to Smith: 80. Actual students Troy Union to Larson: 125.

**Somerset Apartments detail.** Fall 2027 elementary projection of 319 students, distributed as Hamilton 0, Schroeder 60, Bemis 69, Martell 39, Leonard 52, Wattles 52, Morse 47, Troy Union 0, Costello 0, Wass 0, Hill 0, Barnard 0. All Somerset Apartments students go to Boulan Park Middle School.

**Option C.** Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 625, Smith 682. Updated after the AARC concluded, based on questions asked by the group. All Troy Union students go to Smith. All students living in community housing follow their currently assigned elementary school to that elementary school's assigned middle school. Somerset Apartments' 319 students go to Boulan Park from 6 elementary schools. Number of schools affected: 5. Approximate students moved: 630. Number of goals met: 3. Pros: right sizes middle schools, resolves double splits, meets all three goals, keeps cohorts of students together. Cons: unresolved single splits, Hamilton splits from elementary to middle school, and Wattles, Smith and Baker have a split from middle to high school. Special education impact notes potential staffing increases at Smith, an opportunity for students with IEPs receiving services only or a resource room program to remain in a cohort with peers, potential for students placed in categorical programs to be displaced from peers if the placement is not at Smith, and continued staffing based on building need. English learner staffing continues based on need. Transportation routes and bus numbers may shift, with a goal of consistent routes and driver numbers and a longest route of 30 minutes or less.

**Option C - ONLY TU.** Baker 517, Boulan Park 793, Larson 625, Smith 591. Updated after the BOE Workshop on 1/14/25. All Troy Union students go to Smith; all students living in community housing go to Boulan Park Middle School (current policy); Somerset Apartments' 319 students go to Boulan Park from 6 elementary schools. Schools affected: 3. Approximate students moved: 250. Goals met: 2. Pro: resolves double splits. Cons: unresolved single splits, Hamilton splits from elementary to middle school, and Wattles, Smith and Baker have a middle-to-high school split. Special education and English learner staffing continue based on building need; transportation goals match Option C, with a longest route of 30 minutes or less.

**Option C - ONLY SA.** Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 750, Smith 557. Updated after the BOE Workshop on 1/14/25. Troy Union has no changes; all students living in community housing follow their currently assigned elementary school to that school's assigned middle school; Somerset Apartments' 319 students currently go to Boulan Park from 6 elementary schools. Schools affected: 3. Approximate students moved: 380. Goals met: 2. Pro: keeps cohorts of students together. Cons: does not resolve the Troy Union double split, unresolved single splits, Hamilton splits from elementary to middle school, and Wattles, Smith and Baker have a middle-to-high school split.

**Option C - TU to Larson.** Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 830, Smith 477. Updated after the BOE Workshop on 1/14/25. Troy Union all to Larson; all students living in community housing follow their currently assigned elementary school to that school's assigned middle school; Somerset Apartments' 319 students go to Boulan Park from 6 elementary schools. Schools affected: 6. Approximate students moved: 380. Goals met: 2. Pros: resolves double splits, keeps cohorts of students together. Cons: unresolved single splits, Hamilton splits from elementary to middle school, and Wattles, Smith and Baker have a middle-to-high school split.

**No Change.** All Somerset Apartment students go to Boulan Park. Four middle schools with 2,940 pupils (December 2024) and 2,526 pupils (2027). Existing Boundary (2024): Baker (Blue) 631, Boulan (Orange) 847, Larson (Green) 863, Smith (Yellow) 599. Maintain Existing Boundary/Policy (2027): Baker (Blue) 517, Boulan (Orange) 793, Larson (Green) 750, Smith (Yellow) 466. Schools affected: 0. Goals met: 1. Pros: no students affected, community support. Cons: does not right size middle schools, continues the disparity, maintains the double splits.

**Timeline and assumptions.** 2025/2026 - prepare for adjustments; 2026/2027 - changes implemented. Students will continue to have access to advanced programming. TSD will ensure families with multiple middle school students enrolled at the same time have the option to keep siblings at the same middle school. Middle school legacy: students currently enrolled in 5th, 6th, 7th or 8th grade (classes of 2032, 2031, 2030 and 2029) will not be impacted and may continue in the building they are in the Fall of 2025. Option to move: a current 5th or 6th grader slotted to attend a new school may do so in the 2025/2026 school year, ahead of the proposed changes. Curriculum is consistent across all four middle schools and athletics are uniform.

**Phases and next steps.** Phase 1 Discovery - committee formed, research and planning, potential recommendations developed. Phase 2 Recommendation (January) - the committee provides the Board with options and the Board determines whether to move forward. Phase 3 Feedback (February - April) - four listening sessions, one at each middle school, plus a community survey. Phase 4 Determination (April/May) - TSD provides the Board a summary of feedback and the Board determines any future changes. Next steps: February/March community meetings at the 4 middle schools; March/April community survey; April/May Board of Education consideration and decision.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Document and setting.** Attendance Area Review Committee (AARC) Proposal presentation for the Troy School District, delivered to the Board of Education on January 14, 2025. It presents the committee's full option set - Options A, B, C, D and E plus a No Change scenario - for redrawing middle school attendance boundaries across the district's four middle schools: Baker, Boulan Park, Larson and Smith.

**Why the review.** Historic district practice is to review enrollment patterns and challenges every 5-10 years. Previous AARC groups met in 2015 and 2018. A 62-member Facilities Review Committee ran a 6-month process in 2021/22 to create recommendations for the 2022 bond proposal, with staff, student, cabinet and Board of Education feedback. District and community challenges include enrollment 'splits' as students transition from elementary to middle school or middle to high school, a double split at Troy Union, single splits at Smith, Baker, Wattles and Hamilton, world class programmatic experience, and current ratios at each middle school, where enrollment ranges from 590 to 870 per building. Additional factors are enrollment projections, birth rate and schools of choice, the new Smith Middle School built for an optimal enrollment of 750, and Metro Parent rankings placing all four middle schools in the Top 6 in Michigan.

**Optimal middle school size.** Ideal parameters are a Learning Community size of 125 students, average class size of 25 students, full-time teachers teaching 5 sections (5 x 25 = 125), two Learning Communities per grade level (250 in grade 6), and grades 6-8 totaling 750 students. Learning Communities can flex up to 900 students as class size increases above an average of 25, or to fewer than 750 students as class size dips below an average of 25, which increases costs. Benefits of optimal enrollment include elective staffing trending toward more full-time staff in the building and grade-level enrollment allowing 3 lunch periods aligned with grade levels.

A smaller school brings more partial staff, impact on school culture, limited availability of when courses are offered (example: only 2 sections of art offered), increased costs from lower class sizes, staff with split areas of focus across two content areas, and too few students for extracurricular courses such as jazz band, theatre and yearbook. A larger school may require staffing 'overages' (example: needing more than a 1.0 orchestra teacher), teachers giving up prep periods to teach overages, physical space congestion in classrooms, hallways and the cafeteria, saturated club and athletic opportunities, and limited ability to support new or move-in families due to high enrollment.

**Process to date.** The district hired Plante Moran as demographers for yearly and future enrollment projections. The AARC group was formed in 2024 with 25 members representing each elementary and middle school - 15 administrators and 10 community members - with applications requested in September from administrators, staff, families and cabinet. The 3-month process met on October 14, October 28, November 11, November 25 and December 9, and cabinet discussions have been held weekly since August 2024. Criteria and data utilized included enrollment, grade cohorts and boundaries, birth rates, resident/non-resident/employee feeder paths and patterns, current maps, demographic data covering ethnicity, English learners, students with disabilities, economics and content area performance, transportation implications, historical cohort data over time, and previous AARC information. Historical enrollment data slides carry a January 2024 label.

**Committee work.** TSD directed the committee to focus on a four middle school future and on how best to achieve a balanced distribution of enrollment. Committee feedback and further evaluation of data gave the district pause about how to better understand and uphold community priorities and values, with examples including programmatic experience, location and community schools, enrollment size in school, and duration of bus ride.

**Surrounding districts.** Rochester Community School District, Utica Community Schools, Walled Lake Consolidated Schools, Huron Valley Schools, West Bloomfield School District and Chippewa Valley Schools are noted as considering or moving through the same process.

**Goals.** Goal 1: right-size middle schools, equal student ratios. Goal 2: resolve double splits. Goal 3: no impact on high schools.

**Current pathways.** Troy Union to Smith/Larson to Athens/Troy; Wass, Hill and Costello to Larson to Athens; Barnard to Baker to Athens; Morse and Wattles to Baker to Athens/Troy; Martell and Leonard to Smith to Troy; Hamilton to Smith/Boulan to Troy; Schroeder and Bemis to Boulan to Troy. The double split is Troy Union Elementary students splitting between Smith and Larson middle schools, with the Smith students splitting again between Athens and Troy High. The elementary single split is Wattles and Morse Elementary students attending Baker MS being split between Troy HS and Athens HS. The middle school single split is Hamilton Elementary students splitting between Smith and Boulan Park MS, with both then attending Troy HS.

**Current and future student counts.** The four middle schools hold 2,940 pupils (2024) and a projected 2,526 pupils (2027). Existing Boundary (December 2024): Baker (Blue) 631 students, Boulan (Orange) 847 students, Larson (Green) 863 students, Smith (Yellow) 599 students. Maintain Existing Boundary (2027): Baker (Blue) 556, Boulan (Orange) 721, Larson (Green) 713, Smith (Yellow) 536.

**Fall 2027 projected middle school enrollment (2,526 students).** Hamilton 226, Schroeder 216, Bemis 237, Martell 189, Leonard 212, Wattles 205, Morse 204, Troy Union 205, Costello 219, Wass 219, Hill 187, Barnard 207. All options are based on the Fall 2027 projected enrollment.

**Option A.** Baker 631, Boulan Park 657, Larson 611, Smith 627. A portion of Morse and Wattles east of Rochester Rd. could split at the high school level. All of Hamilton goes to Smith, all of Morse goes to Boulan Park, all of Costello goes to Baker, and all of Troy Union goes to Larson. Number of schools affected: 9. Number of goals met: 3. Pros: right sizes middle schools, resolves a double split at Troy Union, middle school boundaries are geographically close to their middle school location, resolves all elementary-to-middle school splits, meets all three goals. Cons: Morse and Wattles maintain a middle-to-high school split, it affects the highest number of schools and students, it has two middle-to-high school splits at Baker and Boulan Park, and it impacts 4 elementary schools.

**Option B.** Baker 563, Boulan Park 739, Larson 611, Smith 613. Hamilton split, current, total 226: 150 to Boulan Park (2/3) and 76 to Smith (1/3). Morse split, new, total 204: 136 to Boulan Park (2/3) and 68 to Baker (1/3). Wattles split, current, total 205: 136 to Smith (2/3) and 69 to Baker (1/3). All of Costello goes to Baker, all of Troy Union goes to Larson, and all of Wattles goes to Smith. Number of schools affected: 8. Number of goals met: 2. Pros: partially right sizes middle schools, resolves a double split at Troy Union, resolves all middle-to-high school splits, meets most of the goals, and creates two distinct feeders to Athens and Troy High with the split happening after elementary. Cons: Morse, Wattles and Hamilton have an elementary-to-middle school split, several schools and students are affected, and a lot of disruption at the elementary level.

**Option C.** Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 625, Smith 682. Updated after the AARC concluded, based on questions asked by the group. Hamilton split, total 226, current practice: 150 to Boulan Park (2/3) and 76 to Smith (1/3). All Troy Union students go to Smith. All students living in community housing follow their currently assigned elementary school to that elementary school's assigned middle school. Number of schools affected: 5. Number of goals met: 3. Pros: right sizes middle schools, resolves double splits, meets all three goals, keeps cohorts of students together. Cons: unresolved single splits, Hamilton splits from elementary to middle school, and Wattles, Smith and Baker have a middle-to-high school split.

**Option D.** Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 611, Smith 696. Hamilton split, current, total 226: 150 to Boulan Park (2/3) and 76 to Smith (1/3). All of Troy Union goes to Larson and all of Costello goes to Smith. Number of schools affected: 4. Number of goals met: 3. Pros: right sizes middle schools, resolves a double split at Troy Union, impacts fewer schools. Cons: Hamilton splits from elementary to middle school; Costello, Wattles and Morse split from middle to high school.

**Option E.** Baker 563, Boulan Park 589, Larson 611, Smith 763. Wattles split, current, total 205: 136 to Smith (2/3) and 69 to Baker (1/3). Morse split, total 204: 136 to Boulan Park (2/3) and 68 to Baker (1/3). All of Troy Union goes to Larson and all of Costello goes to Baker. Number of schools affected: 9. Number of goals met: 3. Pros: partially right sizes middle schools, resolves a double split at Troy Union, resolves all middle-to-high school splits, meets all three goals, and creates two distinct feeder patterns to Athens and Troy High with the split happening after elementary. Cons: Morse and Wattles have an elementary-to-middle school split, several schools and students are affected, and it impacts 9 buildings.

**No Change.** Current middle school boundary with four middle schools, 2,940 pupils (December 2024) and 2,526 pupils (2027). Existing Boundary (2024): Baker (Blue) 631, Boulan (Orange) 847, Larson (Green) 863, Smith (Yellow) 599. Maintain Existing Boundary (2027): Baker (Blue) 556, Boulan (Orange) 721, Larson (Green) 713, Smith (Yellow) 536. Number of schools affected: 0. Number of goals met: 1. Pros: no students affected, community support. Cons: does not right size middle schools, continues the disparity, maintains the double splits.

**Timeline and assumptions.** 2025/2026 - prepare for adjustments; 2026/2027 - changes implemented. Advanced programming: students will continue to have access. Siblings: TSD will ensure families with multiple middle school students enrolled at the same time have the option to keep siblings at the same middle school. Middle school legacy: students currently enrolled in 5th, 6th, 7th or 8th grade (classes of 2032, 2031, 2030 and 2029) will not be impacted and will have the option to continue in the building they are in the Fall of 2025. Option to move: a current 5th or 6th grader slotted to attend a new school may do so in the 2025/2026 school year, ahead of the proposed changes. Curriculum: the curriculum offered at all four middle schools is consistent across the district, and athletics are uniform.

**Phases and next steps.** Phase 1 Discovery - the committee was formed and developed potential recommendations. Phase 2 Recommendation (January) - the committee provides the Board of Education with options and the Board determines whether to move forward. Phase 3 Feedback (February - April) - four listening sessions, one at each middle school, plus a community survey. Phase 4 Determination (April/May) - TSD provides the Board a summary of feedback and the Board determines any future changes. Next steps: February/March community meetings at the 4 middle schools; March/April community survey; April/May Board of Education consideration and decision.
