https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education regular meeting held November 19, 2024, at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, called to order by President Schmidt at 7:00 p.m. with approximately 140 people in the audience. The Board recognized Hamilton Elementary School as a 2024 National Blue Ribbon School and honored the district Communications Department for 15 Michigan School Public Relations Association awards. The most consequential business was acceptance of the district's audited 2024 financial statements from Plante Moran, which carried an unmodified opinion with no findings or questioned costs, followed by a series of contract awards including $1,239,877.00 to Heritage and Company, Inc. for landscape work at the new Smith Middle School.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Meeting**
Troy Board of Education regular meeting, November 19, 2024, Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Present in addition to Mr. Schmidt: Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, and Wilson. Dr. Philippart was absent. Also present: Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Pagel, Malutan, and Trudel. Approximately 140 members of the audience attended. The meeting adjourned at 9:43 p.m. Minutes submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary.

**Recognition / Mission Moment**
Hamilton Elementary School was recognized for its designation as a National Blue Ribbon School, honored at a ceremony in Washington, D.C. on November 7th and 8th by U.S. Secretary of Education Miguel Cardona. Only 356 schools nationwide were chosen for the honor in 2024.

The Communications Department was recognized for receiving 15 Michigan School and Public Relations Association (MSPRA) awards, the most the team has ever received: three awards of excellence and 12 awards of merit. Staff named: Melissa Verduyn, Thomas Butcher, Adam Burns, Linda Alfonso, Patrice Rowbal, and Alison Hendry. Awards were received in October, with recognition to follow at the MSPRA conference in March.

**Consent Agenda**
Moved by Mr. Hauff, supported by Mr. Haupt, to approve items A, B, C, and D: minutes of the October 1, 2024 Board Workshop; minutes of the October 15, 2024 Board Meeting; Treasurer's Report for September 2024; and rescheduling the January 7, 2025 Board Workshop to January 14, 2025. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

**Curriculum**
Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent of Elementary Instruction, and Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent of Secondary Instruction, presented a student achievement data review covering summative and formative assessments and a county comparison of M-Step, PSAT, and SAT scores.

**Business**
Michael Walsh, Audit Partner from Plante Moran, presented highlights of the 2023-2024 fiscal year audit; a draft report had been presented in detail at the November 12, 2024 Board Workshop. Results included an unmodified opinion with no findings or questioned costs in the 2024 financial statement and the 2024 federal program audit, plus the ASBO Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting for 2023. Finance Director Aurel Malutan and Assistant Superintendent Dan Trudel were recognized.

| Item | Vendor | Amount | Fund |
|---|---|---|---|
| Three UNOX ovens (Hill, Leonard, Troy Union) | Stafford Smith | $118,203.00 | Food Service Fund |
| New Smith Middle School landscape work | Heritage and Company, Inc. | $1,239,877.00 | Capital Projects Fund |
| 2025 roof replacement | (awarded as listed) | — | Capital Projects Fund |
| New servers and back-up software | People Driven Technology | $443,866.88 | Capital Projects Fund and General Fund |
| Two electric school buses | Hoekstra Transportation | $815,082.00 | 74b Clean Bus Energy Grant |

All business motions, including acceptance of the audited 2024 financial statements, passed Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

**Public Communication and Other**
No one spoke on agenda items. Thirteen community members addressed the Board during non-agenda public communication; no action was taken. Student representatives Diana D'Aloisio (Athens High School), Kristian Vitanovich (Troy College and Career High School), Nurayda Albeez (International Academy-East), and Adam McManus (Troy High School) reported on school events. Board members congratulated Audra Melton, Ayesha Potts, and Stephanie Zendler on winning the election and thanked Mr. Hauff, Mr. Schmidt, and Dr. Wilson for their years of service. The next Board Workshop was announced for December 3rd at 6:00 p.m. in the Administration Building and the next regular meeting for December 17th at 7:00 p.m. in the Services Building.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Official minutes of the regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, held November 19, 2024, at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, and Wilson were present; Dr. Philippart was absent. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Pagel, Malutan, and Trudel. Approximately 140 members of the audience were in attendance. The minutes were respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, and carry the notation GH/jh.

RECOGNITION / MISSION MOMENT — NATIONAL BLUE RIBBON AWARD, HAMILTON ELEMENTARY SCHOOL. The Board recognized Hamilton Elementary School for its designation as a National Blue-Ribbon School, an award honoring the school as one of the very best schools in the United States. Hamilton was recognized by U.S. Secretary of Education Miguel Cardona at a ceremony in Washington, D.C. on November 7th and 8th. Only 356 schools from around the country were chosen for this honor in 2024. The minutes note that the award affirms the hard work of students, staff, parents, and the Hamilton community, and quote Secretary Cardona's press release statement that "The National Blue Ribbon Schools Award is a testament to the exceptional achievements of students and educators at each of these schools," that the 2024 National Blue Ribbon Schools are "raising the bar for our nation's students, serving as models for effective teaching and intentional collaboration in their schools and communities," and calling on the country to look to these schools for inspiration "as we champion education as the foundation of a brighter future for every child."

RECOGNITION — 2024 MICHIGAN SCHOOL PUBLIC RELATIONS ASSOCIATION (MSPRA) AWARDS. The Board recognized the Troy School District Communications Department and invited team members forward. The Communications team received 15 Michigan School and Public Relations Association (MSPRA) awards, the most the team has ever received. Staff thanked by name were Melissa Verduyn, Thomas Butcher, Adam Burns, Linda Alfonso, Patrice Rowbal, and newest team member Alison Hendry. The department was recognized with three awards of excellence and 12 awards of merit.

Awards of Excellence were received in the Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion category for "Elevating Voices: In Comfortably Uncomfortable Conversations" podcast; the Marketing Materials category for Early College with LTU; and the Special Purpose category for Coffee with the Superintendent.

Awards of Merit were received in the Marketing Materials category for the Career Accelerator Program; Marketing Materials for the College and Career Fair; Marketing Materials for the Summer School Catalog; Newsletter category for TSD News Supplement - Spring 2024 - Summer 2024; Special Purpose category for Board of Education Community Conversation; Special Purpose category for Smith Middle School Orchestra; Video category for "Why Flexible Seating"; Video category for "Danielle Clippard - Outstanding Support Staff 2024"; Video category for "Autism Acceptance: Morse Friendship Cookies"; Video category for "Beyond: Flying Drones with Jack Kelly"; Video category for "Celebrating Manufacturing Day"; and Audio/Podcast category for "Inside TSD with Dr. Rich Machesky - June 2024." The team received the awards in October and will be recognized at the MSPRA conference in March. The minutes record the district's pride in the department's creative talent and its dedication to sharing the stories and successes of the Troy School District and to "world-class excellence."

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS: None. PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (AGENDA ITEMS): None.

GENERAL — CONSENT AGENDA. It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Troy Board of Education approve items A, B, C, and D on the consent agenda: minutes of the October 1, 2024 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the October 15, 2024 Board of Education Meeting; the Treasurer's Report for September 2024; and rescheduling the January 7, 2025 Board Workshop to January 14, 2025. The vote was Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

PERSONNEL: None.

CURRICULUM — STUDENT ACHIEVEMENT DATA REVIEW. Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent of Elementary Instruction, and Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent of Secondary Instruction, shared a report updating the Board on student achievement data. They explained how the data is used to drive the district's systems and processes, discussed summative and formative assessments, and reviewed county comparisons of M-Step, PSAT, and SAT scores.

BUSINESS — 2023/2024 AUDIT REPORT. Mr. Michael Walsh, Audit Partner from Plante Moran, presented to the Board of Education on the audit of the 2023-2024 fiscal year. A draft copy of the District's Audit Report had been presented in detail to the Board at the November 12, 2024 Board of Education Workshop. Mr. Walsh provided highlights and reported an unmodified opinion with no findings or questioned costs in the 2024 financial statement and in the 2024 federal program audit results, and mentioned the ASBO Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting for 2023. Governmental funds, revenue and expenditures were reviewed, along with student population, foundation allowance, and changes in federal funding. The audit partners and Board members recognized the Business Services team, Finance Director Aurel Malutan and Assistant Superintendent Dan Trudel, for their work managing the budget.

2023/2024 AUDIT — ACTION. It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mr. Hauff that the Board of Education accept and approve the Troy School District's audited 2024 financial statements as presented by Plante Moran. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

OVEN REPLACEMENT FOR HILL, LEONARD, AND TROY UNION. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Anne that the purchase of three UNOX ovens be awarded to Stafford Smith in the amount of $118,203.00, approved as an expenditure of the Food Service Fund. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

NEW SMITH MIDDLE SCHOOL — LANDSCAPE CATEGORY. It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Hauff that the bid for landscape work at the new Smith Middle School be awarded to Heritage and Company, Inc. in the amount of $1,239,877.00, approved as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

2025 ROOF REPLACEMENT PROJECT. It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mrs. Alic that the bid for roof replacement be awarded as set out in the resolution and that the amount be approved as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund. The award detail appears in a table that is not captured in the extracted text of these minutes. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

INFRASTRUCTURE UPGRADES. It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Alic that the contract for new servers and back-up software be awarded to People Driven Technology in the amount of $443,866.88, approved as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund and General Fund. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

ELECTRIC BUSSES PURCHASE. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Anne that the bid for two electric school buses be awarded to Hoekstra Transportation in the amount of $815,082.00, approved as an expenditure of the 74b Clean Bus Energy Grant. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (NON-AGENDA ITEMS). Thirteen community members addressed the Board during public communication. No action was taken by the Board.

OTHER: None.

REPORTS FROM HIGH SCHOOL STUDENT REPRESENTATIVES. Diana D'Aloisio, student representative for Athens High School, shared a report on events and activities at her school. Kristian Vitanovich, student representative for Troy College and Career High School, shared a report on his school. Nurayda Albeez, student representative for International Academy-East, shared a report on her school. Adam McManus, student representative for Troy High School, shared a report on his school.

BOARD COMMENTS. Board members shared upcoming events of possible community interest and congratulated Audra Melton, Ayesha Potts, and Stephanie Zendler for winning the election. They shared sentiments and thanked Mr. Hauff, Mr. Schmidt, and Dr. Wilson for their dedication and years of service as Board members to Troy School District students and the community. Mr. Schmidt announced that he would not be in attendance for the December workshop or meeting and shared sentiments about his years of service on the Troy Board of Education. He announced that the next Board Workshop would be held in the Administration Building on December 3rd at 6:00 p.m., and the next regular meeting on December 17th in the Services Building at 7:00 p.m.

ADJOURNMENT. The meeting adjourned at 9:43 p.m.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Presented to the Troy School District Board of Education on December 3, 2024, the Accountability Plan slide deck reports progress against the four "World Class for All" pillars: Green (Early Childhood to Career), Red (Equity and Well-Being), Blue (Deep Learning), and Gold (Building Capacity of Students, Staff, and Families). Each pillar is laid out as objectives, December 2024 celebrations and key results, and challenges and recommendations. Among the reported results, GSRP preschool slots increased from 98 to 160, the Career Accelerator Program grew to 60 students, and more than 290 students from the Class of 2024 earned completer status in a Career and Technical Education course.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Format and purpose**
PowerPoint presentation delivered at the December 3, 2024 Troy School District Board of Education meeting. The framing slide states that the "World Class for All" pillars hold the team accountable to Objectives and Key Results. Each of the four color-coded pillars is presented in the same sequence: objectives, December 2024 celebrations and key results, and challenges and recommendations.

**Green Pillar - Early Childhood to Career**
Objectives: invest in high-quality early childhood education, including advocating for universal preschool for all three- and four-year-olds; expand college and career pathways through high-quality CTE that connects underrepresented students to in-demand careers; and build a consistent K-12 career readiness plan.
Key results: GSRP slots increase from 98 to 160; Portrait of A Learner; K-8 career readiness engagement with Media Specialists and Maker Space; the 99b Computer Science / Computational Thinking Grant; K-12 CS alignment with Oakland Schools and MDE; Early Middle College with LTU; a Business Round Table; Career Accelerator Program increase to 60 students; 8th grade interviews and portfolio integrated with middle school Celebrations of Learning; and Athens named one of two schools in the state to pilot the Ignite Program (Mechatronics). More than 290 students from the class of 2024 earned CTE completer status across eleven listed fields including Mechatronics, Automotive Technician, Computer Programming, Finance, and Woodworking.
Challenges: transition to a 5 Day Model; preparation for universal preschool; the stigma of career readiness; embedding career readiness through building leaders; digital citizenship K-12; growing computer science; and shifting from electives to CTE programs.

**Red Pillar - Equity and Well-Being**
Objectives center on equity and well-being, funding investments for the whole child, an elevated district-wide focus on Alignment, Access, and Agency, and assessing needs for a world class learning environment. Key results: an SEL curriculum pilot and SEL-focused programming K-12; Behavioral Threat Assessment and Suicide Risk Assessment committee work; Belonging Focus Group Sessions and Student Equity Council expansion; the Community Book Read; and all building teams trained in restorative culture as of November 2024. Challenges note over 1600 SEL lessons in Everyday Speech utilized September through November, partnership with Margaret Coggins and the BTA Team, NTAC adoption, and suicide awareness professional learning in Winter 2024.

**Blue Pillar - Deep Learning**
Objectives: MTSS systems of support that empower student voice, improved technology access and training, global best practices (NPDL, The 6 C's, learning partnerships), and upgraded facilities. Slides cover furniture, playgrounds, and student designs and input, noting 36 teachers piloting furniture K-12 alongside student quotations. Curriculum and pedagogy items include full days of professional learning on October 31st and November 1st, implementation of NWEA and Common Lit standardized assessments, pilot work in Geometry, review in Spanish and French, an elementary ELD Newcomer curriculum pilot, and a Grades 11/12 ELA Course Study Team. MTSS work includes partnership with New Solutions K-12 and Solution Tree, a teacher consultant model for Special Education, and an artificial intelligence leadership committee. Challenges: coordinating MTSS across teams, substitute teacher coverage, and systemness.

**Gold Pillar - Building Capacity**
Objectives address educator preparation, pipelines for underrepresented educators, job-embedded professional learning, and co-designed experiences for the OneTroy community. Key results list the Fielding International Partnership, NSK12, Solution Tree, Community Book Read, Learning Nights at all schools, counseling systemness 6-12, website launch feedback sessions, and WEB, LEAP, and the Student Leadership Conference. Challenges include partnership with Celebrate Hope, attracting experienced staff from outside the district, retention strategies, leadership cohorts, and a new teacher learning series.

**Closing**
A "What's Next?" slide quotes that the world's best school systems ensure all stakeholders understand the purpose, priorities, and goals of the system, with leaders clarifying a few very specific non-negotiables while encouraging autonomy and creativity at all levels.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Troy School District Accountability Plan presentation delivered to the Board of Education on December 3, 2024, in PowerPoint form. The opening slides identify the district and school (Troy) and establish the framework: the "World Class for All" Pillars hold the team accountable to Objectives and Key Results. The body of the deck walks through four color-coded pillars in turn, each with an objectives slide, a December 2024 celebrations and key results slide, and a challenges and recommendations slide.

GREEN PILLAR - EARLY CHILDHOOD TO CAREER
Objectives: continue to invest in high-quality early childhood education, including advocating for access to universal preschool for all three- and four-year-olds; expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students by offering high-quality career and technical education, with the plan connecting underrepresented students to in-demand careers in high-growth industries through partnerships with colleges, employers, and stakeholders, enabling work-based learning, credential earning, and college credit opportunities; and build a consistent career readiness plan for students K-12.
December 2024 celebrations and key results: an increase in GSRP slots from 98 to 160; consistent priority on percent Preschool Experience Data; Portrait of A Learner; career readiness engagement opportunities K-8 partnered with Media Specialists and Maker Space; the 99b Computer Science / Computational Thinking Grant; K-12 computer science alignment with Oakland Schools and the Michigan Department of Education; expanded maker-centered learning spaces to the high school; continued prioritization of post-secondary learning partnerships throughout K-12; Early Middle College with LTU; a Business Round Table; a Career Accelerator Program increase to 60 students; 8th grade interviews and portfolio integrated with middle school Celebrations of Learning; Athens named as one of two schools in the state to pilot the Ignite Program (Mechatronics); and a process of reviewing and updating CTE programs to make improvements, build stronger connections with business and industry, and provide students the opportunity to earn credentials.
A dedicated slide records that more than 290 students from the class of 2024 earned completer status in one of the district's CTE courses, listing Education, Radio & Television Broadcasting, Marketing, Finance, Drafting & Design Technology, Cooking and Culinary Arts, Automotive Technician, Computer Programming, Mechatronics, Business, and Woodworking.
December 2024 challenges and recommendations: transition to a 5 Day Model; preparation for universal preschool (expanding access); mindshifting the stigma of career readiness to prioritize relevance to learning in classrooms; supporting all building leaders to embed career readiness initiatives in classrooms and beyond; Portrait of a Learner, leveraging and embracing its connection to the current strategic plan; prioritizing digital citizenship for K-12; growing and developing computer science in the K-12 curriculum; and shifting from electives to CTE programs.

RED PILLAR - EQUITY AND WELL-BEING
Objectives: ensuring a focus on equity and well-being; funding additional investments to support the needs of the whole child; an elevated district-wide focus on Alignment, Access, and Agency; and assessing needs and taking action to meet the demands of a world class learning environment in all school communities.
December 2024 celebrations and key results: an SEL curriculum pilot and SEL-focused programming K-12; Behavioral Threat Assessment (BTA) and Suicide Risk Assessment committee work; elevating student experience through Belonging Focus Group Sessions and Student Equity Council expansion; family and community engagement via the Community Book Read and the Continuing the Conversation Series; and restorative culture and community, with all building teams trained as of November 2024.
Challenges and recommendations: community engagement and partnerships with continued intentional collaboration and connection; encouraging and implementing aligned structures; equity teamwork across buildings; SEL curriculum and SEL support/instruction K-12, noting that over 1600 SEL lessons in Everyday Speech were utilized September through November; continued partnership with Margaret Coggins and the BTA Team, including behavioral threat assessment consistency through NTAC adoption, suicide awareness professional learning in Winter 2024, and consistent expectations across all levels and teams; restorative practices including counseling, team, and department fundamentals training, train-the-trainer work to build capacity, and community involvement and awareness; and Belonging as a North Star, continued through an Inclusive Newsletter, professional learning, and student support.

BLUE PILLAR - DEEP LEARNING
Objectives: create and sustain systems of support at all levels that deepen learning and empower student voice (MTSS), with access to deep learning described as imperative for all children; improve technology access for students and families while providing quality training to leverage technology to deepen learning; continue to pursue the global best practices of all content areas (NPDL, The 6 C's, learning partnerships); and assess the need and take action for upgraded facilities to meet the demands of a world-class learning environment in all school communities.
Separate slides are devoted to Furniture, Playgrounds, and Student Designs and Input for Playgrounds and Furniture. The student input slide records 36 teachers piloting furniture K-12 and quotes students: "We need places to climb and play sports to get our energy out!"; "I like rockers because I can rock on them and sit on the carpet to read. It's easy to concentrate and it's comfy."; "My favorite stuff is something I can move with."; and "We want shade and nice places to relax with our friends in nature."
Curriculum and pedagogy: focused attention on Professional Learning Communities at the secondary level; targeted learning on Universal Design and MTSS at the secondary level; continued learning around learning environments in coordination with bond initiatives; development of an Artificial Intelligence leadership committee; development of a Computer Science leadership team; and continuing to grow digital portfolios for students to document learning over time. A second curriculum slide lists October 31st and November 1st as full days of professional learning - elementary on classroom environments and MTSS in mathematics, secondary on universal design, plus choice sessions - along with implementation of NWEA and Common Lit standardized assessments and ongoing development of the MTSS process, and continued curricular work comprising pilot work in Geometry, a review process in Spanish and French, a pilot of the elementary ELD Newcomer curriculum, and a Grades 11/12 ELA Course Study Team.
Multi-Tiered Systems of Support: partnership with New Solutions K-12 and a plan for implementation of its recommendations. Elementary MTSS work continues to monitor benchmark data, develop capacity in math, and solidify tier-one instruction in all classrooms. Secondary MTSS teams meet regularly to support student needs, consider system data to be utilized, build a continuum of services to include a teacher consultant model for Special Education, and partner with Solution Tree to build instructional leadership capacity.
Challenges and recommendations: coordinating MTSS implementation across teams (principals, teachers, content areas, support staff); continuously supporting all content areas; substitute teacher coverage; systemness and building capacity of all staff; and helping staff see connections across content area and level.

GOLD PILLAR - BUILDING CAPACITY OF STUDENTS, STAFF, AND FAMILIES
Objectives: improving educator preparation, strengthening pipelines for underrepresented educators, and supporting current educators; continuing to provide job-embedded professional learning experiences for all staff; and providing professional learning opportunities for staff, community, and students with the goal of co-designing impactful experiences to better the OneTroy community.
Key results: job-embedded learning for staff through the Fielding International Partnership, NSK12, Solution Tree, the Community Book Read, and Learning Nights at all schools; use of early release days to prioritize conversations with collaborative teacher teams around student learning and emerging professional learning communities; building systemness with counseling 6-12 around program opportunities; engaging stakeholders in feedback sessions on the website launch; and building student capacity through WEB, LEAP, and the Student Leadership Conference.
Challenges and recommendations: continued partnership with Celebrate Hope; continued investigation into attracting experienced staff from outside of the district; retention strategies; building community partnerships; continued collaboration among departments within Sub Cabinet; leadership cohorts; and a new teacher learning series.

CLOSING
The final content slide is titled "What's Next?" and carries the quotation: "The world's best school systems ensure that all stakeholders understand the purpose, priorities, and goals of the system. Leaders clarify a few very specific non-negotiables that must be honored throughout the system and at the same time they encourage autonomy and creativity at all levels to foster ownership and innovation."

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
"Exploring Our Data Story" was presented to the Troy School District Board of Education at its meeting of November 19, 2024. The stated objectives were to review district goals, provide context to enhance understanding of data, and share how data is utilized to drive district systems and processes.

ASSESSMENT FRAMEWORK
A slide titled "Beyond the Cover: Understanding Summative & Formative Assessment" organizes the district's measures: building a strong foundation and early childhood enrollment; district-level summative assessments consisting of M-STEP (Gr 3-7), PSAT 8 / SAT 11, and College Board Advanced Placement; classroom-level formative assessments consisting of Fountas & Pinnell (K-5), Bridges Math (K-5), Common Lit (ELA 6-12), and NWEA - Math (6-Alg 1); and exit data, specifically the TCCHS graduation rate.
Under "Snapshots of Progress," the presentation recognizes the limitations of summative M-STEP and PSAT/SAT data: cohort tracking allows monitoring of student cohort performance over time; comparative insights allow assessment against other districts; and granularity issues mean summative data lacks detailed analysis for specific performance insights.

M-STEP
Chart slides are presented for ELA M-STEP Grades 3-7 with county comparison and FRL rate, for M-STEP Math Grades 3-7 with county comparison and FRL rate, and for Middle School M-STEP Grades 6 and 7 covering English Language Arts and Mathematics. The underlying values for these graphics are not carried in the document text.

PSAT 8 RESULTS
The PSAT 8 Evidence-Based Reading & Writing (EBRW) chart plots Troy School District (TSD), Oakland Schools, and the State across 2018-19, 2021-22, 2022-23, and 2023-24. TSD: 87.1, 81, 85.6, 84.2. Oakland Schools: 70.3, 67, 68.4, 71.4. State: 61.9, 59.7, 59.7, 64.5.
The PSAT 8 Math chart, over the same four periods, shows TSD at 75.1, 67.5, 69, and 64.3; Oakland Schools at 52.5, 44.6, 45.5, and 42.3; and the State at 41.4, 36.2, 36.2, and 32.6. A further slide is labeled "2023-24 PSAT 8" and compares the OS LEA Average with TSD.

SAT 11TH GRADE RESULTS
SAT 11th grade Evidence Based Reading & Writing (EBRW) over 2018-19, 2021-22, 2022-23, and 2023-24: TSD 82.9, 75.3, 76.9, 77.3; Oakland Schools 62.9, 59, 59.3, 59.6; State 55.3, 51.6, 52.2, 51.3.
SAT 11th grade Math over the same periods: TSD 73.6, 61.6, 61.3, 59.5; Oakland Schools 46.7, 39.3, 38.9, 35.7; State 36.3, 30, 29.9, 26.3.
SAT Overall Performance, defined as the percent of 11th grade students who meet or exceed expectations in both Math and EBRW, is charted on an axis spanning 2018-19, 2019-20, 2020-21, 2021-22, 2022-23, and 2023-24 with a 0 to 80 scale. Plotted values are 69.8, 58.8, 59.7, and 57 for TSD; 44.5, 37.3, 37.1, and 34.4 for Oakland Schools; and 33.9, 28.1, 28.2, and 25.1 for the State. TSD exceeds both Oakland Schools and the State on every summative measure shown.

REFLECTIONS AND USES OF SUMMATIVE DATA
Summative data informs the MTSS process, collaboration, and ongoing adjustments, along with a partnership with NSK12 to evaluate supports and structure for students with services in ELD, Special Education, and other areas. Areas of focus are access to Tier 1 core instruction for all; access to content-strong staff, framed as who is teaching the content and intervention; additional time for learning, framed as more time with content-strong staff; and ongoing professional learning, with the October 31 and November 1 Trailguide given as an example.

USING DATA TO INFORM INSTRUCTION
Under MTSS Decision Making, "MTSS Time" covers building data and trends; the principle that MTSS is for all children; bringing students with IEPs into scheduling discussions; reviewing progress monitoring of any student on a plan; working on team dynamics; starting with celebrations; and reviewing all data points. Chart slides display the Fountas & Pinnell Benchmark by grade level and a Math Benchmark by grade.
For NWEA mathematics, the district has established a universal screener for middle school mathematics; middle school math specialists use it to identify which students need further, more diagnostic assessment within the MTSS process; and it allows the district to participate in a third-party study with Illustrative Mathematics. A slide addresses NWEA informing classroom-level decisions.
The Common Lit assessment is described in five functions: assessment as a baseline, establishing a starting point for student performance; identifying needs, recognizing students who require immediate support; data-driven instruction, using results to inform whole-class lessons and small group activities; monitoring growth, measuring student progress over time; and goal setting, engaging students in setting personal learning objectives based on assessment results. A sample classroom report from Common Lit is shown.

NEXT STEPS
"Reading Between the Lines" lists district improvement needs: examples such as screening and diagnostic tools to improve the MTSS process; formation of work groups to build capacity and continued partnership; and shared ownership of the MTSS process.

CELEBRATIONS
Investment in Early Childhood is listed first among celebrations.
International Academy East IB Diploma acquisition is reported by graduation year: 82% in 2019, 90% in 2020, 87% in 2021, 88% in 2022, 72% in 2023, and 81% in 2024.
AP Honor Roll results are given for Troy High School and Athens High School across 2023-24 and 2022-23:
| AP School Metric | Troy HS 2023-24 | Troy HS 2022-23 | Athens HS 2023-24 | Athens HS 2022-23 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| School Overall | Gold | Gold | Gold | Silver |
| College Culture | 75% (381/510) | 69% (364/527) | 70% (253/362) | 61% (232/378) |
| College Credit | 67% (341/510) | 65% (341/527) | 58% (209/362) | 50% (189/378) |
| College Optimization | 30% (153/510) | 30% (158/527) | 23% (83/362) | 27% (102/378) |
Definitions given: College Culture is the percent of students in the graduating class who took an AP exam at any point in high school regardless of score; College Credit is the percent of the graduating class who score 3 or higher on an AP exam in high school; College Optimization is the percent of the graduating class who took 5 or more AP exams in high school, where at least 1 exam was taken in 9th or 10th grade. The document notes that research finds 6 or more APs do not improve college graduation rates beyond the optimal total of 5 such courses in high school, and that the Honor Roll also recognizes schools that encourage students earlier on their AP journey so as not to overload them with AP courses in their junior or senior years. Award thresholds are listed as Platinum, Gold, Silver, and Bronze: College Culture 80%, 65%, 50%, 40%; College Credit 50%, 35%, 30%, 25%; College Optimization 15%, 10%, 5%, 2%.
Enrollment in AP 11 ELA by school year, showing percent of 11th graders enrolled, total 11th graders, and 11 English AP enrollment:

A College Board quotation states that AP courses help students tackle college-level work, develop critical and useful skills for future AP courses, college, and career, and stand out to scholarship organizations and in the college application process.
Seal of Biliteracy recipients by year of graduation: 9 in 2019, 3 in 2021, 3 in 2022, 5 in 2023, 15 in 2024, and 18 marked with an asterisk for 2025.
The TCCHS 4-year graduation rate, expressed as the percent of students who graduated in four years, is charted for 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024 at 32, 48, 47, 64, 77, and 83.
Career and Technical Education completer status: more than 290 students from the Class of 2024 earned completer status in one of the district's CTE courses, spanning Mechatronics, Computer Science, Automotive Technician, Cooking & Related Culinary Arts, Drafting & Design Technology, Finance & Financial Management Services, Education, Television & Radio Broadcasting, Woodworking, Merchandizing, Sales & Marketing Operations, and others.

The presentation ends with "Sharing Troy's Success Stories" and a thank you.

**Meeting and Attendance**
Troy Board of Education regular meeting, October 15, 2024, Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m.; it adjourned at 8:11 p.m. Minutes submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary. Present besides Mr. Schmidt: Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart, and Wilson; Superintendent Machesky; administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Pagel, Foren, and Trudel. Approximately 25 members of the audience attended.

**Recognition and Mission Moment**
Student Spotlight recognized creative achievement in the TSD Creative Guild; Thomas Butcher introduced Athens senior Maisie Justes and described her journey as a filmmaker. The U.S. Department of Education designates October as Learning Disabilities / Dyslexia / ADHD / Down Syndrome Awareness Month; Governor Whitmer declared October Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan.

**Resolutions adopted**

| Resolution | Moved by | Supported by | Vote |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Learning Disabilities Awareness Month, October 2024 | Dr. Wilson | Dr. Philippart | Yes 7 / No 0 |
| Principal Appreciation Month | Mrs. Alic | Mr. Haupt | Yes 7 / No 0 |
| 2025 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists | Dr. Philippart | Mrs. Alic | Yes 7 / No 0 |

The Learning Disabilities resolution notes that 1 in 5 individuals have a learning disability and joins Governor Gretchen Whitmer in commemorating October 2024 as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan.

**NSPRA Awards**
The Communications Department received 11 national awards through the NSPRA National School Communication Awards: 6 Awards of Excellence, 4 Awards of Merit, and 1 Honorable Mention. Excellence: Troy Union At a Glance Infographic; Elevating Voices: In Comfortably Uncomfortable Conversations Podcast; Discover Kitchen Cookoff Video; Positive Behavior Incentive Systems at Morse Elementary School Video; Why You Should Take a Music Class in Middle School Video; The Press Room on our Website. Merit: Inside TSD with Dr. Rich Machesky Podcast; TSD Weekly Newsletter; Magic of Light at Hamilton Video; Why Flexible Seating Video. Honorable Mention: the district newspaper mailed to homes 3 to 4 times per year inside the Troy Times.

**National Merit**
More than one million students nationwide, from some 21,000 high schools, entered the National Merit Scholarship Program; approximately 16,000 seniors are selected as semifinalists. Troy had sixty-nine, whose names Mrs. Anne read aloud. Semifinalist status requires scoring in the top one and one-half percent on the PSAT with comparable SAT scores. Copies of the resolution will be presented at a reception on November 7th.

Moved by Mr. Hauff, supported by Dr. Philippart; items A through E: minutes of the September 3, 2024 Workshop; minutes of the September 17, 2024 Board Meeting; Treasurer's Report - August 2024; Oakland County Special Education Parent Advisory Committee Representatives; and OCSBA Bylaws Amendment. **Meeting identification.** Minutes of a Board Meeting of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, held October 15, 2024 at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois. The meeting of the Troy Board of Education was held at the Troy School District Services Building located at 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present were Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart, and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Pagel, Foren, and Trudel. There were approximately 25 members of the audience. The meeting adjourned at 8:11 p.m. The minutes are respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the typist notation GH/jh.

**Recognition - Student Spotlight.** The Board introduced the evening's Student Spotlight, the segment in which students are recognized for creative achievements they accomplish in the TSD Creative Guild. The Board invited Thomas Butcher to the podium to introduce Athens senior Maisie Justes and to share about her success in her journey as a filmmaker.

**Mission Moment - Learning Disabilities Awareness Month.** National associations for a number of different learning differences have each declared October as an awareness month, including associations for Dyslexia, Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, and Down Syndrome. To honor and magnify those efforts, the U.S. Department of Education has declared October as Learning Disabilities / Dyslexia / Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder / Down Syndrome Awareness Month. In Michigan, Governor Whitmer provided a more encompassing definition and declared October as Learning Disabilities Month, and the Troy Board of Education adopted its own resolution in response.

The resolution, titled Learning Disabilities Awareness Month, October 2024, was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Dr. Philippart. Its recitals state that the term learning disabilities refers to differences in how our brains work, which may affect the acquisition, organization, retention, understanding, or use of verbal or nonverbal information; that learning disabilities range in severity and may impact the acquisition and use of oral language, reading, written language, and mathematics; that 1 in 5 individuals have a learning disability; that learning disabilities may co-exist with other disabilities and conditions and can affect individuals regardless of race, gender, sexual orientation, or other intersecting factors; that disabilities are a natural part of human diversity but individuals with learning disabilities may face discrimination or marginalization; that every person has strengths and learning disabilities should not keep individuals from realizing their full potential; that specialized assessments and interventions involving home, school, community, and workplace settings can significantly enhance quality of life; that appropriate supports and services allow individuals with learning disabilities to achieve their goals and participate fully in society; and that celebrating unique abilities is essential to an inclusive society embracing the potential of all Michigan residents. The resolving clause has the Troy School District Board of Education join Governor Gretchen Whitmer in commemorating October 2024 as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan. Vote: Yes 7, No 0. Resolution adopted.

**Principal Appreciation Month.** Throughout the State of Michigan, October has traditionally been celebrated as Principal Appreciation Month in recognition of the work of building-level educational leaders. The resolution commending elementary and secondary principals was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt. Its recitals state that energetic and inspiring school leadership is essential if teachers, schools, and districts are to ensure that all Troy students are college and career ready; that K-12 school principals play a vital role in student success and act as liaison between the school and the community it serves, ensuring parents and the community are aware of student and school achievements; that Troy School District principals are dedicated, quality educational professionals committed to providing sound leadership and guidance to their staff and students; and that during this month the district joins educators, parents, and students throughout Michigan to raise awareness of the importance of educational leadership and to thank all principals working in Troy. The resolving clause officially recognizes October as Principal Appreciation Month in Troy. Vote: Yes 7, No 0. Resolution adopted.

**2024 National School Public Relations Association (NSPRA) Awards.** The Board recognized the Troy School District Communications Department and invited them forward. The Communications team received 11 national awards this year through the National School Public Relations Association National School Communication Awards: 6 Awards of Excellence, 4 Awards of Merit, and 1 Honorable Mention. The Awards of Excellence were for the Troy Union At a Glance Infographic; Elevating Voices: In Comfortably Uncomfortable Conversations Podcast; the Discover Kitchen Cookoff Video; the Positive Behavior Incentive Systems at Morse Elementary School Video; the Why You Should Take a Music Class in Middle School Video; and The Press Room on the district website. The Awards of Merit were for the Inside TSD with Dr. Rich Machesky Podcast; the TSD Weekly Newsletter; the Magic of Light at Hamilton Video; and the Why Flexible Seating Video. The Award of Honorable Mention was for the Troy School District newspaper that is mailed to homes 3 to 4 times per year inside the Troy Times. The team received the awards over the summer, certificates were displayed on screens around the room, and the Communications Team had already hung the awards down the hallway to the studio. The Board expressed pride in the department's creative talent and its work strengthening the bond between the schools and the community.

**2025 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists.** More than one million students nationwide, from some 21,000 high schools, entered the National Merit Scholarship Program this year; approximately 16,000 of these seniors are selected to be semifinalists. The Board passed a resolution to commend and congratulate the district's sixty-nine National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists. Mrs. Anne read the names of the following students: Aleezay Ahmad, Nurayda Albeez, Gurgia Bains, Jacob Baker, Arin Barman, David Chen, Terence Chen, Saanvi Duruvasan, Akhilan Ganeshkumar, Octavian German, Sriram Yeshaswi Godugula, Adwayan Goswami, David He, Erin Jeong, Lillian Jing, Sophia Kaltsounis, Atiksh Karanwal, Jeffrey Kim, Krrish Kishore Kumar, Arjun Korrakuti, Pranavi Kumar, Anthony Li, Matthew Li, Michael Li, Edison Lin, Pelon Lin, Ethan Liu, Rishi Lokesh, Suraj Makunur, Arjun Manyem, Brenda Mao, Claire Mao, Nishka Mehta, Joseph Morelli, Vandya Nedle, Kevin Oakes, Ritesh Palla, Rhea Pawar, Rahul Perala, Elizabeth Pfauth, Rohith Pramod, Vishnav Ramesh, Rishabh Rao, Sri Sowmya Sanka, Swathi Seshadri, Aaditya Shah, Kalp Shah, Tanay Shah, Shamanth Shastry, Benjamin Sheng, Shabd Shienh, Abhradeep Shil, Sanjay Shyamsundar, Arnav Sinha, Athrv Siriki, Parnavi Sonar, JoAnn Tu, Alexander Ulrich, Aryan Vadlamudi, Ajay Varghese, Sanjeevkumar Vijayakumar, Aishwarya Viswanathan, Ryan Wang, Jessica Wu, Olivia Xu, Elaine Zhang, Yuchen Zhang, Zhedong Zhao, and Angela Zhou. The minutes call this a remarkable number of semifinalists and a tribute to the staff and parents of the Troy School District. The resolution was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Alic; its recitals note that student achievement is honored through the National Merit semifinalist and finalist recognition programs and that National Merit students reach semifinalist status by scoring in the top one and one-half percent on the National Preliminary Scholastic Aptitude Test (PSAT) and earning comparable scores on the Scholastic Aptitude Test (SAT). Vote: Yes 7, No 0. Resolution adopted.

**Additions and Deletions; Public Communication (Agenda Items).** Both recorded as None.

**General - Consent Agenda.** It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Dr. Philippart that the Troy Board of Education take action to approve items A, B, C, D, and E on the consent agenda: minutes of the September 3, 2024 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the September 17, 2024 Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report - August 2024; Oakland County Special Education Parent Advisory Committee Representatives; and OCSBA Bylaws Amendment. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Personnel and Curriculum.** Both sections recorded as None.

**Business - New Smith Middle School Construction Items.** It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Haupt that the bid for the construction of a new Smith Middle School, including architectural, mechanical, electrical and civil/site work, be awarded as attached in the amount of $8,915,483.00, and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund, Sinking Fund, and Food Services Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Business - Cafeteria Tables, Leonard Elementary School.** It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mr. Hauff that the purchase of cafeteria tables be awarded to Great Lakes Furniture Supply, Inc. in the amount of $48,530.00, and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Bond Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

**Public Communication (Non-Agenda Items) and Other.** Both recorded as None.

**Reports from High School Student Representatives.** Diana D'Aloisio, student representative for Athens High School, shared a report on events and activities at her school. Madie Miller, student representative for Troy High School, filled in for Adam McManus, who was not present, and shared a report on events and activities at her school. Nurayda Albeez, student representative for International Academy-East, shared a report on events and activities at her school. Kristian Vitanovich, student representative for Troy College and Career High School, shared a report on events and activities at his school.

**Board Comments and Adjournment.** Board members shared upcoming events of possible community interest. Mr. Schmidt announced that the next Board Workshop would be held in the Administration Building on November 12th at 6:00 p.m. and that the next regular meeting would be held on October 21st in the Services Building at 7:00 p.m. He also reminded everyone to vote at the upcoming election for the district's millage renewal on November 5th. The meeting adjourned at 8:11 p.m.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Exploring Our Data Story, a Troy School District Board of Education workshop presentation dated November 12, 2024, running 47 slides. Stated objectives are to review district goals, provide context to enhance understanding of data, and share how data is utilized to drive district systems and processes, under the framing heading Setting the Scene.

DISTRICT GOALS. Four numbered goal areas are presented: 1 Early Childhood to Career; 2 Equity & Well-Being; 3 Deep Learning; 4 Building Capacity.

ASSESSMENT INVENTORY. Under Beyond the Cover: Understanding Summative & Formative Assessment, the deck lists building a strong foundation and early childhood enrollment; district-level summative measures of M-STEP (grades 3-7), PSAT 8 / SAT 11, and College Board Advanced Placement; classroom-level formative measures of Fountas & Pinnell (K-5), Bridges Math (K-5), Common Lit (ELA 6-12), and NWEA Math (6 to Algebra 1); and exit data in the form of the TCCHS graduation rate. A slide titled Snapshots of Progress recognizes the limitations of summative M-STEP and PSAT/SAT data under three headings: cohort tracking (summative data helps monitor student cohort performance over time), comparative insights (performance can be assessed against other districts), and granularity issues (summative data lacks detailed analysis for specific performance insights).

M-STEP GRADES 3-7. The ELA chart plots school years 2018-19, 2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24 with three series. TSD: 74.3, 68.9, 67, 65.6. OS (Oakland Schools): 53.6, 50.1, 49.7, 49.4. State: 44.3, 40.7, 40.7, 40.5. The mathematics chart, same years and series, plots TSD 70.1, 64.7, 65.7, 67.4; OS 48.9, 42.6, 43.7, 45; State 38.7, 33.3, 34.7, 35.6. Additional slides break out Elementary M-STEP grades 3-5 and Middle School M-STEP grades 6 and 7 for English language arts and mathematics, and two further slides present ELA M-STEP and Math M-STEP county comparisons with free and reduced lunch rate; these slides carry no extracted figures.

M-STEP SCIENCE. The science slide is organized by Elementary, Middle School and High School with series for 2021-22, 2022-23, 2023-24, OS Avg. and State Avg. The figures appearing on the slide are 20, 59.1, 48, 6.25, 63.72, 36.27, 27.27, 64.64 and 45.21, together with comparison averages of 47.8, 47.4 and 43.6 and of 40.4, 38.8 and 37.5.

M-STEP SOCIAL STUDIES. Organized the same way, the social studies slide shows 30.59, 45.13, 42.7, 36.12, 49.94, 33.72, 34.88, 47.59 and 45.95, with comparison values of 37.4, 44.7 and 24.1 and of 18.9, 29.7 and 39.6. A later slide is titled M-STEP Social Studies By School.

PSAT 8. The Evidence-based Reading & Writing chart covers 2018-19, 2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24: TSD 87.1, 81, 85.6, 84.2; Oakland Schools 70.3, 67, 68.4, 71.4; State 61.9, 59.7, 59.7, 64.5. The mathematics chart for the same years: TSD 75.1, 67.5, 69, 64.3; Oakland Schools 52.5, 44.6, 45.5, 42.3; State 41.4, 36.2, 36.2, 32.6. A separate slide compares 2023-24 PSAT 8 results for the OS LEA average against TSD.

SAT. The SAT Overall Performance chart spans 2018-19, 2019-20, 2020-21, 2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24 with an axis running 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80; plotted values are TSD 69.8, 58.8, 59.7 and 57; Oakland Schools 44.5, 37.3, 37.1 and 34.4; State 33.9, 28.1, 28.2 and 25.1. The SAT Total, met and/or exceeded expectations chart for 2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24 shows AHS at 51.1, 53 and 50.3 and THS at 67.5, 70 and 67.2. The SAT EBRW percent met or exceeded chart for the same three years shows AHS 70.1, 76 and 72.7 and THS 81.7, 81.5 and 82.5. The SAT Math percent met or exceeded chart shows AHS 53.5, 54.6 and 53.8 and THS 70.6, 71.8 and 69.2. District-level SAT Evidence Based Reading & Writing across 2018-19, 2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24 shows TSD 82.9, 75.3, 76.9 and 77.3; Oakland Schools 62.9, 59, 59.3 and 59.6; State 55.3, 51.6, 52.2 and 51.3. District-level SAT Math across the same years shows TSD 73.6, 61.6, 61.3 and 59.5; Oakland Schools 46.7, 39.3, 38.9 and 35.7; State 36.3, 30, 29.9 and 26.3. There are additional slides titled SAT Overall Performance By School and a 2023-24 SAT slide charting percent economically disadvantaged against EBRW and math, whose data labels extracted only partially.

REFLECTIONS AND USES OF SUMMATIVE DATA. The deck describes the MTSS process, collaboration and ongoing adjustments, and a partnership with NSK12 to evaluate supports and structure for students with services in ELD, special education and other areas. Areas of focus are access to Tier 1 (core instruction for all), access to content-strong staff (who is teaching the content and intervention), and additional time for learning (more time with content-strong staff). Ongoing professional learning is cited with the example of the October 31 and November 1 Trailguide. Further slides cover Using Data to Inform Instruction, MTSS Decision Making, and MTSS Time, the last listing building data and trends, MTSS is for ALL children, meeting on students with IEPs to discuss scheduling, reviewing progress monitoring of any student on a plan, working on team dynamics, starting with celebrations, and reviewing all data points.

FORMATIVE AND CLASSROOM-LEVEL TOOLS. Slides present the Fountas & Pinnell benchmark by grade level and a math benchmark by grade. The Math Recovery Assessment slide states that the elementary benchmark is utilized for universal screening, that diagnostic assessments about where to go with instruction are given by math specialists, and that next steps are determined for intervention and instruction; a sample class-level report follows. The NWEA update with mathematics states that a universal screener has been established for middle school mathematics, that middle school math specialists use it to identify which students need further, more diagnostic assessment within the MTSS process, and that it allows the district to participate in a third-party study with Illustrative Mathematics; a slide on NWEA informing classroom-level decisions follows. The Common Lit assessment slide organizes uses under assessment as a baseline (establishing a starting point for student performance), identifying needs (recognizing students who require immediate support), data-driven instruction (using assessment results to inform whole-class lessons and small group activities), monitoring growth (measuring student progress over time), and goal setting (engaging students in setting personal learning objectives based on assessment results), followed by a sample classroom report.

NEXT STEPS. Under Reading Between the Lines, district improvement needs are listed as examples of screening and diagnostic work to improve the MTSS process, formation of work groups to build capacity and continued partnership, and shared ownership of the MTSS process.

CELEBRATIONS. Investment in Early Childhood. International Academy East IB Diploma acquisition: 2024 81%, 2023 72%, 2022 88%, 2021 87%, 2020 90%, 2019 82%.

AP Honor Roll, with Athens High School and Troy High School compared for 2022-23 and 2023-24. School overall: Athens Silver then Gold; Troy Gold then Gold. College Culture: Athens 61% (232/378) then 70% (253/362); Troy 69% (364/527) then 75% (381/510). College Credit: Athens 50% (189/378) then 58% (209/362); Troy 65% (341/527) then 67% (341/510). College Optimization: Athens 27% (102/378) then 23% (83/362); Troy 30% (158/527) then 30% (153/510). Definitions given: College Culture is the percent of students in the graduating class who took an AP exam at any point in high school regardless of score; College Credit is the percent scoring 3 or higher on an AP exam in high school; College Optimization is the percent who took 5 or more AP exams where at least one was taken in 9th or 10th grade, with the note that research finds 6 or more APs do not improve college graduation rates beyond the optimal total of 5 such courses. Award thresholds are listed as College Culture Bronze 40%, Silver 50%, Gold 65%, Platinum 80%; College Credit Bronze 25%, Silver 30%, Gold 35%, Platinum 50%; College Optimization Bronze 2%, Silver 5%, Gold 10%, Platinum 15%.

Enrollment in AP 11 ELA by school year, showing 11 English AP enrollment, total 11th graders, and percent of 11th graders enrolled: 2020, 357 of 935, 38%; 2021, 307 of 905, 34%; 2022, 356 of 924, 39%; 2023, 315 of 932, 34%; 2024, 402 of 948, 42%. The slide quotes the College Board on AP courses helping students tackle college-level work, develop critical and useful skills for future AP courses, college and career, and stand out to scholarship organizations and in the college application process.

Seal of Biliteracy by year of graduation: 2019, 9; 2021, 3; 2022, 3; 2023, 5; 2024, 15; 2025, starred 18.

TCCHS 4-year graduation rate, percent of students who graduated in four years, charted for 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024 with values of 32, 48, 47, 64, 77 and 83.

Career and Technical Education completer status: more than 290 students from the Class of 2024 earned completer status in one of the district's CTE courses, with programs listed as Mechatronics, Computer Science, Automotive Technician, Cooking & Related Culinary Arts, Drafting & Design Technology, Finance & Financial Management Services, Education, Television & Radio Broadcasting, Woodworking, Merchandizing, Sales & Marketing Operations, and others. The deck closes with Sharing Troy's Success Stories and a thank-you slide.

Content covers the MTSS process, collaboration, ongoing adjustments, and a partnership with NSK12 to evaluate supports and structure for students with services in ELD, special education and other areas. MTSS Time lists building data and trends, MTSS is for ALL children, meeting on students with IEPs to discuss scheduling, reviewing progress monitoring of any student on a plan, working on team dynamics, starting with celebrations, and reviewing all data points.

FORMATIVE ASSESSMENT PAGES. Fountas & Pinnell Benchmark by grade level; Math Benchmark by grade; Math Recovery Assessment, noting the elementary benchmark is used as a universal screener, that diagnostic assessments about where to go with instruction are given by math specialists, and that next steps are determined for intervention and instruction; a sample class-level report; an NWEA update with mathematics establishing a universal screener for middle school mathematics, used by middle school math specialists to identify which students need further diagnostic assessment through the MTSS process and allowing participation in a third-party study with Illustrative Mathematics; a page on NWEA informing classroom-level decisions; and the Common Lit assessment page framed around assessment as a baseline, identifying needs, data-driven instruction, monitoring growth, and goal setting, followed by a sample classroom report.

Meeting and attendance
Regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education, September 17, 2024, at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Present with him were Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt and Wilson; Dr. Philippart was absent. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Pagel, Jansen, Haezebrouck, Griffor, Trudel and Milanov. Approximately 75 members of the audience attended. Minutes submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary (GH/jh).

Recognitions
- Student representatives to the Board for 2024-2025: Kristian Vitanovich (Troy College and Career High School), Nurayda Albeez (International Academy - East), Diana D'Aloisio (Athens High School) and Adam McManus (Troy High School).
- All-State athletes for spring 2024, recognized by Mr. Jansen: Michelle Baik, Claire Balintfy, Ethan Bieniek, Louis D'Souza, Lauren DeJonckheere, Chase Duncan, Jacob Esser, Dylan Esser, Julian Farrell, Marin Fox, Jason Hamilton, Erin Humphrey, Olivia Jasniewicz, Nainka Jasti, Quinn Kelly, Hannah Lee, Michael Lim, Myles Linden, Nate Linden, Zach Macleish, Vishvaa Ravishankar, Kian Schneeweis, Nika Tananko, Sydney Taylor and Evan Watson.
- Student Spotlight: Thomas Butcher introduced Smith Middle School 7th graders Azra Yildiz and Seowoo Kim, recognized for work in the TSD Creative Guild.
- Michigan Association of School Boards awards presented by Dr. Machesky: Emina Alic and Matt Haupt, Certified Board Member Award and Award of Merit (all Level 1 courses and 45 education credits); Vital Anne, Master Board Member Award (Levels 1, 2 and 3 courses and a minimum of 368 education credits); Karl Schmidt, 12 years of service; Nancy Philippart, 16 years of service; and the TSD Board, Standard of Excellence Award.

Proclamation
On motion by Dr. Wilson, supported by Mrs. Anne, the Board adopted the Oakland Community Health Network proclamation recognizing September 2024 as National Suicide Prevention Month, citing World Suicide Prevention Day on September 10, CDC data that more than 48,000 people die by suicide each year, suicide as the second leading cause of death for ages 10 to 34, fourth for ages 35 to 54 and eighth for ages 55 to 64, and the work of NAMI and the 988 lifeline. Vote: 6 yes, 0 no, Philippart absent. Resolution adopted.

Section 1 update
Chris Bunch, Executive Director of Six Rivers Land Conservancy, updated the Board on the Section 1 Property, Turtle Woods Preserve, reporting that Oakland County Parks revised its new application and that the next Trust Fund Board meeting would be held in October.

Consent agenda
Moved by Mr. Hauff, supported by Mr. Haupt, approving items A through D: minutes of the August 20, 2024 Special Board Meeting, the August 20, 2024 Closed Session, and the August 20, 2024 Board of Education Meeting, plus the Treasurer's Report for July 2024. Vote 6-0, Philippart absent.

Personnel and curriculum
John Pagel, Assistant Superintendent for Employee Services, reported on the hiring process and the factors driving annual teacher hiring, including retirements and resignations, full-year leaves of absence, FTE status and student enrollment; the District hired 31 new teachers this year. The personnel recommendations were approved on motion by Mrs. Alic, supported by Mr. Hauff, 6-0 with Philippart absent. Natalie Haezebrouck, Director of Teaching and Learning, presented on summer professional learning, including curriculum development, the UDL Conference, the administrative kick-off, the TSD Math and Literacy Project for the Pre-K Institute and Troy Institutes K-12, New Teacher Orientation and restorative practices.

Other business
No additions or deletions, no agenda-item public communication and no business items. Three community members addressed the Board during non-agenda public communication, with no action taken. The Board certified Matt Haupt, Gary Hauff, Nicole Wilson and Karl Schmidt as delegates to the MASB 2024 Delegate Assembly on October 24 at 7:00 p.m., with Nancy Philippart as alternate, and approved delegations of no more than four members to the 2025 NSBA Advocacy Institute in Washington, D.C. (February 2-4, 2025) and the 2025 NSBA Annual Conference in Atlanta (April 4-6, 2025). Meeting adjourned at 8:51 p.m.

Minutes of the Troy Board of Education regular board meeting held Tuesday, September 17, 2024 at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan, carried on the October 15, 2024 agenda for approval. President Karl Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt and Wilson were present; Dr. Philippart was absent. Superintendent Machesky attended along with administrators DiPilato, Pagel, Jansen, Haezebrouck, Griffor, Trudel and Milanov. Approximately 75 members of the audience were present. The minutes are signed Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the typing notation GH/jh.

Recognition of student representatives. Mr. Schmidt introduced and welcomed the high school student representatives to the Board for the 2024-2025 school year. Kristian Vitanovich of Troy College and Career High School is a senior, AP student and student leader, a member of the TCC Student Council, a musician and songwriter active in the Music Club, and front man and lead guitarist of the TCC Rock House Band; he learned guitar one year earlier and has taken up cello and piano to advance his songwriting, and plans to attend college with aspirations of becoming a high school teacher. Nurayda Albeez of International Academy - East is a senior pursuing an IB Diploma, a member of the Superintendent Student Advisory Board since her freshman year and its president for the year, president of the IA Student Government, a former State Officer for the Michigan HOSA organization who facilitated statewide leadership conferences, and the recipient of the President's Volunteer Service Gold Award for three consecutive years after completing over 650 hours of community service; she is a former Barnard Bluejay and Baker Bobcat. Diana D'Aloisio of Athens High School is a senior scholar-athlete on the Athens Varsity Girls Golf Team, Vice President of the National Honor Society and a board member of the Athens Spanish Club, who plans to attend an in-state college and pursue a career in the medical field. Adam McManus of Troy High School is a senior serving as Student Government and Leadership Executive Board President, DECA Chapter President, Spanish Club President and a senior board member on the Principal-Student Advisory Board, and represents Troy High School and Oakland County on the Michigan Association of Student Councils and Honor Societies.

All-State athletes, spring 2024. Mr. Jansen and the Board recognized: Michelle Baik, senior, Troy High, girls' tennis; Claire Balintfy, senior, Athens, girls' lacrosse; Ethan Bieniek, freshman, Athens, boys' track; Louis D'Souza, senior, Troy High, boys' track; Lauren DeJonckheere, junior, Athens, girls' soccer; Chase Duncan, junior, Troy High, girls' lacrosse; Jacob Esser, senior, Athens, boys' track; Dylan Esser, senior, Athens, boys' track; Julian Farrell, junior, Athens, boys' track; Marin Fox, senior, Troy High, girls' tennis; Jason Hamilton, junior, Troy High, boys' track; Erin Humphrey, senior, Troy High, girls' lacrosse; Olivia Jasniewicz, sophomore, Troy High, girls' soccer; Nainka Jasti, sophomore, Troy High, girls' tennis; Quinn Kelly, junior, Troy High, boys' track; Hannah Lee, senior, Troy High, girls' tennis; Michael Lim, senior, Troy High, boys' lacrosse; Myles Linden, junior, Athens, boys' track; Nate Linden, sophomore, Athens, boys' track; Zach Macleish, junior, Troy High, boys' lacrosse; Vishvaa Ravishankar, senior, Troy High, boys' track; Kian Schneeweis, junior, Troy High, boys' track; Nika Tananko, senior, Troy High, girls' tennis; Sydney Taylor, senior, Troy High, girls' soccer; and Evan Watson, senior, Athens, boys' track.

Student Spotlight. The Board introduced the year's first Student Spotlight, which recognizes creative achievements in the TSD Creative Guild. Thomas Butcher was invited to the podium to introduce two 7th grade students from Smith Middle School, Azra Yildiz and Seowoo Kim, and to share their work.

National Suicide Prevention Month. Oakland Community Health Network asked school boards throughout Oakland County to partner with it by approving a proclamation designating September as National Suicide Prevention Month at their September board meetings. It was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mrs. Anne to adopt the resolution, whose recitals note that September is known as National Suicide Prevention Month, that World Suicide Prevention Day is observed each year on September 10, that suicidal thoughts can affect anyone regardless of age, gender, race, orientation, income level, religion or background, that according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention each year more than 48,000 people died by suicide, that suicide is the second leading cause of death for people 10 to 34 years of age, the fourth leading cause among people 35 to 54 years of age and the eighth leading cause among people 55 to 64 years of age, that organizations such as the National Alliance on Mental Illness and the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, 988, work to help individuals in crisis, and that OCHN is committed to being a Zero Suicide organization. The resolved clause records that Oakland Community Health Network recognizes September 2024 as National Suicide Prevention Month and calls upon individuals, government agencies, public and private institutions, businesses, faith-based organizations and schools to recommit to increasing awareness and understanding of suicide prevention. Vote: yes 6, no 0, absent Philippart. Resolution adopted.

Michigan Association of School Boards awards. Dr. Machesky presented the Board with honors received during the past year. Trustees Emina Alic and Matt Haupt were recognized for the Certified Board Member Award and Award of Merit, requiring completion of all Level 1 courses and 45 education credits. Vital Anne was recognized for the Master Board Member Award, requiring completion of Levels 1, 2 and 3 courses and a minimum of 368 education credits. President Karl Schmidt was recognized for 12 years of dedicated service and Trustee Nancy Philippart for 16 years of dedicated service. The entire Board was congratulated for earning the Standard of Excellence Award, placing the Troy Board of Education among a handful of Michigan school district governing bodies demonstrating commitment to student achievement and exemplary leadership, with the minutes noting the Troy community is fortunate to have seven Board members committed to life-long learning and positive policy making.

Additions and deletions: none. Public communication on agenda items: none. Business: none.

Section 1 update. Mr. Chris Bunch, Executive Director for Six Rivers Land Conservancy, provided an update on the Section 1 Property, Turtle Woods Preserve. He indicated that Oakland County Parks revised their new application and that the next Trust Fund Board meeting will be held in October.

General consent agenda. Moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Troy Board of Education approve items A, B, C and D on the consent agenda: minutes of the August 20, 2024 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the August 20, 2024 Closed Session Meeting; minutes of the August 20, 2024 Board of Education Meeting; and the Treasurer's Report for July 2024. Vote: yes 6, no 0, absent Philippart.

Personnel, staffing update. John Pagel, Assistant Superintendent for Employee Services, shared a report on the District's hiring process and the factors influencing the number of teachers hired each year, including retirements and resignations, full-year leaves of absence, FTE status and student enrollment. This year the District hired 31 new teachers. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Hauff that the Board approve the personnel recommendations as stated. The new hires listed are Sara Abrin, Lauren Alarie, Hailey Ateek, Kelly Barker, Alyssa Baxendale, Benjamin Borglin, Britiany Bowers, Bradley Ciaramitaro, Isabella Contesti, Brittany Cwiertniewicz, Lillian DeLyon, Jenna Demeter, Riley Frazier, Heidi Haligowski, Lora Herbert, Tanille Hill, Madison Hutchins, Hannah Jackowicz, Steve Johansson, Monika Kitchen, Breanne Massie, Devron Minor, Alice Ochoa, Colleen Osis, Kirsten Paik, Stephanie Pindar, Shauna Pruess, Faith Pustover, Katie Schrepferman, Lauren Walkley and Kevin White. Vote: yes 6, no 0, absent Philippart.

Curriculum, summer learning. Director of Teaching and Learning Natalie Haezebrouck shared a PowerPoint presentation on the District's summer professional learning, covering summer curriculum development, participation at the UDL (Universal Design for Learning) Conference, the administrative kick-off meeting, and the TSD Math and Literacy Project for the Pre-K Institute and Troy Institutes K-12. She reported that New Teacher Orientation week went well and discussed restorative practices for building teams and future ready learning environments. Board members discussed the new calendar and their satisfaction that it is more culturally responsive; Ms. Haezebrouck noted that tool kits will be provided to help teachers respond to students and the diverse cultures in the school community. There was also discussion of the new furniture and the possibility of hosting job-embedded learning opportunities in buildings that have piloted it.

Public communication, non-agenda items. Three community members addressed the Board; no action was taken.

Reports from high school student representatives. Nurayda Albeez (International Academy - East), Kristian Vitanovich (Troy College and Career High School), Diana D'Aloisio (Athens High School) and Adam McManus (Troy High School) each reported on events and activities at their schools.

Other business. Moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Anne that the Troy Board of Education certify Matt Haupt, Gary Hauff, Nicole Wilson and Karl Schmidt as delegates to the MASB 2024 Delegate Assembly on October 24 at 7:00 p.m., with Nancy Philippart as alternate. Vote: yes 6, no 0, absent Philippart. Moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mrs. Alic that the Board approve a delegation of no more than four Board members as representatives at the 2025 NSBA Advocacy Institute in Washington, D.C., February 2-4, 2025. Vote: yes 6, no 0, absent Philippart. Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Board approve a delegation of no more than four Board members as representatives at the 2025 NSBA Annual Conference for Public Education Leaders in Atlanta, Georgia, April 4-6, 2025. Vote: yes 6, no 0, absent Philippart.

Board comments and adjournment. Board members welcomed new staff and welcomed everyone back to the start of the school year. Mr. Schmidt announced Coffee with the Board on Tuesday, October 8th from 6-7 p.m. at Hamilton Elementary School, the next Board Workshop on October 1st at 6:00 p.m. in the Administration Building, and the next regular meeting on October 15th in the Services Building at 7:00 p.m. The community was invited to attend the League of Women Voters' Meet the Candidate Forum on Wednesday, September 25th at 7:00 p.m. in the Troy School District Services Building. The meeting adjourned at 8:51 p.m.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Barton Malow Builders' August 20, 2024 award recommendation letter to Assistant Superintendent of Business Services Dan Trudel covers Bid Package #3B for the New Smith Middle School, with the attached bid tabulation from the July 30, 2024 public bid opening. Sixteen bid categories are recommended for award, from masonry through temperature controls, producing a total contractor direct cost of $31,554,812, a contingency at 8% of $2,524,385, and a total construction cost of $34,079,197. Barton Malow notes the project was advertised on the state website for four and a half weeks and drew 105 bids, and projects the total cost of the school, including previously awarded work and contingency, at fifty-six million dollars ($56 million).
